source: སྦྱོར་ལམ། གསུམ་པ་གདམས་དོན་ལ་སྒོམ་བྱུང་གི་ཐོག་མ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་འཆད་པ་ལ། རང་རྒྱུ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན་རྫོགས་རྗེས་སུ་བྱུངབའི་མངོན་རྟོགས་ཀྱི་རིགས་སུ་གནས་པ། བདེན་པ་མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པ་དང་རྗེས་སུ་མཐུན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་ལམ་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དེ། ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ལས་ཁྱད་ཆོས་ལྔའམ་དྲུག་གི་སྒོ་ནས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱན་ལས། དམིགས་པ་དང་ནི་རྣམ་པ་དང་། །ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར། དམིགས་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པ་དང་། རྒྱུ་བྱེད་ཚུལ་དང་། ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་ཚུལ་དང་། བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་རྣམ་རྟོག་སྤངས་བྱའི་གཙོ་བོ་ལྡན་ཚུལ་དང་། ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེན་པོའི་དབྱེ་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཁྱད་པར་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་ལ་ངོ་བོའི་སྒོ་ནས་དྲོད་སོགས་བཞི་དང་། གནས་སྐབས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་རེ་རེ་ལ་ཆུང་འབྲིང་ཆེན་པོ་གསུམ་གསུམ་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཡོད། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་དང་ཉི་ཁྲི་སོགས་ན་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་རྣམ་དང་སྦྱོར་རྒྱུའི་མདོ་རེ་ཡོད་ལ། འདི་ལ་དྲོད་རྩེ་བཟོད་མཆོག་བཞི་ལ་རེ་རེ་ལས་མདོ་མེད་པས།
translation: Path of Preparation: The third section explains the path of preparation, which is the beginning of the meditative cultivation of the meaning of the instructions. Its definition is: the Mahayana mundane path that abides in the lineage of realization, which arises after having completed the portion of the Mahayana path of liberation that is its own cause, and which accords with the realization of the truths. Such a Mahayana path of preparation is superior to the Hīnayāna path of preparation by way of five or six distinct qualities. As the *Ornament* states, "The object of observation, the aspect, and so forth," it is superior by way of the object of observation, the aspect, the mode of engaging in the cause, the mode of apprehension, the manner of possessing the primary abandonment of the conceptualization of grasping at truth, and the division into small, medium, and great. Regarding this, in terms of its essence, there are the four [levels] such as heat, and in terms of its stages, there are twelve, with three—small, medium, and great—for each. While the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, the *Viṃśatisāhasrikā*, and others contain individual sutras for the objects of observation, aspects, and causes of practice for all paths of preparation, for this [text], there is no sutra for each of the four—heat, peak, patience, and supreme dharma—individually.

heading: **ངོ་བོ་དམིགས་རྣམ་རྒྱུ་གསུམ་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར།**

source: དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ། དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ་ནི། གཟུགས་མེད་ཚོར་བ་མེད། ཅེས་པ་ནས། རྣམ་ཤེས་ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། འདིར་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོས་བསྡུས་པ་དབང་པོ་ལྔ་དོན་ལྔ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ནི། རྡུལ་དུ་མ་འདུས་ཤིང་བསགས་པ་ཡིན་པས་ཆ་དུ་མ་དང་བཅས་ལ། དེ་ཡང་རང་གི་ཆ་ཤས་རྣམས་དང་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་གཅིག་དང་དུ་མ་གང་དུ་གྲུབ་ཅེས་དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་ལ། ཆ་ཤས་རྡུལ་ཕྲན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཕྱོགས་ཆ་དང་བཅས་པས་སྔར་ལྟར་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེདཔའི་ཕྱིར། གཟུགས་འདི་ནི་སྣང་ཡང་བདེན་པར་མེད་པ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རང་གཞན་གྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་བདེ་སྡུག་བཏང་སྙོམས་ཀྱི་ཚོར་བ་འདི་དག་ལའང་གཅིག་ཏུ་དྲལ་གྱི་རིགས་པས་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་དང་འདྲ་བར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཕུང་བོ་དང་སེམས་ཡུལ་ལ་གཡོ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་བྱུང་སེམས་པ་སོགས་འདུ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་བདེན་པར་མེད་ལ། ཚུལ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པའམ་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་དོ། །ཅེས་པ་འདིས་སྡུག་བདེན་གྱི་གཙོ་བོ་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་ལྔ་དྲོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །རྣམ་པ་ནི། གནས་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ན། ཞེས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་བདེན་པར་གནས་པ་སྡེ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ཞེས་པ་འདིས་སྟེ། འདིས་བདེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་དྲོད་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེ་རྣམ་པ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟུན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
translation: The object of observation of heat: The object of observation of heat is indicated by the passage from "Form is not, feeling is not" up to "consciousness." The meaning is this: Here, the five sense faculties, the five objects, and so forth, which are included within the aggregate of form, are composed of many particles and are accumulated, and thus they possess many parts. If one analyzes them with the reasoning that investigates the ultimate—asking whether they are established as one or many by way of their own nature—there is not even the slightest thing established by its own essence. Furthermore, since the particles that are their parts also possess directional parts, if one analyzes them as before, there is not even the slightest thing established as true. Therefore, although this form appears, it does not exist as true. Likewise, if one analyzes these feelings of pleasure, pain, and equanimity, which are included within one's own or others' continua, with the reasoning that dissects them into one and many, they are not established as true. Similarly, the aggregate of perception and the compositional factors, such as the mental factor of intention that moves the mind toward an object, also do not exist as true. Regarding such a mode, there is not even the slightest thing that is consciousness or established as true. By this, it is shown that the five aggregates, which are the primary objects of the truth of suffering, are the object of observation of the wisdom of heat. The aspect is indicated by the passage, "The abode is not even an atom." This is because it states that there is not even an atom of that which is apprehended as truly abiding. By this, it is shown that the wisdom of heat, which does not conceptually construct true existence, is the aspect.

heading: **དྲོད་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The distinction of the cause is indicated by the two lines, "He does not dwell in all phenomena," and so forth. The meaning is this: when these phenomena, such as the five aggregates, are not examined, they are established merely as conventional designations that are pleasant to experience; however, when they are examined and analyzed, one gains a special, definitive understanding that they are like dreams and illusions, devoid of even an atom of inherent existence. At that time, a bodhisattva who dwells in the stages of the path of preparation of the Great Vehicle, such as the heat stage, does not dwell in all phenomena from form up to the omniscience of the Buddha by way of clinging to them as truly existent, nor does he dwell in any of the extremes of permanence or annihilation. Rather, he practices—that is, he engages in—the perfection of wisdom. In this way, by relying on the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects, without grasping at any conventional phenomena such as form through a meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom that is one-pointedly placed in suchness, and as this wisdom increases and expands further and further, one will attain the unsurpassed, great awakening of the mind-stream of the Sugatas.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The object of focus of the peak: The object of focus of the peak is indicated by the single verse beginning with "How." The meaning is this: For example, a wandering ascetic—known as a craftsman or as one who wears a garland—realized through the power of his own wisdom that he could not attain liberation, which is freedom from all the sufferings of cyclic existence, by relying merely on the views of his own tradition that posit the existence of a person (pudgala) or on the meditative absorption of the formless realms that he had attained. Thus, he came before the Teacher, the Buddha, and asked what the path to attaining liberation was. When the Teacher taught the subtle selflessness of the person and phenomena, he developed supreme conviction and trust in it. By relying on the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), which is the path of realizing that there is not even the slightest object of focus of grasping at true existence, he attained nirvana, where the appropriation of the aggregates—which are propelled by karma and defilements—is destroyed, or rather, the continuity of wandering in cyclic existence is severed. Similarly, any bodhisattva who knows that all phenomena, such as form, are devoid of true existence in that way, is sustained by special methods such as great compassion (mahākaruṇā). Consequently, he does not touch the extreme of peace—nirvana without remainder—and instead dwells in the wisdom that realizes the equality of existence and peace as being empty of true existence. This is taught as the object of focus of form and so forth that is free from signs.

In this way, by relying on the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness endowed with the supreme of all aspects, without grasping at any conventional phenomena such as form through a meditative equipoise of primordial wisdom that is one-pointedly placed in suchness, and as this wisdom increases and expands further and further, one will attain the unsurpassed, great awakening of the mind-stream of the Sugatas.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་དམིགས་པ།**
source: རྣམ་པ་ནི། ཡང་འདི་ཤེས་རབ་ཅེས་སོགས་ཆིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། ཡང་འདི་མཉམ་དུ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཐར་བར་བསྒྲོད་པའི་ལམ་གཅིག་པུ་འདི་ནི། གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཕུང་པོའམ་རྫས་སམ་ཡོན་ཏན་ནམ། ལས་སམ། སྤྱིའམ། ཁྱད་པར་རམ། འདུ་བ་གང་ཡིན། གང་ཟག་སུ་ཡི་ཡིན། མཐའ་བཞི་གང་ལས་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་གང་ཡང་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དོན་དམ་པར་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། རིགས་པ་དེ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གཟུགས་ནས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་བར་གྱི་ཆོས་འདི་ཐམསཅད་རང་གི་ངོ་བོས་སྟོང་པར་རྟོག་ཅིང་དཔྱོད་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །དེ་ལྟར་གཅིག་དུ་བྲལ་དང་རྡོ་རྗེ་ཟེགས་མའིགཏན་ཚིགས་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིག་པ་ཡང་དག་གིས་ཉེ་བར་བཏགས་ནས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པར་མཐོང་བ་ན་ཞུམ་པ་མེད་ཅིང་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པ་ཡི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་ཉེ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་རྒྱུའི་ཁྱད་པརདང་། རྣམ་པར་དཔྱད་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་མཐོང་བ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཡིན་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །
translation: As for the aspect, this is taught by a single verse beginning with "Also this perfection of wisdom..." The meaning is: This perfection of wisdom, which is the sole path leading to liberation—realizing that all phenomena are simultaneously empty by nature—is what is being taught. When one examines and investigates, asking, "Is it the aggregates such as form, or the substances, or the qualities, or the actions, or the universals, or the particulars, or the combinations? Whose is it? From which of the four extremes does it arise?" one finds that it is none of these, because in ultimate reality there is no arising. By that very logic, one contemplates and investigates all these phenomena, from form up to the knowledge of all modes, as being empty of their own essence. In this way, by relying upon valid reasoning—such as the arguments of being free from one or many, or the diamond slivers—when one sees them as empty by nature, the bodhisattva who is undaunted and fearless regarding the meaning of the abiding nature is close to perfect enlightenment. Thus, it is taught that the distinction of the cause and the seeing of phenomena as lacking inherent nature when analyzed is the aspect.

heading: **བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ།**
source: བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ།བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་མི་ཤེས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། གལ་ཏེ་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་གདོང་མ་ནས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའི་དོན་མི་ཤེས་བཞིན་དུ་གཟུགས་ལ་རང་གི་ངོ་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་གཟུགས་སུ་མངོན་པར་འདུ་ཤེས་ཤིང་། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཚོར་བ་དང༌། སེམས་པ་སྟེ་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་བ་དང་རྣམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོར་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་སྤྱོད་པར་བྱེད་ན་མཚན་མ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པར་མ་ཟད་སྟོང་ཉིད་ལ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་ཚེ་གཟུགས་ཕུང་པོ་འདི་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པའོ་ཞེས་རྣམ་པར་རྟོག་ནའང་མངོན་པར་འདུ་བྱེད་པའི་སེམས་པ་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་སྣང་བ་མ་ཁེགས་པས།  དེ་ལྟར་བསྒོམ་ཀྱང་དེ་འདྲའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ནི་མཚན་མ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་གྱི། རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་གནས་ལ་ཡིད་ཆེས་པའི་དད་པ་ཐོབ་སྟེ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་རྣལ་མ་གནས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །འདིས་དོན་དམ་པར་ངོ་བ་ཉིད་མེད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་བྱས་པའི་གཟུགས་སོགས་དམིགས་པར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཁ་ཅིག །མདོ་འདིས་དོན་དུ་བསམ་ནས་དགག་བྱ་བདེན་གྲུབ་བཀག་པའི་མེད་དགག་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དེ་ཙམ་གནས་ལུགས་མཐར་ཐུག་མ་ཡིན་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་མི་རུང་བར་འདོད་པ་སོགས་ནི་འཐད་པ་མ་ཏེ། རིགས་པ་དང་ལུང་ཚད་མས་གནོད་པའི་ཕྱིར།  རྩ་ཤེས་ཊིཀ་ཆེན་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་དངོས་པོ་རྣམས་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པ་མིན་ནོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པ་ན་འདི་རྣམས་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་ངོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་དུ་མི་རུང་བ་མིན་གྱི་དངོས་པོ་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་འདི་བདེན་ནོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེས་ན་ཆོས་རྣམས་སྟོང་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་བཟུང་ན་ཡང་གསོར་མི་རུང་བར་གཞུང་འདིས་བསྟན་པར་འདོད་པ་ནི་མ་བརྟགས་པར་སྨྲ་བ་ཆེན་པའོ། ། སློབ་དཔོན་གཉིས་ཀས་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་དུ་ལྟ་བ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ལ་དངོས་པོར་ཞེན་པ་ལ་གསུངས་ལ་དེ་ནི་སྟོང་ཉིད་བདེན་པར་བཟུང་བའམ་སྟོང་ཉིད་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཡོད་པར་འཛིན་པ་ཡིན་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་མེད་དོ་སྙམ་དུ་འཛིན་པ་ཙམ་ག་ལ་ཡིན། ཞེས་དང་། དེ་ལྟར་གཞུང་གི་དོན་ལོག་པར་བཟུང་ན་ནི་དོན་དམ་པའི་བདེན་པ་མི་སྲིད་ཅེས་སྐུར་བ་འདེབས་པ་དང་། སྲིད་ཀྱང་དེ་ངེས་པའིངེས་ཤེས་བསྐྱངས་ན་མཚན་འཛིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་བཟུང་ནས་ཡང་དག་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་དུ་ངེས་པའི་ལྟ་བ་སྐྱོང་བའི་གེགས་ཆེན་པོ་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས།  ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་པོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་མོ་ལ་ཇི་ལྟར་སྤྱད་པ་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་དུ། ཕུང་པོ་ལྔ་པོ་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་སྟོང་པ་རྣམ་བར་ཡང་དག་བར་རྗེས་སུ་ལྟའོ། །ཞེས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་པ་ལྟ་དགོས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་། མདོ་འདི་ཉིད་ལས་ཀྱང་། གང་ཚེ་འདུས་བྱས་འདུས་མ་བྱས་དང་དཀར་ནག་ཆོས། ཤེས་རབ་རྣམ་པར་བཤིག་ནས་བརྔུལ་ཙམ་མི་དམིགས་ཚེ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་དྲག་ན་ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་གྲངས་འགྲོ། །ཞེས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་རྣམས་ལ་དཔྱད་པས་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་མི་དམིགས་པར་མཐོང་ན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་དུ་འགྲོ་བར་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ལུང་རིགས་གཞན་ཡང་མང་མོད་ཀྱང་ཡི་གེས་འཇིགས་ནས་མ་སྤྲས་སོ། །
translation: The object of patience: The object of patience is taught by a single verse beginning with "If one does not know..." The meaning is: If, without knowing the meaning that all phenomena such as form are empty of intrinsic nature from the very beginning, one superimposes upon form the notion that it is a form established by its own essence, and similarly, if one acts with the notion of truly clinging to feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness, then one is not only acting upon signs, but even when one is single-pointedly absorbed in emptiness, if one conceptualizes, "This form aggregate is empty by nature," one is still acting upon the mental formations that construct, and the appearance of the five aggregates is not blocked. Thus, even if one meditates in that way, such a bodhisattva is acting upon signs; they have not attained the faith of conviction in the state of nature-less arising, and they are not abiding in the genuine perfection of wisdom. By this, it is taught that one is observing form and so forth, which are characterized by being devoid of essence in ultimate reality. Some hold that this sutra, considering the meaning, implies that the mere emptiness of negation—where the object of negation, true existence, has been negated—is not the ultimate abiding nature, and they hold that it is improper to grasp that "form and so forth are empty of true existence." Such views are not tenable, as they are contradicted by valid reasoning and scripture. In the Great Commentary on the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, it is stated: "When it is taught that 'in this way, things do not exist by way of their own essence,' it does not mean that one should not grasp that 'these are empty of true existence'; rather, it means that one should not grasp that 'this emptiness of things of true existence is true.'" Therefore, to hold that this text teaches that even if one grasps that "phenomena are empty," it is not to be accepted, is a great error of speaking without investigation. Both masters explained that the meaning of "viewing emptiness as a position" refers to the fixation on emptiness as a functional entity; this is the grasping of emptiness as truly existent or the grasping of emptiness as existing by way of its own essence—how could it possibly refer to the mere apprehension that things lack intrinsic nature? They further stated that if one misinterprets the meaning of the text in this way, one is disparaging it by saying that ultimate truth is impossible, and even if it were possible, by holding that cultivating certainty about it leads to grasping at signs, one becomes a great obstacle to cultivating the view that correctly determines the genuine meaning. The Heart Sutra also, in response to the question of how to practice the profound perfection of wisdom, states: "One should correctly and thoroughly look upon those five aggregates as being empty by nature." This teaches that one must look upon them as empty by nature. Furthermore, this very sutra states: "When one has analyzed conditioned and unconditioned, white and black phenomena with wisdom, and does not observe even an atom, then, if the world is wise, one goes to the perfection of wisdom." This teaches that if one sees, through the analysis of phenomena by wisdom, that not even an atom is observed, one proceeds to the perfection of wisdom. Although there are many other scriptures and reasonings, I have not elaborated upon them for fear of excessive length.

[3-30] translation already produced for this document:
As for the aspect, this is taught by a single verse beginning with "Also this perfection of wisdom..." The meaning is: This perfection of wisdom, which is the sole path leading to liberation—realizing that all phenomena are simultaneously empty by nature—is what is being taught. When one examines and investigates, asking, "Is it the aggregates such as form, or the substances, or the qualities, or the actions, or the universals, or the particulars, or the combinations? Whose is it? From which of the four extremes does it arise?" one finds that it is none of these, because in ultimate reality there is no arising. By that very logic, one contemplates and investigates all these phenomena, from form up to the knowledge of all modes, as being empty of their own essence. In this way, by relying upon valid reasoning—such as the arguments of being free from one or many, or the diamond slivers—when one sees them as empty by nature, the bodhisattva who is undaunted and fearless regarding the meaning of the abiding nature is close to perfect enlightenment. Thus, it is taught that the distinction of the cause and the seeing of phenomena as lacking inherent nature when analyzed is the aspect.

heading: **བཟོད་པའི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The aspect is taught by the single verse beginning with, "Whatever is not form." The meaning is: one does not apprehend form as form established by its own essence; likewise, one does not apprehend feeling as established by nature, nor does one apprehend perception, the bodhisattva, and so forth as established from their own side. Furthermore, one does not engage or abide in consciousness in a way that apprehends it as established by its own mode of existence or essence. In short, for one who is in meditative equipoise resting in emptiness, the appearance of the five aggregates is blocked, and one practices without abiding in any object through belief in its truth. That practitioner of meditative equipoise does not perceive, "I am practicing emptiness," because they possess a stable wisdom that is free from all grasping at the truth of the three spheres. Having thus taught the aspect, the manner of performing the cause is as follows: one who possesses the intellect that realizes the three—the agent, the action, and the object—as unborn in truth, touches the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle, which is the supreme pacification of distractions and so forth, such as the meditative absorption named "heroic stride," and so forth, thereby completely attaining the classes of realization of the three vehicles. By this, it is taught that realizing what is ultimately without essence as being the essence of form and so forth is the aspect. "Forbearance" means being free from the manifestation of fear regarding the profound phenomena of non-arising.

heading: **ཆོས་མཆོག་གི་དམིགས་པ།**
translation: The Aspect: This is taught in one verse, beginning with "Practicing in this way..." The meaning is this: if one practices in this way, without any arrogant assumption of truth regarding any phenomenon whatsoever, one is practicing the wisdom of the Sugatas. This is because that bodhisattva fully understands that the very fact that no phenomenon can be practiced in an ultimate sense is the supreme practice of the heirs of the Victorious One. The perfection of wisdom, which is the phenomenon to be practiced, such as the path of preparation; the bodhisattva, who is the practitioner; and the practice itself, which is the application—none of these are apprehended as true. Such practice, which does not apprehend the three spheres, is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. This shows the state without arrogant assumption and also indicates the special nature of the cause. Although there are twelve divisions of the path of preparation—three each for the heat and so forth, being small, medium, and great—and although the differences in their non-apprehending aspects could be correlated with the extensive, intermediate, and other sutras, one should understand that even though they cannot be directly correlated here due to the brevity of the sutra text, they are taught by implication.

[3-34] translation already produced for this document:
The Aspect: This is taught in one verse, beginning with "Practicing in this way..." The meaning is this: if one practices in this way, without any arrogant assumption of truth regarding any phenomenon whatsoever, one is practicing the wisdom of the Sugatas. This is because that bodhisattva fully understands that the very fact that no phenomenon can be practiced in an ultimate sense is the supreme practice of the heirs of the Victorious One. The perfection of wisdom, which is the phenomenon to be practiced, such as the path of preparation; the bodhisattva, who is the practitioner; and the practice itself, which is the application—none of these are apprehended as true. Such practice, which does not apprehend the three spheres, is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom. This shows the state without arrogant assumption and also indicates the special nature of the cause. Although there are twelve divisions of the path of preparation—three each for the heat and so forth, being small, medium, and great—and although the differences in their non-apprehending aspects could be correlated with the extensive, intermediate, and other sutras, one should understand that even though they cannot be directly correlated here due to the brevity of the sutra text, they are taught by implication.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་བཟུང་རྟོག**
translation: Regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as an obscuration of knowledge, if we divide it primarily, there are two: the conceptualization of the apprehended as defiled and the conceptualization of the apprehended as purified. If we divide it by way of branches: regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as defiled, there are nine types, such as the consciousness of attachment that clings to the ignorance of the afflicted as being truly existent as an object of enjoyment. Regarding the conceptualization of the apprehended as purified, there are nine types, such as the consciousness of attachment that clings to the aggregates of the purified as being truly existent as an object of enjoyment. Concerning these two types of conceptualization of the apprehended, the single verse beginning with "Whatever is not existent" indicates the object of the conceptualization of the apprehended as defiled, by way of the opposite of what is taught by the literal meaning of the object of the conceptualization of the apprehended as purified, which is the ignorance that is confused about the state of the two truths. Furthermore, any apprehended object of the defiled or purified, when analyzed by reasoning such as the refutation of production from the four extremes, is not truly existent because it cannot withstand such analysis; it is said to be without inherent existence because it is established by scripture and reasoning. Ordinary beings, having examined these phenomena correctly, posit them as existing only conventionally and not existing ultimately; yet these two—existing conventionally and not existing ultimately—are also phenomena that do not exist truly, for they are merely posited by the power of understanding both, and cannot withstand analysis by reasoning. Therefore, if a Bodhisattva knows that, just as a magical pebble appears as a chariot or an ox, yet the two—the appearance and the emptiness of it—are not contradictory, so too the two—that phenomena exist conventionally and do not exist ultimately—are not contradictory, and furthermore, that they proceed as one assisting the other, then they will certainly emerge from the extremes of existence and peace, and will attain non-abiding nirvana. Thus it is said.

[3-35] translation already produced for this document:
The distinction of the fruition, the associated, the abandonment, and the realization. Second, regarding the explanation of the distinction of the conceptualizations to be abandoned: there are two, the conceptualization of the apprehended and the conceptualization of the apprehender.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་འཛིན་རྟོག**
translation:
The second type of cognitive obscuration, the conceptualization of grasping, is divided fundamentally into two: the conceptualization of grasping at substantial existence and the conceptualization of grasping at nominal existence. When divided by way of their branches, there are nine types of conceptualization of grasping at substantial existence, such as grasping at the enjoyment of objects by focusing on the grasping of a self that is independent. Likewise, there are nine types of conceptualization of grasping at nominal existence, such as grasping at the enjoyment of objects by focusing on the grasping of a person as nominally existent. These two types of conceptualization are taught in a single verse, beginning with the words, "In this context, the five aggregates..." In that regard, the first of the nine objects of focus—the grasping at an "I" that is nominally imputed upon the five aggregates—is taught by the explicit words, and from the opposite perspective, the self that does not depend upon the aggregates is taught as the object of focus for the grasping at substantial existence.

In this context of training on the path, one understands that all phenomena, such as the five aggregates, are like illusions—appearing yet lacking true existence. Furthermore, one does not make a distinction between the true and the untrue by positing that the illusion is false while the aggregates are truly existent; rather, one understands the five aggregates themselves to be like illusions, dreams, and mirages. By being free from the consciousness of various conceptualizations and by practicing in a state where all elaborations are pacified, one engages in the supreme perfection of wisdom. In this context, being free from the conceptualization of subject and object does not mean that the seeds have been abandoned, but rather that one is free from their manifestation.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་འཛིན་རྟོག**
translation: The third point, demonstrating the distinction of the spiritual friend who is a mentor, is taught in one verse beginning with "Possessing a virtuous friend." Regarding this, there are two types of mentors: external and internal. The external mentor, being skilled in means, teaches that "there are such faults of Māra and such actions," and acts to turn one away from them. Then, in accordance with the capacity of the trainee's mind, they gradually lead them along the paths of the small and intermediate persons—such as [contemplating] impermanence and suffering—and when the continuum is well-ripened, they act as a mentor by way of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom, such as emptiness. The internal mentor, possessing the special union of method and wisdom, acts to restrain one from the two [faults of] engaging in the lesser vehicle and clinging to true existence.

heading: **ཤེས་སྒྲིབ་འཛིན་རྟོག**
translation: The meaning of the words is as follows: Bodhisattvas possess virtuous spiritual friends who lead them onto the path of virtue by teaching them, in a complete manner, the profound reality of emptiness and the methods and wisdom such as the generation of bodhicitta, dedication, and aspiration. Furthermore, they possess both external and internal mentors—the latter being the insight (vipaśyanā) and so forth that constitutes the wisdom realizing emptiness, which is seized by special methods. Through this, having heard the perfection of wisdom, which is the mother that gives birth to the victorious ones, they do not become afraid, they never change, they realize the meaning of reality, and they do not decline from the Great Vehicle. Having thus demonstrated the distinction of the mentor by way of the direct approach, it is also taught by way of the reverse approach: any beginner who lacks faith in the Great Vehicle, who possesses a sinful friend who turns them away from it, and who is separated from the internal mentor that realizes the meaning of the perfection of wisdom through one's own power, is one who relies on others. This is like an unbaked clay pot that disintegrates when touched by water; just as pouring water into a pot that has not been fired in a kiln causes it to dissolve and the pot to be destroyed, this person, too, because they are afraid of emptiness, abandons the perfection of wisdom, and just as the pot is destroyed, all their previously existing practice and conduct are destroyed.

source: ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པ།བཞི་པ་ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། རྟོགས་པ་ཡིན་ནི། ཆོས་དྲུག་དང་། ནས། རིགས་ཞེས་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། རང་གི་རྟེན་ཆོས་སུ་གྱུར་བའི་དྲི་མ་དང་བཅས་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་གང་ཞིག །ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་འགྱུར་དུ་རུང་བ། རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཀྱང་ཡིན། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དངོས་ཀྱི་རྟེན་གཞི་ཡང་ཡིན་པའི་གཞི་མཐུན་པ་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། རིགས་ལ་སྒྲས་བརྗོད་རིགས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་དང་། རྗེས་འགྱུར་གྱི་རིགས་གཉིས་ཡོད། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དྲོད་སོགས་བཞི་དང་མཐོང་སྒོམ་གཉིས་ཏེ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཆོས་དྲུག་དང་། གཉེན་པོའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། སྤོང་བའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། སྤངས་བྱ་དེ་དག་ཏུ་གཏུགས་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། ཤེས་རབ་སྙིང་བརྩེར་བཅས་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། སློབ་མ་ཉན་ཐོས་སོགས་དང་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། གཞན་དོན་གོ་རིམ་དུ་བྱེད་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ། ཡེ་ཤེས་རྩོལ་བ་མི་མངའ་བར་འཇུག་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྟེན་རང་བཞིན་གནས་རིགས་དང་བཅུ་གསུམ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་ན་ཡོད།
translation: Mahāyāna Practice. Fourth, the naturally abiding disposition (prakṛtistha-gotra) that serves as the support for Mahāyāna practice. The Ornament states: "Realization is the six dharmas, and so on, called the disposition." Regarding this, there are three sections: definition, classification, and scope. As for the first, the definition of the naturally abiding disposition is: that which is the nature of the mind (cittatā) accompanied by adventitious stains, which serves as one's own support, and which is capable of being transformed into the Svābhāvikakāya. It is also the nature of the mind in the continuum of a bodhisattva, and it is a common locus that is also the actual basis of support for Mahāyāna practice. Regarding the classification of the disposition by way of the disposition expressed by name, there are two: the naturally abiding disposition and the developmental disposition (samudānīta-gotra). Regarding the classification of the naturally abiding disposition that serves as the support for Mahāyāna practice, there are thirteen: the six dharmas of realization, namely the four [levels] beginning with heat (ūṣmagata) and the two [paths of] seeing and meditation; the practice of the antidote; the practice of abandonment; the practice of focusing on those things to be abandoned; the practice accompanied by wisdom and compassion; the practice that is uncommon to the śrāvaka disciples and others; the practice of performing the benefit of others in sequence; and the naturally abiding disposition that serves as the support for the practice of engaging in wisdom without exertion. As for the scope, it exists from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum (dharmadhātu-viśuddhi).

heading: **ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: Although the extensive sutras teach the thirteen individually, here, because the words are condensed, they indicate the naturally abiding lineage in a general way, as shown by the two lines beginning with "Why is this...?" Furthermore, if one asks why this person is designated as a "bodhisattva," the answer is that if the mind were established as truly existent, it would not provide the space for qualities to arise, and thus the name "bodhisattva" would not be obtained. However, because the naturally luminous nature of the mind—the basis from which all Buddha-qualities arise—is capable of having faults removed and capable of having qualities arise, through the wisdom of hearing, thinking, and meditating that realizes the suchness of the mind, one cuts through, without remainder, all attachment or grasping at phenomena such as form as being truly existent. By completely abandoning and exhausting the conceptual thoughts, along with their seeds, that are attached to all knowable phenomena as being truly existent, and by eventually attaining great enlightenment, one obtains the name "bodhisattva." For example, just as space provides the space for other things that have form, and the stages of the sun gradually rising in space obtain names such as "morning" and "forenoon," so too is this the case. The *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "Impure, impure-pure, and thoroughly pure, in sequence, are called sentient being, bodhisattva, and Tathāgata." Thus, the name "sentient being" is applied to the stage of being impure due to stains, "bodhisattva" to the stage of being partially pure, and "Tathāgata" to the stage of being entirely pure. Here too, one should understand that the thirteen bodhisattvas designated for the various stages of practice are all designated based on the stages where the stains of that naturally abiding lineage—the suchness of the mind which acts as the basis or the space for the arising of qualities—are gradually purified and where qualities progressively increase.

source: གཉིསཔ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དགེ་མི་དགེ་ལུང་མ་བསྟན་གསུམ། འཇིག་རྟེན་སོར་སྐྱས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ། འཇིག་རྟེན་ལས་འདས་པའི་འཕགས་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བསམ་གཏན། ཟག་བཅས་ཉེར་ལེན་གྱི་ཕུང་པོ། དྲན་སོགས་ཟག་མེད། འདུ་བྱས་ལམ་བདེན། འདུས་མ་བྱས་འགོག་བདེན། ཐེག་གསུམ་མཐུན་མོང་གི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསམ་གཏན། ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྟོབས་བཅུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད། ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཐོག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་དམིགས་པ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོ་རྣམ་དག་ལམ་གྱི་དམིགས་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་ལ་བྱེད་དགོས་ཏེ། སེམས་བདེན་སྟོང་ལ་དམིགས་ནས་བསྒོམས་ན་སྤྲིན་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་ཟད་པ་དང། ཆུ་བུར་ཆུ་ལ་ཐིམ་པ་ལྟར་འགོག་པ་རང་སྟེང་དུ་མཐོང་བ་དང་དྲི་མ་ཆོས་དབྱིངས་སུ་ཟད་པ་དང་འགོག་བདེན་དོན་དམ་བདེན་པར་འཇོག་པ་སོགས་འོངས་ཤིང་གནད་གཅིག་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང༌། འདིར་སྟོང་ཉིད་གཙོ་བོར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་ན་རིགས་སྟོན་པའི་གཞུང་དང་ཟློས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཞེ་ན། རང་བཞིན་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་རིགས་དང་རྣམ་འགྱུར་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པ་དམིགས་པ་ཞེས་བཤད་བས་རིགས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་སུ་བདེན་སྟོང་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་གཞན་ཐམས་ཅད་དེའི་ཁྱད་ཆོས་སུ་སྒྲུབ་པས་ཆོས་ཅན་གྱི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་བརྗོད་ལ།དམིགས་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཁྱད་གཞི་དང་བདེན་མེད་ཁྱད་ཆོས་ལྟ་བུར་བརྗོད་པས་སྐྱོན་མེད་ཅེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས།
translation: Regarding the second, when classifying this, there are three: virtuous, non-virtuous, and neutral. There are the aggregates of worldly beings, the meditative concentrations of the continuum of the noble ones who have transcended the world, the contaminated aggregates of grasping, the uncontaminated [phenomena] such as mindfulness, the truth of the path which is conditioned, the truth of cessation which is unconditioned, the meditative concentrations which are qualities common to the three vehicles, and the eleven [qualities] which are uncommon, namely the ten powers. Although all phenomena are objects of observation for the practice of the Great Vehicle, one must primarily focus on the ultimate object of observation, the path of perfect purity. This is because if one meditates by focusing on the mind as empty of true existence, results such as seeing the cessation within oneself—like clouds vanishing into the sky or bubbles dissolving into water—the exhaustion of stains into the expanse of reality, and the establishment of the truth of cessation as the ultimate truth will come about, and because the essential point is the same. If one asks how there is no fault of redundancy with the treatises that teach the lineage when emptiness is directly taught here as the primary [subject], Gungthang Jamyang stated: "Because it is explained that the lineage is the primary nature and the object of observation is the primary manifestation, in the context of the lineage, emptiness of true existence is stated as the basis and all other things are established as its attributes, expressed in the manner of a property-possessor; whereas in the context of the object of observation, all phenomena are stated as the basis and the lack of true existence is expressed as if it were an attribute, so there is no fault."

translation: Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the scope. The first is: the ultimate result for the sake of which one engages in practice is the definition of the purpose of practicing the Great Vehicle. Regarding the classification, there are three: the great bodhisattva, the great abandonment, and the great realization. The scope exists only in the Buddha. The meaning of the three types of such great purposes is indicated by the single verse beginning with "Why is that?" If one asks, "Why is that person given the name 'great bodhisattva'?" it is because they have become the protector and ally of the great assembly of sentient beings and their many gatherings, and thus have become supreme; because they have become great, they are a "great mind." Furthermore, because sentient beings have different realms and inclinations, they rely on the forty-eight views based on the past, the fourteen views based on the future—making sixty-two wrong views—as well as the three hundred wrong views and so forth; these infinite wrong views are difficult to destroy and numerous because they have been familiarized with since beginningless time, and thus they are "great." Because one teaches the doctrine of emptiness and so forth to sever their continuity, one is "eliminating," and since one must first abandon them oneself, this is "great abandonment." Having directly indicated these two, and because when one is free from obscurations, one realizes all phenomena just as one sees forms, the obscurations that hinder realization are indicated as abandoned; thus, the "great realization" of the omniscient primordial wisdom that realizes them is also understood by implication. Therefore, because one engages in the practice of the path for the sake of attaining the result of the three bodies, one is explicitly called a "great bodhisattva."

heading: **གོ་སྒྲུབ།**
source: གོ་སྒྲུབ།བདུན་པ་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ནི། རྒྱུན་ལས། དེ་དག་སོ་སོར་སྦྱིན་ལ་སོགས། །ནས། དྲུག་གིས་ཇི་བཞིན་བཤད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། ཐེག་ཆེན་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་ལ་བརྟེན་ནས་དོན་གཉིས་ཕུན་ཚོགས་སུ་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་པའི་ཆེན་པོ་དྲུག་ལྡན་གྱི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར། ཐེག་ཆེན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན་དཔེར་ན། གཡུལ་འགྱེད་པ་ལ་གོ་གྱོན་པ་དང༌། གཡུལ་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་དང་། དགྲ་ལས་རྒྱལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གྲོགས་དང་མཚོན་ཆ་དང་། དགྲ་ལས་རྒྱལ་བ་དང་འདྲ་བར་གོ་སྒྲུབ། འཇུག་སྒྲུབ། ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ། ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ་དང་བཞི་ཡོད། དང་པོ་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ་ས་མཚམས་གསུམ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། སྦྱིན་སོགས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་རེ་རེའི་ནང་དུ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་དང་ཚང་བར་བསྡུས་ནས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་བསམ་པའི་བྱ་བ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོས་ཟིན་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར། གོ་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཁྱེན་པ་དོན་ཅིག །གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན།  སྦྱིན་པ་ནས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་བར་དྲུག་ཡོད། རྒྱས་པོར་ཕྱེ་ན། སྦྱིན་སོགས་རེ་རེ་ལ་དྲུག་དྲུག་སྟེ་སོ་དྲུག་ཡོད།  གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། གོ་སྒྲུབ་དེ་ནི་གཏོང་བ་ཆེ་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན། དོན་ནི། བཤད་མ་ཐག་པ་དེ་ཙམ་མ་ཟད་གཞན་ཡང་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པ་ོབགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ན་ཡང་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པ་ོཞེས་བྱ་ལ། གོ་ཆ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། སྤྱོད་འཇུག་ལས། བདོག་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་འབྲས་བཅས་ཏེ། །སྐྱེ་བོ་ཀུན་ལ་གཏོང་སེམས་ཀྱིས། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ལྟར།  ལུས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་དགེ་རྩ་ཐམས་ཅད་གཏོང་པ་ནི་གཏོང་བ་ཆེ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ་སྦྱིན་པའི་གོ་ཆའི་སྒྲུབ་པ་དང་། ཉེས་སྤྱོད་སྡོམ་པ་དང༌། དགེ་བ་ཆོས་སྡུད་པ་དང༌། སེམས་ཅན་དོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་སོགས་འཆལ་ཚུལ་སྤོང་བའི་སེམས་དཔའ་འམ་བློ་ཆུང་བ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་གོ་སྒྲུབ་དང༌། མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་ནི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཕྱི་མ་བཞི་སྟེ། དེ་ཡང་ཕར་ཕན་གཏགས་པའི་ལན་དུ་ཚུར་གནོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་དང་དྲིན་ལན་ལོག་པར་འཇལ་བ་སོགས་ནི་བཟོད་དཀའ་ནའང་དེས་ཀྱང་མི་རྫི་བའི་བཟོད་པ་དང་། རྐང་ལག་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བ་སོགས་བྱ་དཀའ་བའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སྐྱོ་ངལ་མེད་པའི་བརྩོན་འགྲུས་དང་། ཐེག་དམན་ཡིད་བྱེད་དང་མ་འདྲེས་པར་རྩེ་གཅིག་པའི་བསམ་གཏན་དང༌། བྱ་བྱེད་ལས་གསུམ་བདེན་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་གོ་སྒྲུབ་སོགས་རང་རང་ག་ིམི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་འཇོམ་པའི་མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་དང་། རྒྱལ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་མཆོག་ལ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནས་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་གྱི་བར་ལམ་འབྲས་བུ་དང་བཅས་པ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་བགོས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། བུདྡྷ་ཤྲཱིས་རྐང་པ་ཕྱི་མ་འདི་འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་ལ་སྦྱར་ཡང་སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་ལྟར་རོ། །
translation: Armor Practice. The seventh is armor practice. The *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* states: "From 'Those, each giving, and so forth' up to 'explained according to the six.'" This is the bodhisattva’s yoga, which possesses the six greatnesses and accomplishes the two benefits in perfection, based on the generation of the Mahāyāna mind. It is the definition of Mahāyāna practice. When divided, for example, it is like donning armor for battle, entering the battlefield, having the allies and weapons to defeat the enemy, and defeating the enemy; there are four: armor practice, engagement practice, accumulation practice, and the practice of definite emergence. Regarding the first, armor practice, there are three aspects: definition, division, and scope. The first is the bodhisattva’s yoga, which is seized by a vast intention to practice by condensing all six perfections within each individual perfection. This is the definition of armor practice; it is synonymous with the bodhisattva’s wisdom. Second, regarding its division, there are six, from the armor practice of generosity to the armor practice of wisdom. When divided in detail, there are thirty-six, six for each, such as generosity. Third, regarding its scope, it exists from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum. This armor practice is indicated by the two lines, "Great giving, and so forth." The meaning is that, not only what has just been explained, but because one has donned great armor, one is called a great bodhisattva. What is that armor? As stated in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*: "With the intention to give all that one possesses, along with the results, to all beings..." Thus, giving away one’s body, enjoyments, and all roots of virtue of the three times is the armor practice of generosity, which possesses great giving. The armor practice of ethical discipline is that of a bodhisattva or one of lesser intellect who abandons corrupt conduct, such as the discipline of restraining from non-virtue, the discipline of gathering virtue, and the discipline of benefiting sentient beings. The "great power" refers to the latter four perfections. Even when it is difficult to bear, one is not overcome by those who do harm in return for help or who repay kindness with ingratitude; this is the armor practice of patience. One has no weariness or fatigue in the difficult conduct of the heirs of the Victorious One, such as giving away limbs; this is the armor practice of perseverance. One has one-pointed meditative concentration that is not mixed with the mental engagement of the lesser vehicle; this is the armor practice of meditative concentration. One realizes that the three—the agent, the action, and the object—are devoid of truth; this is the armor practice of wisdom. These possess great power to overcome their respective opposing forces. Because one is engaged in practicing the path and its fruit, from the generation of the mind for the supreme Mahāyāna of the Victorious Ones up to omniscience, one has donned great armor. Although Buddhajñāna applies this final line to engagement practice, the Master applies it to armor practice.

heading: **འཇུག་སྒྲུབ།**
source: འཇུག་སྒྲུབ།བརྒྱད་པ་འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། བསམ་གཏན་གཟུགས་མེད་སྦྱིན་སོགས་དང༌། །ནས། ཤེས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་རྒྱུ་འབྲས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ཅི་རིགས་པ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གཙོ་བོར་གྱུར་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་བ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན་དགུ་ཡོད་དེ། བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་བསམ་གཏན་གཟུགས་མེད་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་སྒྲུབ་པ་དང༌། ཕར་ཕྱིན་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང་། འཕགས་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང༌། ཚད་མེད་བཞི་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང་། མི་དམིགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང༌། འཁོར་གསུམ་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའི་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང་། ཆེད་དུ་བྱ་བའི་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང༌། མངོན་པར་ཤེས་པའི་འཇུག་པའི་དེ་དང་། རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་དང་དགུ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ནི། སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་རོ། །སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱ་པ་སོགས་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་རྣམས་སོ་སོར་གསུངས་ཀྱང་འདིར་ཚིག་བསྡུས་པའི་དབང་གིས་འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་སྤྱི་ཙམ་སྟོན་པར། གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་བགོས་ཤིང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ནམ་མཁའ་ལྟར་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་མ་ལུས་པ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ།  སྙིང་སྟོབས་ལྡོག་ཏུ་མེད་པའི་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་བགོས་ཤིང་ཕྱོགས་བཅུའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་ན་གནས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ལྟ་བ་ངན་པ་དང་སྔུག་བསྔལ་སེལ་ཞིང་ལྷའི་བུའི་བདུད་ཀྱི་སྒྱུ་རྩལ་མཐའ་དག་འདུལ་བ་ལ་བརྩོན་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཕྱིར་ན་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་སྤྱིར་བསྟན་ནས་ཁྱད་པར་རྣམས་ཤུགས་ལ་འཕངས་སོ། །
translation: The eighth, the practice of engagement: regarding the practice of engagement, the Ornament states: "Meditative concentrations, formless [absorptions], giving, and so forth, up to... should be known." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the boundaries. The first: the definition of the practice of engagement is the yoga of a bodhisattva seized by the wisdom of engagement, which is the practice of taking up the various causes and effects of the Great Vehicle, with the peak practice as the primary focus. The second: when classified, there are nine: the practice of engagement in the bodhisattva’s meditative concentrations and formless absorptions; that of engagement in the perfections; that of engagement in the noble paths; that of engagement in the four immeasurables; that of engagement in non-conceptualization; that of engagement in the complete purity of the three spheres; that of engagement in the purpose to be achieved; that of engagement in the superknowledges; and the practice of engagement in the omniscience of all aspects. The third: the boundaries are from the heat level of the path of preparation up to the end of the continuum. Although the specific details are taught individually in the Hundred Thousand [Verse Perfection of Wisdom] and other texts, because the words are condensed here to show only the general nature of the practice of engagement, the meaning of the two lines stating "having donned the great armor, and so forth" is: in order to practice the entire, limitless, sky-like path of the Great Vehicle, such as the six perfections, one dons the great armor of an irreversible intention of courage, and strives to eliminate the wrong views and sufferings of sentient beings dwelling in the ten directions of the world-realms, and to subdue all the deceptive arts of the māras who are sons of the gods; for that reason, one is highly termed a "bodhisattva mahāsattva." Thus, having generally indicated the practice of engagement, the specific details are implied.

heading: **ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ།**
source: ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ།དགུ་པ་ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། བརྩེ་དང་སྦྱིན་ལ་སོགས་པ་དྲུག །ནས། ཤེས་པར་བྱ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། ཚོགས་གཉིས་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོས་ཟིན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ཆོས་མཆོག་འབྲིང་མན་ཆད་ལས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་ཤིང༌། རང་འབྲས་བྱང་ཆེན་འབྱིན་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར། ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཚོགས་དང་། སྦྱིན་པ། ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས། བཟོད་པ། བརྩོན་འགྲུས། བསམ་གཏན། ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དང༌། ཞི་གནས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དང་། ལྷག་མཐོང་གི་ཚོགས་དང་། དེ་ཟུང་འབྲེལ་གྱི་ཚོགས་དང༌། ཐབས་མཁས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དང་། ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དང་། བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དང༌། ལམ་གྱི་ཚོགས་དང༌།  གཟུངས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དང༌། སའི་་ཚོགས་དང༌། གཉེན་པོའི་ཚོགས་དང་བཅུ་བདུན་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ཆོས་མཆོག་ཆེན་པོ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་ན་ཡོད། དེ་ཡང་གོ་སྒྲུབ་ལས་འཕྲོས་ནས་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ཡིན་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་དུ་ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ་དང་པོ་བཅུ་དང་། འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་ལས་འཕྲོས་ནས་ཐེག་ཆེན་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་དེ་གང་ཡིན་ཇི་ཙམ་གྱིས་ཞུགས་པ་ཡིན། གང་ནས་ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་། གང་དུ་གནས་པར་འགྱུར། གང་ཞིག་འབྱུང་བ་ལགས་ཞེས་དྲིས་པ་ལ། དང་པོ་ཐབས་མཁས་ནས་གཟུངས་ཀྱི་བར་དང་། གཉིས་པ་སའི་ཚོགས་དང་། གསུམ་པའི་ལན་དུ་མཐོང་སྤང་གཉེན་པོའི་ཚོགས་དང་། བཞི་པ་ལ་སྒོམ་སྤང་རྟོག་པ་དང་པོའི་གཉེན་པོ་དང་། ལྔ་པའི་ལན་དུ་སྒོམ་སྤང་ལྷག་མ་གསུམ་གྱི་མཉེན་པོར་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། འདིར་ཡང་དཔེར་ན་སྒྱུ་མཁན་གྱིས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་ཇི་ཙམ་གྱིས་གོ་ཆ་བགོས་པ་ཡིན་དྲིས་པའི་ལན་གྱི་ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ་དང་པོ་བཅུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ཞིང་། དེ་ཡང་ཚིགས་བཅད་དང་པོས་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོས་ཚོགས་བསྟན། དེ་ནས་དམ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་གོ་ཆ་མཆོག་ཅེས་པའི་བར་གྱི་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བ་ཡན་ཆད་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་དགུ་བསྟན། ཅི་ཕྱིར་འདི་ནི་ཞེས་པ་ནས། ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་མཆོག་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན། ཞེས་པའི་བར་གྱི་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གྱིས་ཚོགས་ལྷག་མ་བདུན་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། དེ་དག་གི་དོན་ནི། དཔེར་ན་སྒྱུ་མ་བྱེད་པ་ལ་བྱང་བའི་མཁས་པའམ་སྒྱུ་མ་མཁན་གྱིས་སྒྱུ་མ་སྤྲུལ་པའི་གནས་ལམ་པོ་ཆེའི་གཞི་མདོར་སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས་ཆེན་པ་མངོན་པར་སྤྲུལ་བར་བྱས་ཏེ། translation: The Practice of Accumulation. Ninth, regarding the practice of accumulation: The *Ornament* states, "From love and generosity, the six... up to... should be known." This passage addresses its definition, its divisions, and its three boundaries. First, the definition of a bodhisattva’s yoga of the practice of accumulation is: a practice that, by being seized by the vast two accumulations, is superior to the intermediate level of the Mahayana path of preparation’s "supreme dharma" and which produces its own result, great enlightenment. Second, regarding its divisions, there are seventeen: the accumulation of great compassion, the accumulation of generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, the accumulation of calm abiding, the accumulation of superior insight, the accumulation of their union, the accumulation of skillful means, the accumulation of primordial wisdom, the accumulation of merit, the accumulation of the path, the accumulation of dhāraṇī, the accumulation of the stages, and the accumulation of antidotes. Third, regarding the boundaries, it exists from the great level of the Mahayana path of preparation’s "supreme dharma" up to the end of the continuum. Furthermore, following the discussion of the practice of armor, in response to the question of how one dons the armor, the first ten accumulations are taught. Following the discussion of the practice of engagement, in response to the questions—what is this Mahayana into which one engages, to what extent has one engaged, from where does one definitively emerge, where will one abide, and what will arise—the first is from skillful means up to dhāraṇī, the second is the accumulation of the stages, the third is the accumulation of the antidotes to what is to be abandoned by seeing, the fourth is the antidote to the first conceptualization to be abandoned by meditation, and the fifth is taught as the antidote to the remaining three to be abandoned by meditation. Here, too, the two verses beginning with "For example, as a magician..." teach the first ten accumulations in response to the question of to what extent the armor has been donned. The first verse teaches the accumulation of great compassion. Then, the single verse ending with "...the supreme armor of the noble ones" teaches the nine accumulations up to the union of calm abiding and superior insight. The three verses from "Why is this..." up to "...is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom" teach the remaining seven accumulations. The meaning of these is as follows: For example, a skilled magician or one trained in magic, at a crossroads or a large public square, manifests a great assembly of people. When he displays the illusion of cutting off the many various heads of the majority of these people, those who are "killed" are merely magical manifestations and lack consciousness; therefore, because they have no fear or suffering, and no sin or the like arises for the one who kills them, in that same way, a bodhisattva also, having thoroughly understood that all these beings tormented by immeasurable suffering are, like an illusion, devoid of any truly established existence, acts for the benefit of beings through great compassion—knowing the conventional way in which it is appropriate to establish all beings without exception in happiness and protect them from suffering—without having even the slightest fear or trepidation. The reason why sentient beings are like magical manifestations is also as follows: what is called a "sentient being" is merely designated in dependence upon these five aggregates, which are the basis of imputation. In reality, form, feeling, perception, mental factors, and consciousness are not bound by the ignorance of grasping at truth, nor are they liberated by any wisdom that realizes the lack of truth, and so forth. The reason for this is that there is no valid cognition that proves these five aggregates exist in an ultimate sense. Having understood it in that way, the lack of any shrinking heart regarding the manner of engaging in the practice of the complete enlightenment—which, although not existing ultimately, exists conventionally—is the supreme armor of the noble individuals, the bodhisattvas.

heading: **ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ།**
translation: Why is this path named the Great Vehicle of the bodhisattva? Because the word "vehicle" also carries the meaning of a "conveyance," it is called a vehicle in the sense of a conveyance because the Great Vehicle—which is comprised of the accumulation of love, generosity, and so forth—is that upon which any person mounts in order to ferry, that is, to cause all sentient beings to be led beyond sorrow. This is because this path causes both oneself and all others to proceed to the level of a buddha. The essence of this Great Vehicle is like space, because it opens a refuge of liberation for immeasurable sentient beings, and it is a great mansion, because it possesses an infinite array of qualities such as retention, eloquence, meditative stabilization, clairvoyance, and miraculous powers. Because those persons who have entered such a path of the Great Vehicle attain, in the interim, joy of mind and physical ease and happiness, and ultimately attain the distinct bliss of non-abiding nirvāṇa, it is called the supreme vehicle or the Great Vehicle. In ultimate reality, there is no person who, having mounted the Great Vehicle, can be observed to be proceeding toward the fruition of the ten stages and so forth.

heading: **ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ།**
translation: If one asks, "How is it that, relying upon this vehicle, it is taught that one proceeds from cyclic existence to the fruition of nirvāṇa?" it is not that one proceeds from a truly established cyclic existence to a truly established nirvāṇa. Rather, because when one searches for both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa through reasoning, one does not observe any proceeding to nirvāṇa, one must posit the attainment of nirvāṇa merely in terms of the exhaustion of cyclic existence. For example, just as the term "extinguished" is applied to the mere aspect of a fire ceasing when its fuel is exhausted—there being no fire that goes anywhere else—in the same way, because of the cause of the exhaustion of birth in cyclic existence due to karma and afflictions, it is well-stated that such a person has attained nirvāṇa, that is, liberation.

translation: The bodhisattva who practices the path does not apprehend a prior limit—the stage of an ordinary being in the past—nor a later limit—the stage of a Buddha in the future—nor the present stage of a noble one, because they have not arisen from their own side, nor will they arise later. Therefore, because the three times are devoid of being one or many that are truly established, they are pure by nature, and cannot be differentiated by any time.

If one asks, "How is it that, relying upon this vehicle, it is taught that one proceeds from cyclic existence to the fruition of nirvāṇa?" it is not that one proceeds from a truly established cyclic existence to a truly established nirvāṇa. Rather, because when one searches for both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa through reasoning, one does not observe any proceeding to nirvāṇa, one must posit the attainment of nirvāṇa merely in terms of the exhaustion of cyclic existence. heading: **ཚོགས་སྒྲུབ།**
translation: That which is called a "bodhisattva" is unconditioned because it is not found when analyzed by reasoning; because it is empty by nature, for that very reason there is no conceptual elaboration of attachment to the truth of form and so forth. Knowing that there is not even the slightest focus of grasping at truth in this way is what is called practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom.

translation: The Practice of Definite Emergence. The tenth, the practice of definite emergence, is stated in the Ornament as: "The objective, equality, and so forth... are called the practice of definite emergence." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. The first: the yoga of the pure bhūmis that unfailingly leads to the omniscient state is the definition of the practice of definite emergence. The second, its divisions: there are eight, namely, the practice of definite emergence for the sake of the three great objectives, that of equality, that of the benefit of sentient beings, that of spontaneous presence, that of transcending the extremes, that of definite emergence into the omniscient state, and the practice of definite emergence that has the path as its object. The third, the boundaries: they exist in the three pure bhūmis. Gungthang Jamyang stated that the extensive sutras explain these eight through the perspective of the basis of the quality and the quality of emptiness, and that this is a definite emergence through non-apprehension itself, in order to understand that one must practice through the perspective of non-apprehension at the beginning, middle, and end. Although Buddhashrī connects the practice of definite emergence starting from the words "whoever rides," according to our own tradition's master, the meaning taught by the five verses beginning with "the wise bodhisattva" is that when a bodhisattva who is skilled in the manner of positing conventionalities and who practices the conduct of the children of the Victorious One—such as the practice of definite emergence for the sake of the reality of suchness—analyzes with reasoning such as the refutation of production from the four extremes, they contemplate the meaning of being unborn by nature, and having realized the meaning of the unborn, they act and abide in this way.

That which is called a "bodhisattva" is unconditioned because it is not found when analyzed by reasoning; because it is empty by nature, for that very reason there is no conceptual elaboration of attachment to the truth of form and so forth. Knowing that there is not even the slightest focus of grasping at truth in this way is what is called practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom.

heading: **ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation:
The meaning of the phrase "at the time of" (dus kyi tshe), as stated, is to refute the view held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others that time is permanent. For example, in the world, when one says, "At the time of such-and-such a previous event," one understands that the present has changed from that previous state. Thus, the phrase "at the time of" signifies that time is changing, and thereby it is able to refute the permanence of time, as stated in the *Detailed Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom*.

How, then, does this exist? Even if one generates great compassion—the love that desires all beings to be free from suffering—if one is attached to the reality of a "self" and "sentient beings," then this lack of the perception of sentient beings is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of the definitive departure for the sake of all purposes.

If one asks what fault arises from perceiving sentient beings: if one generates the perception that oneself and sentient beings truly exist, and likewise generates the perception that suffering also truly exists, then one practices the perfections, such as generosity, with difficulty. Thinking, "I shall work for the benefit of sentient beings and eliminate their suffering," the bodhisattva who, through attachment to the reality of a "self" and "sentient beings," thoroughly conceives of them as truly existent, is bound by the mental continuum of grasping at truth. Therefore, from that fault of grasping at "self" and "other," all faults, such as attachment and aversion, arise. As the Lord of Logic said:

If there is a self, there is the perception of an other.
From the division of self and other, attachment and aversion arise.
From being thoroughly entangled with these,
All faults come to be.

Therefore, practicing in this way is not the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom.

heading: **ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: If one asks, "How, then, should one practice?" it is reasonable to work for the benefit of others and liberate them from suffering because sentient beings and suffering do not exist truly. Regarding that lack of true existence, among the two—phenomena and persons—and among the two—self and others—if one first looks at how this appears to one's own mind, it is easy to identify the object of negation. By virtue of that, it is also easy to ascertain emptiness, the negation of existence that negates that object of negation. Therefore, a bodhisattva should first know that they themselves lack intrinsic nature. Then, just as one is not established by intrinsic nature, one should know that all sentient beings are also not established by intrinsic nature. Just as all sentient beings lack intrinsic nature, one should know that all phenomena, such as the generation of bodhicitta, lack intrinsic nature. Having realized that, one understands the union of the two truths, where the essence is inseparable, by not conceptualizing true existence in either the ultimate, which is unborn, or the conventional, which has birth. By knowing the state of the two truths as they are and abiding in the meaning of the lack of true existence, one is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, the supreme path of definitive emergence.

heading: **ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: If one asks what is to be attained by that non-conceptual primordial wisdom, it is the Buddha’s mind—the non-conceptual primordial wisdom that abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, having abandoned the extremes of arising and truly passing away or ceasing, in an ultimate sense, regarding all phenomena, such as the ten phenomena including the generation of bodhicitta, or all phenomena from form up to the omniscience, which are all the names of phenomena in the nine worlds that can be expressed. This mind has abandoned all decay and harm without exception, and because there is no decline from it, it is deathless; there is nothing else superior to that supreme primordial wisdom of omniscience. Because it brings about the attainment of that very phenomenon which is supreme and unsurpassed, this path of conceptualizing all phenomena as being ultimately unobservable is the supreme perfection of wisdom, the path of definitive emergence that is to be practiced. By the phrase "the supreme deathless primordial wisdom" and so forth, the two aspects of the path of definitive emergence—the abandonment and the realization of one's own benefit—are indicated.

Regarding that lack of true existence, among the two—phenomena and persons—and among the two—self and others—if one first looks at how this appears to one's own mind, it is easy to identify the object of negation. heading: **ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: Any bodhisattva who, having gained certainty through valid cognition regarding the stages of the path of definitive emergence and so forth, practices and experiences them as previously taught without doubt or hesitation, is said to be endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom seized by skillful means; such a person should be known as one who abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, both in cyclic existence and in peace.

[3-58] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks what is to be attained by that non-conceptual primordial wisdom, it is the Buddha’s mind—the non-conceptual primordial wisdom that abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, having abandoned the extremes of arising and truly passing away or ceasing, in an ultimate sense, regarding all phenomena, such as the ten phenomena including the generation of bodhicitta, or all phenomena from form up to the omniscience, which are all the names of phenomena in the nine worlds that can be expressed. This mind has abandoned all decay and harm without exception, and because there is no decline from it, it is deathless; there is nothing else superior to that supreme primordial wisdom of omniscience. Because it brings about the attainment of that very phenomenon which is supreme and unsurpassed, this path of conceptualizing all phenomena as being ultimately unobservable is the supreme perfection of wisdom, the path of definitive emergence that is to be practiced. By the phrase "the supreme deathless primordial wisdom" and so forth, the two aspects of the path of definitive emergence—the abandonment and the realization of one's own benefit—are indicated.

heading: **ངེས་འབྱུང་སྒྲུབ་པ།**
translation: To have fully realized that the phenomena of the basis, path, and result are devoid of intrinsic nature, equal in being empty of true existence, and of a single taste, is to practice the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of accomplishing definitive emergence. This is what is meant. Because this text summarizes all the meanings of the hundred-thousand-line scripture, it would have been appropriate to arrange the chapters in accordance with that, but because those of lesser intellect would not understand it, it was not so arranged; likewise, it was not done in accordance with the twenty-thousand-line scripture either. It is stated in the difficult-points commentary that the chapters were arranged in accordance with the eight-thousand-line scripture so that it might be easily understood and known to have a single meaning. Having thus finished explaining the ten phenomena that characterize omniscience, the indication of the chapter titles and the conclusion of the section in connection with the Abhisamayālaṅkāra is as follows: from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, a Profound Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities, Clarifying the Reality of Dependent Arising*, this is the first chapter, on entering into omniscience, and the commentary on the first section.

Any bodhisattva who, having gained certainty through valid cognition regarding the stages of the path of definitive emergence and so forth, practices and experiences them as previously taught without doubt or hesitation, is said to be endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom seized by skillful means; such a person should be known as one who abides in the equality of being empty of true existence, both in cyclic existence and in peace.

heading: ལམ་ཤེས།
source: ལམ་ཤེས།རྣམ་མཁྱེན་དེ་ཐོབ་པར་བྱེད་པ་ལས་དེའི་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་རྒྱུ་ལམ་ཤེས་ལ་སློབ་དགོས་པས་གཉིས་པ་ལམ་ཤེས་བཤད་པ་ལ། རྒྱན་ལས། མོག་མོག་པོར་བྱེད་པ་ལ་སོགས་དང༌། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལམ་ཤེས་ཉིད་ནི་དེ་འདྲར་བཤད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་ལྟར། རང་རྒྱུད་ལྡན་གྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་སྟོང་ཉིད་མངོནསུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཟིན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་འཕགས་པའི་མཁྱེན་པ་དེ། ལམ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། ལམ་ཤེས་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དེ་ལ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད་དེ། ལམ་ཤེས་ཡན་ལག་དང་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས། རང་རྒྱལ་གྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ། སྒེམ་ལམ་གྱི་བྱེད་པ། མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ། དེའི་ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟོད་བཀུར་བསྔགས་གསུམ། བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་སྒོམ་ལམ། སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ། རྣམ་དག་སྒོམ་ལམ་རྣམས་སུ་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར།
translation: Knowledge of the path: Since one must train in the knowledge of the path—the uncommon cause of omniscience—in order to attain that omniscience, the second section explains the knowledge of the path. As stated in the *Ornament*: "From 'making dim' and so forth, up to 'the knowledge of the path itself is explained in that way,'" the wisdom of an arya bodhisattva, which is possessed of the realization of emptiness directly within the continuum of a person who possesses their own continuum, is the definition of the knowledge of the path. There are eleven phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the path: the knowledge of the path of the path-knowledge limbs, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of seeing of the Mahāyāna, the function of the path of meditation, the path of meditation of aspiration, the three of praise, honor, and exaltation as its benefits, the path of meditation of dedication, the path of meditation of rejoicing, the path of meditation of accomplishment, and the path of meditation of utter purity.

heading: **ལམ་ཤེས་ཡན་ལག**
source: ལམ་ཤེས་ཡན་ལགདང་པོ་སྟོན་པར། ལྷ་རྣམས་རུང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ནས། དེ་ཡི་ལས། ཤེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ།
translation: To reveal the first limb of the knowledge of the path, from "in order to make the gods favorable" up to "its activity is known," it is said. Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the boundaries.

[3-61] translation already produced for this document:
Knowledge of the path: Since one must train in the knowledge of the path—the uncommon cause of omniscience—in order to attain that omniscience, the second section explains the knowledge of the path. As stated in the *Ornament*: "From 'making dim' and so forth, up to 'the knowledge of the path itself is explained in that way,'" the wisdom of an arya bodhisattva, which is possessed of the realization of emptiness directly within the continuum of a person who possesses their own continuum, is the definition of the knowledge of the path. There are eleven phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the path: the knowledge of the path of the path-knowledge limbs, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the śrāvakas, the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the pratyekabuddhas, the path of seeing of the Mahāyāna, the function of the path of meditation, the path of meditation of aspiration, the three of praise, honor, and exaltation as its benefits, the path of meditation of dedication, the path of meditation of rejoicing, the path of meditation of accomplishment, and the path of meditation of utter purity.

heading: **མཚན་ཉིད།**
translation: The definition: As for the first, that special quality which is conjoined with great compassion, and which is included within any one of the three—the cause, the essence, or the result of the knowledge of the path—is the definition of the limb of the knowledge of the path.

[3-63] translation already produced for this document:
The definition: As for the first, that special quality which is conjoined with great compassion, and which is included within any one of the three—the cause, the essence, or the result of the knowledge of the path—is the definition of the limb of the knowledge of the path.

heading: **ས་མཚམས།**
translation: The boundaries: As for the third, the boundaries, it exists from the time of not having entered the path up to the stage of a Buddha. That limb of the knowledge of the path is taught by one verse, beginning with "Whoever, in form..." According to the *Sampuṭa-ṭīkā* of the Buddha’s feet, it appears correct to apply this to the "congruent with definite discrimination" which is the cause of the knowledge of the path; however, here, the *Sampuṭa-ṭīkā* of the Master is primarily taken as the basis. The meaning of its words is: a bodhisattva does not abide in the form aggregate in the manner of being fixated on it as truly existent, and likewise does not abide in feeling; and one who does not abide because of being fixated on perception as truly existent, and likewise does not abide in volitional factors, and does not abide in consciousness, or in any object whatsoever by way of being fixated on it as truly existent—to realize those directly as empty of truth and free from proliferation, and to remain in meditative equipoise upon that, is to abide in their suchness, which is the reality of those things. Such a state is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the knowledge of the path.

The boundaries: As for the third, the boundaries, it exists from the time of not having entered the path up to the stage of a Buddha. That limb of the knowledge of the path is taught by one verse, beginning with "Whoever, in form..." According to the *Sampuṭa-ṭīkā* of the Buddha’s feet, it appears correct to apply this to the "congruent with definite discrimination" which is the cause of the knowledge of the path; however, here, the *Sampuṭa-ṭīkā* of the Master is primarily taken as the basis. The meaning of its words is: a bodhisattva does not abide in the form aggregate in the manner of being fixated on it as truly existent, and likewise does not abide in feeling; and one who does not abide because of being fixated on perception as truly existent, and likewise does not abide in volitional factors, and does not abide in consciousness, or in any object whatsoever by way of being fixated on it as truly existent—to realize those directly as empty of truth and free from proliferation, and to remain in meditative equipoise upon that, is to abide in their suchness, which is the reality of those things. Such a state is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the knowledge of the path.

translation: The Knowledge of the Path of the Śrāvakas. Second, regarding the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Śrāvakas, there are two: its actual essence and its cause, the aids to penetration.

heading: **མཚན་ཉིད།**

Regarding the first: the knowledge of an Ārya of the Mahāyāna that abides in the category of clear realization to be known for the sake of guiding those to be tamed who are of the Śrāvaka lineage, by way of being seized by the three—the generation of bodhicitta, dedication, and the wisdom realizing emptiness—is the definition of the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Śrāvakas.

heading: **ས་མཚམས།**
translation:
Levels. The third is from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. This is taught in a single verse, "Permanent and impermanent," and so forth. Although the *Extensive Explanation of the Perfection of Wisdom* suggests that "permanent, impermanent, pleasant, painful," and so forth, teach the aspects of the first two truths, and "attaining the fruit, the level of an Arhat," and so forth, teach the aspects of the path of cessation, when examining the *Commentary on the Summary* by the Master, I wonder if the passage from "permanent and impermanent" up to "selfless" teaches the aspects of the truth of suffering, and "thusness" and "thus empty" teach the aspects of the latter three truths; those possessed of analytical intelligence should examine this in detail.

The meaning of the words is as follows: regarding phenomena such as form, one does not abide by way of clinging to them as truly existent, such as: the permanence that is non-decaying; the impermanence that is the opposite of that; the pleasure that has the aspect of soothing sensation; the suffering that is associated with contamination; the pleasantness that is agreeable to the mind; the unpleasantness that is disagreeable; the existence of a self of the person that has become its own essence; the selflessness; and thusness—that is, existing in the ultimate sense—and emptiness, meaning that although they appear to be true, they are empty because they are established in that way or as such. Furthermore, one does not abide through clinging to the attainment of the three fruits—Stream-enterer, Once-returner, and Non-returner—nor to the level of a Śrāvaka Arhat, nor to the level of a Pratyekabuddha, and likewise, one does not abide through clinging to the level of a Buddha. In short, one does not abide by way of truly clinging to any phenomenon included within the three—the basis, the path, and the fruit—as being this or that.

This means that the path of the Śrāvaka, which realizes the sixteen aspects such as impermanence directly, is a path to be known by Bodhisattvas, but they do not practice it by way of seeking the enlightenment of the Lesser Vehicle. Rather, it is shown that they perform the three—generation, knowledge, and perfection—for the sake of guiding those of the Śrāvaka lineage, by way of uniting method and wisdom, such as the generation of bodhicitta, dedication, and the wisdom realizing emptiness.

heading: **དེའི་རྒྱུ་ངེས་འབྱེད་ཆ་མཐུན།**
translation: The causes of that, the factors of definite discrimination. Second, in order to demonstrate the causes of that, the factors of definite discrimination, one verse is spoken, beginning with "Just as the Guide..." The meaning is as follows: Regarding the analogy of not abiding in any phenomenon whatsoever, just as the mind of the Guide, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is the unconditioned realm—meaning it does not abide in the expanse of nirvana, which is peaceful merely by the measure of the cessation of birth in existence—likewise, it does not abide in the side of the conditioned, the three realms of cyclic existence, through grasping at truth. A bodhisattva practices without abiding in any extreme of existence or peace. In that way, having realized that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, even though they abide on the path of the factors of definite discrimination and so forth, they abide without grasping at them as true. This is to abide in the very reality of the free-from-elaboration, without abiding in any phenomenon whatsoever in a definitive sense. It is said that this manner of abiding is the abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of the meaning, as taught by the Victor, the King of Dharma. Thus it is said.
