[3-72] translation already produced for this document:
The causes of that, the factors of definite discrimination. Second, in order to demonstrate the causes of that, the factors of definite discrimination, one verse is spoken, beginning with "Just as the Guide..." The meaning is as follows: Regarding the analogy of not abiding in any phenomenon whatsoever, just as the mind of the Guide, the Buddha, the Blessed One, is the unconditioned realm—meaning it does not abide in the expanse of nirvana, which is peaceful merely by the measure of the cessation of birth in existence—likewise, it does not abide in the side of the conditioned, the three realms of cyclic existence, through grasping at truth. A bodhisattva practices without abiding in any extreme of existence or peace. In that way, having realized that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, even though they abide on the path of the factors of definite discrimination and so forth, they abide without grasping at them as true. This is to abide in the very reality of the free-from-elaboration, without abiding in any phenomenon whatsoever in a definitive sense. It is said that this manner of abiding is the abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of the meaning, as taught by the Victor, the King of Dharma. Thus it is said.

heading: **མཚན་ཉིད།**
translation: The definition. The first is: the wisdom of a Mahayana noble that abides in the category of realizations to be known for the sake of guiding disciples of the Solitary Realizer lineage by way of being seized by three excellences, which is the definition of the knowledge of the path that knows the path of the Solitary Realizer.

རང་རྒྱལ་ནི་སྲིད་པ་ཐ་མའི་ཚེ་སངས་རྒྱས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་ལ་མི་ལྟོས་པར་རང་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་བྱེད་པས་རང་བྱུང་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་དང་། སྒྲ་མེད་ལུས་ཀྱི་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱིས་གཞན་ལ་ཆོས་སྟོན་པ་སྟེ་ཁྱད་ཆོས་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཁྱད་ཞུགས་པར་བརྗོད་ནས་རང་རྒྱལ་གྱི་ལམ་ཤེས་པ་ལ་དེའི་ངོ་བོ་སྟོན་དགོས་པས་དེའི་ངོ་བོ་སྟོན་པ་ནི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་གཞི་དང་ལམ་དང་རྣམ་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་མ་རྟོགས་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་གསུམ་པོ་གང་ཡང་ཐོབ་པར་མི་ནུས་པས་སྙིང་པོའི་དོན་གྱི་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་སློབ་དགོས་པ་ནི། སྐྱེ་བོ་གང་དག་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་བའི་སློབ་མ་ཉན་ཐོས་སུ་འགྱུར་བར་བྱའོ་སྙམ་པ་དང་། གཟུང་བ་ཕྱི་རོལ་དོན་འཛིན་གྱི་རྟོག་པ་སྤངས་བྱའི་གཙོ་བོར་བྱེད་པའི་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་སུ་འགྱུར་བ་དང་དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་སུ་འགྱུར་བར་འདོད་པ་སྟེ་མདོར་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་གསུམ་པོ་གང་འཐོབ་པར་འདོད་ན་ཡང། གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོ་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་པའི་བཟོད་པ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་འདི་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་འབྲས་བུ་དེ་དག་གང་ཡང་ཐོབ་བར་མི་ནུས་ཏེ། དཔེར་ན་གྲུ་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཕ་རོལ་དང་ཚུལ་རོལ་ཏུ་འགྲོ་བའི་འཇུག་ངོགས་མི་མཐོང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །འདིས་ལམ་ཤེས་ཐེག་པ་གསུམ་གྱི་ལམ་གྱི་ཡུལ་ཅན་དུ་བསྟན་ཀྱང་གཙོ་བོ་རང་རྒྱལ་གྱིས་བཟུང་རྟོག་སྤང་བར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །ཁ་གཅིག །ཉན་རང་ལ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་བདག་མེད་ཕྲ་མོ་རྟོགས་པ་སོགས་མེད་བར་འདོད་པ་ནི། མདོ་འདི་དང་དངོས་སུ་འགལ་ཞིང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་གང་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲསབུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་གནས་པར་འདོད་པ་དེས་བཟོད་པ་འདི་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་མི་འགྲུབ་བོ། །དེ་བཞིན་སྦྱར་ཏེ་གང་ལ་ལན་གཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོངས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། ལེན་གཅིག་ཕྱིར་འོངས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ལ་གནས་པར་འདོད་པ་དང་། ནས། རང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་གནས་པར་འདོད་པ་དེས་བཟོད་པ་འདི་ལ་མ་བརྟེན་པར་མ་འགྲུབ་བོ། །ཞེས་དང་། རྡོ་རྗེ་གཅོད་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ཅི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་གིས་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་སམ། རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་གསོལ་བ། བཅོམ་ལྡནའདས་དེ་ནི་མ་ལགས་སོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་སླད་དུ་ཞེ་ན། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་དེ་ནི་གང་ལ་ཡང་ཞུགས་པ་མ་མཆིས་པའི་སླད་དུ་སྟེ། དེས་ན་རྒྱུན་དུ་ཞུགས་པ་ཞེས་བགྱིའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། འཕགས་པ་ཡུལ་འཁོར་སྐྱོང་གིས་ཞུས་པའི་མདོ་ལས། སྟོང་པ་ཞི་བ་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པའི་ཚུལ། །མི་ཤེས་པས་ན་འགྲོ་བ་འཁྱམས་གྱུར་པ། །དེ་དག་ཐུགས་རྗེ་མངའ་བས་ཐབས་ཚུལ་དང༌། །རིགས་པ་བརྒྱ་དག་གིས་ནི་འཛུད་པར་མཛད། །ཅེས་འཁོར་བ་ལས་གྲོལ་བ་ལ་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་དགོས་པར་གསུངས་པ་སོགས་ངེས་དོན་གྱི་མདོ་དུ་མ་དང་འགལ་ཞིང་། འཕགས་པ་ཀླུ་སྒྲུབ་དང་ཟླ་བ་གྲགས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱི་ལུགས་ལས་ཕྱི་རོལ་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྩ་ཤེས་ལས། ལས་དང་ཉོན་མོངས་ཟད་པས་ཐར། །ལས་དང་ཉོན་མོངས་རྣམ་རྟོག་ལས། །དེ་དག་སྤྲོས་ལས་སྤྲོས་པ་ནི། །སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་འགག་བར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་དང་། དཔལ་ལྡན་ཟླ་བས། ཉན་རང་ལ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པ་ཡོད་པར་རིགས་པ་གསུམ་དང་ལུང་དུ་མས་སྒྲུབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འཇུག་པ་རང་འགྲེལ་ལས། ལུགས་འདི་ལས་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ལ་ཡང་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཤེས་པ་ཡང་ཡོད་དོ། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་གསལ་བར་ངེས་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་མ་ཡིན་ན་དངོས་པོ་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་པ་དང་བྲལ་བའི་ཕྱིར། འཇིག་རྟེན་པའི་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བ་ལྟར་དེ་དག་ཀྱང་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རང་གི་བློས་རྣམ་པར་དཔྱད་པས་ཀྱང་ཟིལ་གྱིས་གནོན་པར་འགྱུར་ལ། ཕྱི་རོལ་པ་བཞིན་དུ་འདི་དག་གིས་ཁམས་གསུམ་ན་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཕྲ་རྒྱས་ཐམས་ཅད་སྤངས་པར་ཡང་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རང་གི་ངོ་བོ་ལ་དམིགས་པས་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་འགྱུར་བའི་ཕྱིར། གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པར་མ་འགྱུར་ཏེ། བདག་ཏུ་བཏགས་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཕོང་པོ་ལ་དམིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཇི་སྐད་དུ་རིན་ཆེན་འཕྲེང་བ་ལས། ཇི་སྲིད་ཕུང་པོར་འཛིན་ཡོད་པ། །དེ་སྲིད་དེ་ལ་ངར་འཛིན་ཡོད། །ངར་འཛིན་ཡོད་ན་ཡང་ལས་ཏེ། །དེ་ལས་ཡང་ན་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡིན། །ལམ་གསུམ་ཐོག་མཐའ་དབུས་མེད་པ། །འཁོར་བའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་འགལ་མེ་ཡི། །དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ལྟ་བུར་ཕན་ཚུན་གྱི། །རྒྱུ་ཅན་འདི་ནི་འཁོར་བར་འགྱུར། །དེ་ནི་རང་བཞིན་གཉིས་ཀ་དང་། །དུས་གསུམ་ཉིད་དུ་མ་མཐོང་ཕྱིར། །ངར་འཛིན་པ་ནི་ཟད་པར་འགྱུར། །དེ་ལས་ལས་དང་སྐྱེ་བ་ཡང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་ཤིང་། དེའི་ཤེས་བྱེད་དུ་བསམ་གཏན་དཔེ་འཁྱུད་ཀྱི་མདོ་སོགས་དྲངས་སོ། །ཐེག་པ་ཆེ་ཆུང་གི་ཁྱད་པར་ཡང་། ལྟ་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་མི་འཇོག་པར་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྨོན་ལམ་དང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བའི་ཁྱད་པར་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་འཇོག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། ཇི་སྐད་དུ་རིན་ཆེན་འཕྲེང་བ་ལས། ཉན་ཐོས་ཐེག་པ་དེ་ལས་ནི། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་སྨོན་ལམ་དང་། །སྤྱོད་པ་ཡོངས་བསྔོ་མ་བཤད་དེ། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔར་ག་ལ་འགྱུར། །བྱང་ཆུབ་སྤྱོད་ལ་གནས་པའི་དོན། །མདོ་སྡ་ེལས་ནི་བཀའ་མ་སྩལ། །ཐེག་པ་ཆེ་ལས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པ། །དེ་ཕྱིར་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བཟུང༌། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། འོན་ཀྱང་རིགས་པའི་རྣམ་གྲངས་མཐའ་ཡས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྟོང་ཉིད་རྟོགས་མ་རྟོགས་དང་། སྟོང་ཉིད་རྫོགས་པར་སྒོམ་མི་བསྒོམ་གྱི་ཁྱད་པར་ཡོད་ཚུལ་སོགས་ནི་དབུ་མའི་གཞུང་ལ་ཞིབ་ཏུ་སྦྱངས་ཏེ་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །
translation: The direct. First, it is taught by a single verse, "Those who wish to become..." and so forth. This is to clarify the doubt that, since the two—the Hearer and the Solitary Realizer—are similar in that they both seek liberation for their own sake alone, it is not appropriate to teach the path of the Solitary Realizer separately from the Hearer. For the time being, if one teaches that the Solitary Realizer is superior to the Hearer, one can infer the system of their vehicles; thus, the difference between the two is as follows: Hearers, at the time of their final existence, possess two distinct qualities: they attain their own awakening after listening to instructions from others, and after attaining the result, they teach the Dharma to others by means of sound. Solitary Realizers, at the time of their final existence, are called "self-arisen" because they actualize awakening by their own power without relying on the Buddha or others to teach them the Dharma, and they possess the two distinct qualities of being superior by teaching the Dharma to others through the magical display of a body without sound. Having thus stated that they are superior, one must then teach the essence of the path of the Solitary Realizer. Teaching that essence is as follows: as explained previously, since it is impossible to attain any of the three awakenings without realizing that the basis, the path, and all aspects are empty of true existence, one must train in the perfection of wisdom, which is the meaning of the heart. This means that those beings who think, "I shall become a Hearer, a disciple of the Sugata," or those who think, "I shall become a Solitary Realizer," whose primary task is to abandon the conceptualization that grasps at external objects, and likewise those who wish to become a King of Dharma, a Buddha, a Bhagavan—in short, if one wishes to attain any of the three awakenings, one cannot attain any of those results without relying on this path of patience, which is not afraid of the profound reality of emptiness and realizes that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. It is like not being able to see the landing place for going to the far or near shore of the ocean without relying on a boat. This shows that the knowledge of the path is the object of the path of the three vehicles, but it primarily teaches the abandonment of the conceptualization grasped by the Solitary Realizer. Some hold that Hearers and Solitary Realizers do not realize the subtle selflessness of phenomena, but this directly contradicts this sutra. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states: "O sons of gods, therefore, whoever wishes to attain the result of a Stream-Enterer and wishes to abide in the result of a Stream-Enterer will not succeed without relying on this patience. Apply this likewise to those who wish to attain the result of a Once-Returner, and those who wish to abide in the result of a Once-Returner, up to those who wish to abide in the Self-Awakening." And the *Vajracchedikā* also says: "Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Stream-Enterer think, 'I have attained the result of a Stream-Enterer'?" Subhūti replied, "No, Bhagavan. Why? Because, Bhagavan, he has not entered into anything; therefore, he is called a Stream-Enterer." And the *Ārya-Rāṣṭrapāla-paripṛcchā-sūtra* says: "Those who do not know the way of emptiness, peace, and non-arising wander in the world; those who possess compassion lead them through a hundred methods and means." This and many other definitive-meaning sutras state that realizing emptiness is necessary for liberation from cyclic existence, and it is outside the system of Ārya Nāgārjuna, Candrakīrti, and others. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Liberation comes from the exhaustion of karma and defilements. Karma and defilements come from conceptualization. These come from mental fabrication. Fabrication is stopped by emptiness." And the glorious Candrakīrti proves through three reasonings and many scriptural citations that Hearers and Solitary Realizers also have the realization that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. In his own commentary on the *Madhyamakāvatāra*, it is clearly established: "In this system, Hearers and Solitary Realizers also have the knowledge that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature." If it were not so, because they lack the complete knowledge that things are without intrinsic nature, just as they are free from worldly desire, they would be surpassed by the Bodhisattva who has generated the mind of awakening through his own analytical reasoning; and like non-Buddhists, they would not abandon all the subtle propensities that operate in the three realms. Because they focus on the intrinsic nature of form and so forth, they fall into error and do not realize the selflessness of the person, because they focus on the aggregates, which are the basis for the imputation of a self. As stated in the *Ratnāvalī*: "As long as there is grasping at the aggregates, there is grasping at an 'I'. If there is grasping at an 'I', there is karma, and from that, there is birth. The three paths, without beginning, end, or middle, are like a firebrand in the circle of cyclic existence; because they are mutually causal, this is cyclic existence. Because one does not see them as having two natures or as existing in the three times, the grasping at an 'I' is exhausted. From that, karma and birth also [cease]." This is what was said, and as proof, he cited the *Samādhirāja-sūtra* and others. The difference between the Great and Small Vehicles is not established by way of view, but by way of the Bodhisattva's aspiration, vast conduct, and the difference in dedication. As stated in the *Ratnāvalī*: "In the Hearer vehicle, the Bodhisattva's aspiration, conduct, and dedication are not taught; how could one become a Bodhisattva? The meaning of abiding in the Bodhisattva conduct was not taught in the sutras. It was taught in the Great Vehicle; therefore, the wise should hold to it." However, the way in which there is a difference regarding whether or not emptiness is realized and whether or not emptiness is perfectly meditated upon, through countless variations of reasoning, should be understood by studying the Madhyamaka treatises in detail.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
source: ཞར་བྱུང་།གཉིས་པ་དེའི་ཞར་བྱུང་དུ་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཉན་པ་དང་། བསྒོམ་ནས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་པའི་བར་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བསྟན་པ་ནི། ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུམ་གྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཆོས་འཆད་པ་དང་། སློབ་མས་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉན་པ་དང་། བཤད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཆོས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། ཐོས་པའི་དོན་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཡིད་ལ་བྱས་ཏེ། ལམ་སྒོམ་པས་རྒྱུན་ཞུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་འབྲས་བུ་བཞི་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་རྐྱེན་རྒྱལ་སྟེ་རང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་སྒོམ་མི་སློབ་ལམ་སོགས་ཐོབ་པ་དང༌། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་སྐྱབས་དང་དཔུང་གཉེན་མགོན་པ་ོསངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་པ་དང་། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་མཁས་པ་ཕུལ་དུ་བྱུང་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་ལྡན་ཞིང་ལམ་གྱི་ཚུལ་ལ་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བས་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཟུང་དུ་འབྲེལ་བར་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་བསྒོམས་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ཀུན་ཀྱང་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་གྱི་གཏན་ཚིགས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བརྟགས་ཤིང་དཔྱད་ན་བདེན་པར་གྲུབ་པ་ཅུང་ཟད་ཀྱང་མེད་པར་བདེན་པས་སྟོང་པ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་ཏོ། ཡུམ་རྒྱས་པ་ལས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལས་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུར་བལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། བདག་ནི་མྱ་ངན་འདས་པ་ལས་ལྷག་པའི་ཆོས་གཞན་ཞིག་ཡོད་ན་དེ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་བླཏའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང༌། དེ་ནས་ཡང་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་སེམས་ཏེ། འཕགས་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་འདི་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་རང་བཞིན་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་བཙལ་བར་བྱ་སྙམ་པ་དང༌། དེ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་གི་སེམས་ཀྱི་རྟོག་པ་སེམས་ཀྱིས་ཤེས་ནས་ལྷའི་བུ་དེ་དག་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་ཁོ་བོ་ལ་ཆོས་ཉན་པ་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་དང་སྤྲུལ་པ་ལྟ་བུ་དག་ལྟ་བར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པ་ནས། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅན་ད་ེདག་ནི་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ། ལྷའི་བུ་དག་སེམས་ཅནདེ་དག་ནི་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་སྟེ། ནས། ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཉིད་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་དང་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུའོ། །ནས། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ཡང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུ་རྨི་ལམ་ལྟ་བུར་ན་ཆོས་གཞན་ལྟ་ཅི་སྨོས། ཞེས་གསུངས། ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པའི་དོན་དེ་ལ་གང་ཟག་སུ་ཞིག་གུས་ནས་སློབ་ནུས་ཤེ་ན། གང་ཟག་བཞི་པོ་དེ་འདི་དག་ནི་བཤད་མ་ཐག་པའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ཟབ་མོ་དེ་ལ་མི་སྐྲག་སྟེ་བཞི་པོ་དེ་གང་ཞེ་ན། རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་དོན་ལ་མཁས་པ་རང་རྒྱལ་ཚོགས་སྤྱོད་ཙམ་དང༌། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་སྦྱོར་ལམ་པ་དང། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉོན་སྒྲིབ་སོགས་བློ་ཡི་དྲི་མ་བསལ་ཞིང་ཟད་པར་བྱས་ནས་གནས་ལུགས་ཟབ་མོའི་དོན་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་སྤངས་པ་དེ་གསུམ་དང་། བཞི་པ་ནི་ལས་དང་པོ་པ་ཡིན་དུ་ཟིན་ཀྱང་སྔོན་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ལ་ལྷག་པར་བྱ་བ་བྱས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་ད་ལྟ་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་དོན་ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པར་སྟོན་པར་ནུས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཟིན་པའོ། །འདིའི་རྒྱལ་སྲས་བདེན་ལ་མཁས་ཞེས་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་གནས་གོ་དགོས་པས་རྟེན་རང་རྒྱལ་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་ལས་དེ་ལྟར་བསྟན་ཅིང་རང་རྒྱལ་ལ་རྒྱལ་སྲས་སམ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་ནི། རང་དོན་དུ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དང༌། སྒྲ་མེད་པར་ཆོས་སྟོན་པས་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བཤད་པ་ཡིན་ཞེས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ཟབ་བཤད་ལས་གསུངས། འདིས་དངོས་བསྟན་ཕལ་བ་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་གཅོ་བོ་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་བྱས་ན་འགྲིགས་སམ་སྙམ་ཡང་དཔྱད་འཚལ།
translation: Incidental: The second point, which explains that everything from the teaching and listening to the Dharma, up to the attainment of the fruit after practicing, is devoid of true existence and like an illusion, is taught by the three verses beginning with "Teaching the Dharma." The meaning is this: the teacher teaches the Dharma, the student listens correctly, and whatever the Dharma to be taught may be, one reflects correctly upon the meaning of what has been heard. By practicing the path, one attains the four fruits of the śrāvaka, such as the stream-enterer; likewise, one attains the paths of seeing, meditation, and no-more-learning of the pratyekabuddha; likewise, one realizes the enlightenment of the Buddha, the Bhagavat, who is the refuge, protector, and guardian of the three worlds. By the power of practicing the Mahāyāna path—which is endowed with perfect wisdom, skilled in accomplishing one's own and others' benefit, and clear in intellect regarding the methods of the path, thereby uniting method and wisdom—one attains the ultimate fruit, which is non-abiding nirvāṇa. The Tathāgata, the perfectly completed Buddha, has taught that all of these, when examined and analyzed by the reasoning of dependent origination and so forth, are devoid of even the slightest true existence and are empty of truth, like an illusion. The Extensive Mother states: "O sons of the gods, you should view listening to the Dharma from me as being like an illusion and a magical creation," and so forth, up to: "If there were any dharma superior to nirvāṇa, I would also view that as being like an illusion." The Eight Thousand Verse [Prajñāpāramitā] also says: "Then those sons of the gods thought, 'What is the nature of listening to the Dharma from the noble Subhūti that we should seek?' Then, through the power of the Buddha, the venerable Subhūti knew the conceptualizations of those sons of the gods' minds with his own mind and said to them, 'O sons of the gods, you should view listening to the Dharma from me as being like an illusion and a magical creation,' and so forth, up to: 'O sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like an illusion; O sons of the gods, those sentient beings are like a dream,' and so forth, up to: 'The perfectly completed Buddha himself is like an illusion and like a dream,' and so forth, up to: 'Even nirvāṇa is like an illusion and like a dream; what need is there to speak of other dharmas?'" Who, then, is the person capable of learning this meaning as explained with reverence? Those four types of persons do not fear this profound meaning of the ultimate nature just explained. Who are these four? They are the bodhisattva who is learned in the ultimate truth, the pratyekabuddha who is merely at the stage of gathering practice, the non-returning practitioner of the path of preparation, and the noble arhat who has cleared and exhausted the stains of the mind such as the afflictive obstructions and has abandoned doubts regarding the profound meaning of the ultimate nature. The fourth is one who, even if a beginner, is fully embraced by a spiritual friend who is capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom without error, due to having performed superior deeds for the Buddhas of the past. Regarding the phrase "bodhisattva learned in the truth" here, one must understand it as referring to a pratyekabuddha in the actual sense, as the basis is explicitly taught as a pratyekabuddha. The explanation in the Eight Thousand Verse [Prajñāpāramitā] and other texts that a pratyekabuddha is called a "bodhisattva" or "son of the Victor" is because they are called "bodhisattva" for attaining enlightenment for their own benefit, and "great being" (mahāsattva) for teaching the Dharma without words, as stated in the extensive explanations of the perfection of wisdom. I wonder if it is acceptable to interpret the explicitly taught "ordinary" as the pratyekabuddha and the "primary" as the bodhisattva, though this requires further investigation.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
translation: If one asks, "Having thus indicated the basis, is it the case that a bodhisattva trains in the manner of knowing the path of the pratyekabuddhas?"—a bodhisattva is skilled in accomplishing the purposes of those of the three lineages and in practicing the paths of the three vehicles. Having realized all phenomena as empty of true existence and free from conceptual proliferation, they ultimately establish the manner of the single vehicle. Such a person, who engages in the perfection of wisdom—which is the realization of non-conceptualization, seized by special methods such as great compassion—does not train in the stage that brings about the attainment of a śrāvaka arhat for their own sake. Nor do they train in the stage that brings about the attainment of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha who realizes the conditions. Rather, for the sake of attaining the omniscience that lacks nothing in terms of the purposes of the three lineages, they train in accordance with the Dharma from which all buddhas have departed and will depart.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
translation: Training in the path by way of focusing on omniscience and not apprehending true existence, and not training through focusing on the inferior vehicle or through attachment to true existence—by realizing that both of these are not established as truly existent, and thus not training in any path of focusing on the inferior vehicle or attachment to true existence—this is the authentic path of training in the knowledge of the path, which is the bodhisattva’s path of knowledge. Thus it is said.

[3-79] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks, "Having thus indicated the basis, is it the case that a bodhisattva trains in the manner of knowing the path of the pratyekabuddhas?"—a bodhisattva is skilled in accomplishing the purposes of those of the three lineages and in practicing the paths of the three vehicles. Having realized all phenomena as empty of true existence and free from conceptual proliferation, they ultimately establish the manner of the single vehicle. Such a person, who engages in the perfection of wisdom—which is the realization of non-conceptualization, seized by special methods such as great compassion—does not train in the stage that brings about the attainment of a śrāvaka arhat for their own sake. Nor do they train in the stage that brings about the attainment of the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha who realizes the conditions. Rather, for the sake of attaining the omniscience that lacks nothing in terms of the purposes of the three lineages, they train in accordance with the Dharma from which all buddhas have departed and will depart.

heading: **ཞར་བྱུང་།**
translation: That knowledge of the path which is the knowledge of the path of the solitary realizer also does not arise without cause or condition, so its cause, the factors of definite emergence, is taught by the single verse beginning with "The increase of form..." The meaning is this: that in which a bodhisattva does not train and which he abandons is not the training for the sake of grasping—by way of attachment to true existence—the increase or the complete loss, that is, the decrease, in an ultimate sense, of all phenomena of the side of defilement, such as form, or of all phenomena of the side of purification, such as the foundations of mindfulness. Because all these phenomena are by nature pure, they are not apprehended in an ultimate sense as increasing, decreasing, arising, or ceasing. Therefore, one does not train through an application that involves grasping or generating in one's own continuum—out of manifest attachment—any of the diverse aspects of the phenomena from form up to omniscience; rather, one trains by way of not apprehending, such as the factors of definite emergence. For the sake of others, one conventionally grasps and attains even omniscience by way of knowing it to be without nature, and by relying on the practice of the path in which method and wisdom are conjoined, one definitely emerges into—that is, attains—that ultimate state of Buddhahood. This is the way in which bodhisattvas who delight in the qualities of the Great Vehicle train in the path.

[3-83] source:
བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ལམ།བཞི་པ་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། བདེན་དང་བདེན་ལ་བཟོད་པ་དང༌། ནས། ལམ་ཤེས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། །འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེབ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ།
[3-83] translation already produced for this document:
The Path of Seeing of the Bodhisattva. The fourth, the path of seeing of the bodhisattva, is stated in the *Ornament* as: "Patience toward the truths and the truths, up to the moment of the knowledge of the path." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries.

[3-84] source:
མཚན་ཉིད།དང་པོ་ནི། རང་རྒྱུད་ལྡན་གྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་སྟོང་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་བདེན་པ་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད།
[3-84] translation already produced for this document:
The definition. First, the definition of the Mahayana path of seeing is: a Mahayana clear realization of the truths, which is seized by the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness within the continuum of a person who possesses that continuum.

[3-85] source:
དབྱེ་བ།གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་དང༌། རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཡེ་ཤེས་གཉིས། དམིགས་པ་དང་ལྡོག་པའི་ཕྱེ་ན་ཤེས་བཟོད་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཡོད།
[3-85] translation already produced for this document:
The divisions. Second, if divided, there are two: the wisdom of meditative equipoise and the wisdom of subsequent attainment. When distinguished by way of their objects and aspects, there are sixteen moments of patience and knowledge.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: The direct explanation. First, this is indicated by two verses, beginning with "Form is not the perfection of wisdom." The meaning is: what is the nature of the perfection of wisdom that has become the essence of the path of seeing? Form is not one with the perfection of wisdom, which is the subject that realizes its own mode of existence, because they are distinct. There is no perfection of wisdom—the subject of form—that is distinct in essence or exists as distinct in an ultimate sense, because it is not perceived as such. Likewise, the aggregate of consciousness, and the aggregates of perception, feeling, volition, and compositional factors are not one with wisdom, nor do they exist in a manner where the perfection of wisdom—the subject—is distinct in essence, because they are not established as one, distinct, or as object and subject in an ultimate sense. This dharmadhātu, which has become the object of the wisdom of meditative equipoise of the Mahayana path of seeing, is, in the view of that non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise, the suchness of a non-affirming negation that is free from all conventional marks and dualistic conceptual elaborations. It is similar to the designation of the "element of space" (ākāśadhātu) in relation to the mere exclusion of tactile contact, because there is not even an atom of dualistic phenomena such as oneness or distinctness.

[3-86] source:
ས་མཚམས།གསུམ་པ་ནི། མཐོང་ལམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་དེ་ཕན་ཡོན་གྱི་སྒོ་ནས་སྟོན་པ་ལ་དངོས་དང་། འཕྲོས་དོན་གཉིས།
[3-86] translation already produced for this document:
The boundaries. Third, it exists only on the path of seeing. Regarding the explanation of such a Mahayana path of seeing by way of its benefits, there are two: the direct explanation and the incidental meaning.

heading: **དངོས།**
translation: As it is said, "The perfection of wisdom should be sought in the chapter on Subhūti of the Mother Sutra," and in that regard, "Kausika, the perfection of wisdom should not be sought in form, nor should it be sought apart from form, because those phenomena have a single characteristic, which is the characteristic of having no characteristic," and so forth, as has been taught. This verse specifically singles out and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths. As for the general teaching on the aspects of the four truths, among the sixteen aspects such as impermanence that are the objects of the Mahayana path of seeing, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu, which is empty of being established as a self of phenomena or a self of persons; it is without beginning or end, and because it is not limited by directions or boundaries, it is infinite. Regarding the nature of the truth of the origin, which is the cause that produces the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings, it is also infinite because of the equality of the dharmadhātu, which is empty of true existence. Just as the "element of space" is posited in relation to the mere exclusion of tactile contact, the nature of the dharmadhātu of the truth of cessation, where obscurations have been exhausted, is likewise infinite.

As it is said, "The perfection of wisdom should be sought in the chapter on Subhūti of the Mother Sutra," and in that regard, "Kausika, the perfection of wisdom should not be sought in form, nor should it be sought apart from form, because those phenomena have a single characteristic, which is the characteristic of having no characteristic," and so forth, as has been taught. This verse specifically singles out and teaches the aspect of the truth of suffering from among the four truths. As for the general teaching on the aspects of the four truths, among the sixteen aspects such as impermanence that are the objects of the Mahayana path of seeing, the nature or essence of the truths of suffering is the dharmadhātu, which is empty of being established as a self of phenomena or a self of persons; it is without beginning or end, and because it is not limited by directions or boundaries, it is infinite. Regarding the nature of the truth of the origin, which is the cause that produces the aggregates and so forth of sentient beings, it is also infinite because of the equality of the dharmadhātu, which is empty of true existence. Just as the "element of space" is posited in relation to the mere exclusion of tactile contact, the nature of the dharmadhātu of the truth of cessation, where obscurations have been exhausted, is likewise infinite.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Incidental Meaning: The second, the incidental meaning, is this: If one asks why it is asserted that all phenomena are empty of true existence, it is because all phenomena are merely designated by names. Therefore, it is taught that those who are proceeding to the farther shore of perfect view must utterly destroy the perception of clinging to true existence and meditate. The Guide, the Fully Perfect Buddha, has proclaimed and taught that because of perceiving all phenomena as having a self, one remains here in this place of cyclic existence. By destroying the perception of grasping at a self through the wisdom of individual analysis, and by realizing the non-existence of true existence directly, one acts as the direct antidote to all that is to be abandoned by seeing through the path of seeing, and by completely abandoning it through the path of liberation, one proceeds to the farther shore of perfect abandonment.

[3-89] translation already produced for this document:
The wisdom that knows the two truths, the worldly conventional truth and the ultimate truth, which is the truth of the path, is also infinite because it is empty of a self, for all phenomena are of one taste in being empty of true existence.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Therefore, those bodhisattvas on the path of seeing who have attained such a view, which is free from all perceptions of grasping at true existence, abide in the Buddha’s word that teaches, for instance, that they will not turn back in this life, will remember their future births, and, having traversed the stages and paths, will attain buddhahood under such and such a name. If one asks, "Since there is the practice of the path and so forth, does that not mean there is inherent existence?"—if the Sugata, the teacher who has become a valid authority, were to proclaim even for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges that sentient beings exist, it would still be the case that, because they have been unborn by nature from the very beginning and are pure, with no defilements having entered their nature, sentient beings could not possibly exist in an ultimate sense or arise by way of their own nature. Therefore, the direct realization of the meaning of being unborn by nature is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which constitutes the essence of the path of seeing.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: The practice of the path of seeing is taught by way of an example, stating that one will attain the prophecy of the Tathāgata. The Victorious Śākyasiṃha, who has conquered the enemy of the four māras, spoke thus: "At the time when I, the teacher Śākyamuni, was speaking in accordance with this supreme perfection of wisdom, which constitutes the essence of the path of seeing, the supreme being of old, Dīpaṃkara, prophesied to me, 'Young Brahmin, in a future time, you will become a buddha.'" Therefore, those to be trained in later generations should also understand that this is taught in meaning as: "Abiding in this perfection of wisdom, you will be prophesied by the buddhas and will attain complete and perfect buddhahood." Thus, one should apply oneself to the practice of the Great Vehicle path with the persistence of a flowing river. This is the commentary on the second chapter, the chapter on Śakra, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent arising.

[3-91] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, those bodhisattvas on the path of seeing who have attained such a view, which is free from all perceptions of grasping at true existence, abide in the Buddha’s word that teaches, for instance, that they will not turn back in this life, will remember their future births, and, having traversed the stages and paths, will attain buddhahood under such and such a name. If one asks, "Since there is the practice of the path and so forth, does that not mean there is inherent existence?"—if the Sugata, the teacher who has become a valid authority, were to proclaim even for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges that sentient beings exist, it would still be the case that, because they have been unborn by nature from the very beginning and are pure, with no defilements having entered their nature, sentient beings could not possibly exist in an ultimate sense or arise by way of their own nature. Therefore, the direct realization of the meaning of being unborn by nature is the practice of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which constitutes the essence of the path of seeing.

[3-92] translation already produced for this document:
The practice of the path of seeing is taught by way of an example, stating that one will attain the prophecy of the Tathāgata. The Victorious Śākyasiṃha, who has conquered the enemy of the four māras, spoke thus: "At the time when I, the teacher Śākyamuni, was speaking in accordance with this supreme perfection of wisdom, which constitutes the essence of the path of seeing, the supreme being of old, Dīpaṃkara, prophesied to me, 'Young Brahmin, in a future time, you will become a buddha.'" Therefore, those to be trained in later generations should also understand that this is taught in meaning as: "Abiding in this perfection of wisdom, you will be prophesied by the buddhas and will attain complete and perfect buddhahood." Thus, one should apply oneself to the practice of the Great Vehicle path with the persistence of a flowing river. This is the commentary on the second chapter, the chapter on Śakra, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent arising.

heading: **མཚན་ཉིད།**
translation: Definition. Regarding the first: the benefit attained through the power of cultivating the Mahayana path of meditation, which serves as the method for attaining one's own [goal], is the definition of the function of the Mahayana path of meditation.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Divisions. Regarding the second, if one divides these, there are six: the function of pacifying pride and the like by bringing the mind under control; the function of regarding all sentient beings as spiritual friends and thus being respectful and bowing to them; the function of overcoming the afflictions such as the three poisons; the function of not being oppressed by the harms of humans and non-humans; the function of accomplishing perfect, complete enlightenment; and the function of the place where the bodhisattva who is the support resides becoming a site of prostration and worship for all beings.

translation: Levels. Regarding the third: it exists from the first level up to the level of a Buddha. Furthermore, because the aspiration for the goal arises upon seeing the fruit, the function of the path of meditation is taught immediately following the path of seeing, without mentioning the path of meditation itself; this is indicated by a single verse beginning with "Perfection of wisdom..." The meaning is: this perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the path of meditation, is that in which the protectors, the fully awakened Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and all the bodhisattva heirs of the Conqueror, at all times, whether in meditative equipoise or subsequent attainment, engage and abide. Any son or daughter of noble family who, with faith and respect, holds this text in their mind and fully understands all its meanings through the wisdom that is the nature of hearing, reflecting, and meditating, will not be harmed by external poisons, weapons, fire, or water. Not only that, but they will also not be harmed by afflictions such as the poison of reifying true existence, the weapon-like hatred, the fire-like desire, or the water-like ignorance. Even if Māra—such as the powerful Dga'-rab-dbang-phyug who creates obstacles to the path—or the army of Māra, or those who are the black associates of Māra’s faction, seek an opportunity, they will not find one, because of the power of the nature of reality and because the Buddhas and bodhisattvas protect, guard, and conceal them as if they were their own beloved children. Here, the phrase "with respect" indicates the function of bowing to all, and in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, the function of the path of meditation is taught by such statements as "Bodhisattva mahāsattvas should be thoroughly disciplined and free of pride."

Divisions. Regarding the second, if one divides these, there are six: the function of pacifying pride and the like by bringing the mind under control; the function of regarding all sentient beings as spiritual friends and thus being respectful and bowing to them; the function of overcoming the afflictions such as the three poisons; the function of not being oppressed by the harms of humans and non-humans; the function of accomplishing perfect, complete enlightenment; and the function of the place where the bodhisattva who is the support resides becoming a site of prostration and worship for all beings.

heading: **རང་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: The path of meditation of firm conviction for one's own benefit. To explain the first of these, the path of meditation of firm conviction for one's own benefit, it is taught through three verses beginning with "Some, the Sugata..." The meaning is that these paths of meditation are taught by way of their benefits. As stated in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "The Buddha does not pass into parinirvāṇa, and the Dharma does not disappear," and "If the body has no bones or blood, how could there be relics?" In the ultimate sense, the Buddha does not pass into parinirvāṇa, nor does the holy Dharma disappear; until the cycle of existence is emptied, the enlightened activity of his body, speech, and mind occurs without effort and spontaneously, without interruption. Although the wisdom-body lacks relics and the like, one should understand the manner in which he manifests inconceivable, miraculous emanations that pervade space, such as displaying the manner of passing into parinirvāṇa and placing relics in the world in accordance with the receptivity of those to be tamed, being skilled in the means of taming them and possessing an inconceivable power of aspiration. Therefore, if someone were to construct a stūpa of the bodily remains containing the essence of relics of a Sugata who has passed into parinirvāṇa, and if that stūpa were made of the seven precious substances—gold, silver, vaiḍūrya, crystal, copper, red pearls, and the essence of stone—and they were to make offerings to it; and if, not just one, but as many such Sugata stūpas as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges were constructed, and with them they filled all the countless and limitless Buddha-fields, and—taking this as an example by way of a complete examination—if all the beings residing in those countless, infinite fields were to do nothing other than trade, agriculture, and the like, and instead, with superior offerings of divine flowers, highly fragrant incense, and marvelous unguents, were to make offerings day and night, at all three times, without attachment, and were to make offerings in that manner for an eon or more than an eon, they would indeed possess immeasurable merit. However, if a being, for the sake of their own perfect benefit, were to generate conviction and write down this text of the Perfection of Wisdom—which completely teaches the means and wisdom, the Mother of the Sugatas, from which arise the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and other supreme qualities of the Guide, the King of Victors—and were to keep it in hand, make offerings to it with flowers and unguents, and pay even a little homage for a short time, then the merit of the former, having constructed such stūpas of the Sugata's bodily remains and making offerings to them, would not even equal a fraction of the merit of the latter, who has written down this sūtra of the Perfection of Wisdom and made offerings to it, not even by the count of hundreds of thousands of millions.

heading: **གཉིས་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: [Meditation on the meaning of the two, the path of meditation.] To demonstrate the second, the meditation on the meaning of the two, it is taught in four verses beginning with "The Victor's wisdom." The meaning is this: This Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, is a great mantra or an unsurpassed mantra because it pacifies the afflictions in the mental continuum of oneself and all others. Regarding this, in general, a mantra refers to that which is capable of pacifying harm from humans and non-humans merely by being uttered by sages who have attained the truth of speech, and although there are ordinary ones, this perfection of wisdom, as previously explained, is a great and unsurpassed mantra. It is called the "mantra equal to the unequalled" because, by relying upon it, one becomes equal to the unequalled—the Buddha—or because one attains Buddhahood. This is because it pacifies all phenomena belonging to the suffering of the body, such as illness, and mental grief, such as being separated from what is loved, for the immeasurable and manifold realms of sentient beings, and because it causes the attainment of Buddhahood. Those Buddhas who have passed away in the past, and those who currently live and dwell as protectors of the world in the ten directions, have also trained in this mantra equal to the unequalled and have become unsurpassed kings of physicians who dispel the sins, obscurations, suffering, and illnesses of all sentient beings.

heading: **གཉིས་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: When one is fully seized by the wisdom that realizes the three—the agent, the action, and the object—as devoid of true existence, then generosity and the rest become perfections, and the ultimate fruit, the dharmakāya, is accomplished. For example, just as a universal monarch always travels along a certain path, and other kings also travel along that very path and pay homage, and just as the precious wheel and the rest—the seven precious royal attributes and the fourfold gathering of the army—all travel along without ever separating from him due to the power of his merit, in the same way, wherever in the continuum of a person and in whatever stage of the paths and levels this Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, exists or proceeds, from that very point all the paths comprised of the accumulations of merit and wisdom—such as love, compassion, and the mind of enlightenment—and all the qualities of the Buddha-fruit also proceed and are attained. Therefore, a supreme being who seeks unsurpassed enlightenment should have faith in and aspiration for this Mother, the perfection of wisdom. This is the commentary on the third chapter, which concerns the holding of the immeasurable benefits of the perfection of wisdom and the paying of homage to the stūpa, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: **གཞན་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: The Path of Meditation on the Intention for the Benefit of Others. The third section, which teaches the path of meditation on the intention for the benefit of others, explains the meaning of the nine verses beginning with "The Victorious One [said to] Śakra." The Blessed One, having conquered the four māras, placed before Śakra, the lord of gods who possesses the splendor of a hundred ordinary gods, all the Buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges, filled to the brim and overflowing with the relics of the Victorious Ones. When asked to choose between these and a volume of the Perfection of Wisdom, the reply given to the inquiry was: "If there were Buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand in the river Ganges, and all those fields were filled to the brim and overflowing with the relics of the Victorious Ones, I, the lord of gods, would choose this very Perfection of Wisdom written in a volume."

translation: Why would one choose the volume of the Perfection of Wisdom? It is not that I, Śakra, lack respect or faith in the relics; I have the utmost respect for them. However, the reason for choosing the Perfection of Wisdom is that such a perfection of wisdom thoroughly encompasses and permeates all paths, and by relying upon it, those very relics of the Victorious One become worthy of being honored and worshipped by all the beings of the world. Just as ministers and others who rely upon a king are themselves honored and receive service from others, the relics of the Buddha, which possess immeasurable qualities, are established as such by relying upon the perfection of wisdom.

The Path of Meditation on the Intention for the Benefit of Others. The third section, which teaches the path of meditation on the intention for the benefit of others, explains the meaning of the nine verses beginning with "The Victorious One [said to] Śakra." The Blessed One, having conquered the four māras, placed before Śakra, the lord of gods who possesses the splendor of a hundred ordinary gods, all the Buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges, filled to the brim and overflowing with the relics of the Victorious Ones. When asked to choose between these and a volume of the Perfection of Wisdom, the reply given to the inquiry was: "If there were Buddha-fields as numerous as the grains of sand in the river Ganges, and all those fields were filled to the brim and overflowing with the relics of the Victorious Ones, I, the lord of gods, would choose this very Perfection of Wisdom written in a volume."

heading: **གཞན་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: If one were to think, "Although it came about through the power of the perfection of wisdom, since the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa and is now devoid of such activity, the relics are not worthy of being worshipped," then to establish that they are worthy by way of an analogy: A wish-fulfilling jewel, which is endowed with all qualities such as granting what is desired and is of immeasurable value, is worthy of being honored in whatever container—such as a casket, a box, or a reliquary—it is placed or kept. Even if that jewel is removed from that container, one still feels great joy toward the casket that previously held it, thinking, "This is different from others because it is a container that held a precious jewel," and the fact that the container attained such qualities is due to the power of that precious jewel.

Why would one choose the volume of the Perfection of Wisdom? It is not that I, Śakra, lack respect or faith in the relics; I have the utmost respect for them. However, the reason for choosing the Perfection of Wisdom is that such a perfection of wisdom thoroughly encompasses and permeates all paths, and by relying upon it, those very relics of the Victorious One become worthy of being honored and worshipped by all the beings of the world. Just as ministers and others who rely upon a king are themselves honored and receive service from others, the relics of the Buddha, which possess immeasurable qualities, are established as such by relying upon the perfection of wisdom.

heading: **གཞན་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: In the same way, through the qualities of the supreme precious perfection of wisdom, even though the Victor has passed into parinirvāṇa, the relics—which are like its container—have attained immeasurable qualities, such as being worshipped by others and eliminating the obscurations and misdeeds of sentient beings. Therefore, for that reason, any bodhisattva who rejoices in, aspires to, and wishes to fully grasp the immeasurable qualities of the Victor for the sake of others should write down this perfection of wisdom, and should hold, bind, and take it up; for this is the sole gateway to being liberated from all the bonds and obscurations of grasping at characteristics.

If one were to think, "Although it came about through the power of the perfection of wisdom, since the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa and is now devoid of such activity, the relics are not worthy of being worshipped," then to establish that they are worthy by way of an analogy: A wish-fulfilling jewel, which is endowed with all qualities such as granting what is desired and is of immeasurable value, is worthy of being honored in whatever container—such as a casket, a box, or a reliquary—it is placed or kept. heading: **གཞན་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: If one asks, "Since there are other perfections such as generosity, why is the perfection of wisdom alone made the primary focus and established as the three aspirations?" then, in order to show the reason for that, it is said: Because one must practice generosity by way of grasping it through the wisdom that realizes the non-apprehension of the three spheres—the object to be given, the giver, and the recipient—the phenomenon that precedes the perfection of generosity is wisdom; and likewise, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration must also be preceded by wisdom.

In the same way, through the qualities of the supreme precious perfection of wisdom, even though the Victor has passed into parinirvāṇa, the relics—which are like its container—have attained immeasurable qualities, such as being worshipped by others and eliminating the obscurations and misdeeds of sentient beings. Therefore, for that reason, any bodhisattva who rejoices in, aspires to, and wishes to fully grasp the immeasurable qualities of the Victor for the sake of others should write down this perfection of wisdom, and should hold, bind, and take it up; for this is the sole gateway to being liberated from all the bonds and obscurations of grasping at characteristics.

heading: **གཞན་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: Why is it that all virtuous phenomena, such as generosity, when bound by the grasping of characteristics and tainted by the stains of inferior mental engagement, fall into cyclic existence or the extreme of peace and are thus wasted? Because one does not wish for them to be wasted in that way, one dedicates them to unsurpassed, perfect awakening, and through the perfection of wisdom—which is the wisdom that realizes non-apprehension—one fully grasps generosity and the rest as the path of the utterly pure perfection of wisdom. Thus, this perfection of wisdom demonstrates the singular method of the path, wherein all virtuous phenomena, such as generosity, are unified as the cause of buddhahood. For example, in the Jambudvīpa, there are thousands of millions of distinct trees, such as sandalwood and agarwood, which possess a great variety of forms, such as diverse colors, shapes, scents, branches, fruits, leaves, and flowers. Yet, regarding their shadows, they are merely designated by the name of being the "shadow of a tree"; the shadows themselves do not possess the diverse colors, scents, and so forth, that the trees have, nor do the shadows exist in and of themselves as the distinct varieties of the individual trees. In the same way, these five perfections of the Victor, such as generosity, also only attain the name of "perfection" and become supramundane perfections when they are grasped by the wisdom that realizes the non-apprehension of the three spheres; and this occurs through the power of this perfection of wisdom.

heading: **གཞན་དོན་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: Knowing that the abandonment of the faults of artificiality through these three types of conviction is what constitutes familiarization, and in order to abandon that artificiality, the text demonstrates the characteristics of an artificial perfection of wisdom by way of what follows: "If a bodhisattva, while not yet truly understanding the profound meaning of the Mother—the meaning of emptiness—as it is, and while clinging to these five aggregates—namely, form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness—as being true, teaches them as being impermanent, suffering, and lacking a personal self, and so on, and speaks of and meditates upon this as the perfection of wisdom, that is a mere semblance of the perfection of wisdom, or an artificial perfection of wisdom." This is because it merely indicates a path that takes the elaborations of conventional grasping as its object of focus. Those learned ones who have realized the meaning of the actual state of things without error will always teach and uphold the meaning of the scriptural teachings of the perfection of wisdom sutras and the like without error; they will never cause the essence of the teachings to degenerate or perish.

translation: Having thus shown that the semblance of the perfection of wisdom is to be abandoned, the text explains how to train in the authentic perfection of wisdom by way of the reverse approach: "When one does not apprehend form as being truly existent, and likewise does not apprehend feeling, does not apprehend perception as being truly existent, does not apprehend consciousness, and also does not apprehend volition as being truly existent, but thoroughly understands that all phenomena of cyclic existence and transcendence—characterized by the nature and specific attributes of form and so on, such as impermanence—are empty in the manner of being unborn by nature, and teaches others in that way, this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, the authentic perfection of wisdom."

[3-118] translation already produced for this document:
Knowing that the abandonment of the faults of artificiality through these three types of conviction is what constitutes familiarization, and in order to abandon that artificiality, the text demonstrates the characteristics of an artificial perfection of wisdom by way of what follows: "If a bodhisattva, while not yet truly understanding the profound meaning of the Mother—the meaning of emptiness—as it is, and while clinging to these five aggregates—namely, form, perception, feeling, volition, and consciousness—as being true, teaches them as being impermanent, suffering, and lacking a personal self, and so on, and speaks of and meditates upon this as the perfection of wisdom, that is a mere semblance of the perfection of wisdom, or an artificial perfection of wisdom." This is because it merely indicates a path that takes the elaborations of conventional grasping as its object of focus. Those learned ones who have realized the meaning of the actual state of things without error will always teach and uphold the meaning of the scriptural teachings of the perfection of wisdom sutras and the like without error; they will never cause the essence of the teachings to degenerate or perish.

heading: **མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
source: མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན། བདུན་པ་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། ཤེས་རབ་ཕ་རོལ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ། །ནས། བཀུར་བ་དང་ནི་བསྔགས་པར་འདོད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། རང་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་སུ་གྱུར་པའི་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་བསྒོམས་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དེ། མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན་ཉེར་བདུན་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་སྒོམས་པའི་སྐད་ཅིག་གཉིས་པ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། དེ་ལྟར་མོས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལམ་གོང་མར་འཇུག་ཅིང་སྤྲོ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར། སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྟོད་པ་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་དང་བསྔགས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་མཛད་དོ་ཞེས་སྟོན་པར། ལ་ལས་གཱང་གའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་བདུན་གྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། གང་ཟག་གང་ལ་ལས་གངྒཱའི་ཀླུང་གི་བྱེ་མ་ཇི་སྙེད་ཡོད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་ཞིང་རྣམས་ན་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ཇི་སྙེད་ཅིག་འཁོད་པ་དེ་དག་ཀུན་ཉན་རང་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་ཉིད་ལ་བཀོད་པའམ་བརྟུལ་བ་པས། གང་ཟག་གང་གིས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འདི་ཡི་གེར་བྲིས་ཏེ་སེམས་ཅན་མཆོག་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་གླེགས་བམ་དེ་བྱིན་ན་སྔ་མ་བས་འདི་ནི་བསོད་ནམས་ཆེས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་སོ། །
translation: The Benefits of the Path of Meditation of Resolute Belief. The seventh, the benefits of the path of meditation of resolute belief, is as stated in the *Ornament*: "Regarding the perfection of wisdom... [up to] ...it is desired that they be venerated and praised." The definition of the benefits of the path of meditation of resolute belief is the qualities attained through the power of meditating on the path of meditation of resolute belief, which serves as the method for attaining one's own goal. When divided, there are twenty-seven. The scope extends from the second moment of meditating on the path of meditation of resolute belief up to the stage of a Buddha. To show that the Buddhas offer praise, veneration, and commendation to a Bodhisattva who has such resolute belief, in order to encourage them as they enter the higher paths, the meaning of the seven verses beginning with "Some, [like the sands] of the Ganges..." is as follows: Compared to a person who establishes or settles as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in the fields of the Buddhas into the state of a Hearer or Solitary Realizer Arhat, the person who writes down this perfection of wisdom and gives that volume to a supreme sentient being, a Bodhisattva, possesses merit that is far more superior.

[3-119] translation already produced for this document:
Having thus shown that the semblance of the perfection of wisdom is to be abandoned, the text explains how to train in the authentic perfection of wisdom by way of the reverse approach: "When one does not apprehend form as being truly existent, and likewise does not apprehend feeling, does not apprehend perception as being truly existent, does not apprehend consciousness, and also does not apprehend volition as being truly existent, but thoroughly understands that all phenomena of cyclic existence and transcendence—characterized by the nature and specific attributes of form and so on, such as impermanence—are empty in the manner of being unborn by nature, and teaches others in that way, this is practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom, the authentic perfection of wisdom."

heading: **མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: Why is that? Because the former is for the benefit of a portion of sentient beings, whereas the latter becomes the benefit of all sentient beings. Those supreme beings of speech, the Bodhisattvas, having trained in this path, teach here that all phenomena are by nature empty. Having heard, realized, and meditated upon that meaning of emptiness, those of the Hearer lineage with dull faculties quickly touch and attain the liberation that is complete release from cyclic existence; those of the Solitary Realizer lineage with medium faculties, having seen that meaning, attain the awakening of a Solitary Realizer; and those of the Great Vehicle lineage with sharp faculties, having realized that all phenomena of cyclic existence and nirvana are equal in being empty of true existence, come to touch the awakening of a Buddha.

The Benefits of the Path of Meditation of Resolute Belief. The seventh, the benefits of the path of meditation of resolute belief, is as stated in the *Ornament*: "Regarding the perfection of wisdom... [up to] ...it is desired that they be venerated and praised." The definition of the benefits of the path of meditation of resolute belief is the qualities attained through the power of meditating on the path of meditation of resolute belief, which serves as the method for attaining one's own goal. When divided, there are twenty-seven. The scope extends from the second moment of meditating on the path of meditation of resolute belief up to the stage of a Buddha. To show that the Buddhas offer praise, veneration, and commendation to a Bodhisattva who has such resolute belief, in order to encourage them as they enter the higher paths, the meaning of the seven verses beginning with "Some, [like the sands] of the Ganges..." is as follows: Compared to a person who establishes or settles as many sentient beings as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in the fields of the Buddhas into the state of a Hearer or Solitary Realizer Arhat, the person who writes down this perfection of wisdom and gives that volume to a supreme sentient being, a Bodhisattva, possesses merit that is far more superior.

heading: **མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: To illustrate the example of that which does not arise if the cause is absent: just as in the world it is entirely non-existent and impossible for a trunk or a tree to arise without the proximate cause of a sprout, how could branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits arise from that which lacks a trunk? They do not arise.

heading: **མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: In the same way, if the sprout-like bodhicitta—both relative and ultimate, which is the primary meaning taught in the Mother Sutras—is absent, it is entirely non-existent and impossible in the world for a tree-like Victorious One to arise; and if that is absent, how could Indra, Brahmā, Hearers, and the like arise—being comparable to branches, leaves, and so forth, which are the fruits of having practiced the virtues and the path taught by the Buddha’s Dharma—since there would be no cause?

Why is that? Because the former is for the benefit of a portion of sentient beings, whereas the latter becomes the benefit of all sentient beings. Those supreme beings of speech, the Bodhisattvas, having trained in this path, teach here that all phenomena are by nature empty. Having heard, realized, and meditated upon that meaning of emptiness, those of the Hearer lineage with dull faculties quickly touch and attain the liberation that is complete release from cyclic existence; those of the Solitary Realizer lineage with medium faculties, having seen that meaning, attain the awakening of a Solitary Realizer; and those of the Great Vehicle lineage with sharp faculties, having realized that all phenomena of cyclic existence and nirvana are equal in being empty of true existence, come to touch the awakening of a Buddha.

translation: In the same way, if in this world realm there were no scriptural teachings and bodhicitta—which is like the Naga Lord and possesses the essence of emptiness and compassion—how could there arise in this world the stream of wisdom that brings about the benefits and happiness originating from the power of the Sugatas and that serves to eliminate the obscurations of negative karma? Therefore, one should know that generating within one’s own continuum the two types of precious bodhicitta—which is the sole root and source of all the qualities of the path and fruit of the Great Vehicle—and exerting oneself in the methods to ensure it does not degenerate but rather increases and expands further and further, is the root of all excellence.

To demonstrate through the method of negation that without bodhicitta those results do not exist: for example, if the great Naga Lord in Lake Anavatapta were not to exist, how could the rivers such as the Ganges, which arise through his power, flow here in Jambudvīpa? heading: **མོས་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་ཕན་ཡོན།**
translation: For instance, if in this world realm all the various light-emitting creatures—such as stars, lamps, and fireflies that dispel darkness and make forms visible—were to emit their lights all at once to illuminate the directions, the emergence of a single ray from the sun’s orb would be far more excellent and supreme; indeed, the other lights of the various illuminators, such as stars, would not even be able to compare to a mere fraction of the sun’s light. In the same way, śrāvakas and others cannot compare to the qualities of a bodhisattva. Therefore, one should know that the praise and commendation bestowed upon bodhisattvas by the Buddhas is well-founded. This is the commentary on the fifth chapter, the chapter on the enumeration of merit, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

In the same way, if in this world realm there were no scriptural teachings and bodhicitta—which is like the Naga Lord and possesses the essence of emptiness and compassion—how could there arise in this world the stream of wisdom that brings about the benefits and happiness originating from the power of the Sugatas and that serves to eliminate the obscurations of negative karma? It would not arise. If there were no such stream of wisdom, there would be no increase in the qualities of the grounds and paths, such as the perfection of generosity; if those were absent, the three fruits of awakening would not exist, and the immeasurable qualities of a Buddha, such as the ten powers, which are like an ocean of abandoned and realized qualities, would also not exist. Therefore, one should know that generating within one’s own continuum the two types of precious bodhicitta—which is the sole root and source of all the qualities of the path and fruit of the Great Vehicle—and exerting oneself in the methods to ensure it does not degenerate but rather increases and expands further and further, is the root of all excellence.

heading: **རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
source: རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་སྒོམ་ལམ། སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལྟར། རྒྱན་དུའང་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ་། བརྒྱད་པར་གསུངས་ཀྱང་དོན་ལ་འགལ་བ་མེད་པས་འདིར་དེ་ལས་གོ་རིམ་བཟློག་སྟེ་བརྒྱད་པ་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་སྒོམ་ལམ་བསྟན་པས། དེ་ཉིད་སྟོན་པར་རྒྱན་ལས། ཐབས་དང་མི་དམིགས་པ་དག་གིས། །ནས། འདིར་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་པའི་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་བྱུང༌། རང་གཞན་གང་རུང་གི་དགེ་རྩ་ལ་དགའ་བ་བསྒོམ་པའི་སྒྲ་དོན་འདྲེས་རུང་དུ་འཛིན་པའི་རྟོགས་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་རྗེས་ལ་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རངས་སྒོམས་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན། རང་དང་གཞན་གྱི་དགེ་རྩ་ལ་དགའ་བ་བསྒོམ་པའི་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་སྒོམ་ལམ་གཉིས་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ས་དང་པོ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་ཡོད། བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་བསྔོ་བྱའི་དགེ་རྩ་དེ་གོང་འཕེལ་དུ་བྱེད་པ་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་ལ་རག་ལས་པས་ཐོག་མར་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རངས་སྒོམ་ལམ་སྟོན་པར། ཉན་ཐོས་ཚོགས་རྣམས་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་རང་དོན་དུ་ཇི་སྙེད་པའི་སྦྱིན་པ་གཏོང་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་དགེ་བ་དང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་དང་བསྒོམ་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་དང་རབ་ཏུ་ལྡན་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བརྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའང་སྐྱེ་འཕགས་ཀུན་གྱི་དགེ་རྩ་ཐམས་ཅད་མི་དམིགས་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་བསྔོ་བའི་ཐབས་མཁས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་གི་སེམས་སྐད་ཅིག་གཅིག་བསྐྱེད་པ་ལ། ཉན་ཐོས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོས་དེའི་ཆ་ཤས་སུ་གཏོགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་ཆར་ཡང་མི་ཕོད་དེ་ཉན་ཐོས་རྣམས་ནི་ཐབས་ཤེས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་མི་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཞེས་པའོ །
translation: The path of meditation on rejoicing, like the *Śatasāhasrikā* and so forth, is also the path of meditation on dedication in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra*. Although it is taught in the eighth [chapter], there is no contradiction in meaning, so here the order is reversed and the path of meditation on rejoicing is taught as the eighth. To teach this, a verse appears in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* beginning with "By means of skill and non-observation..." and ending with "...is stated here." The realization that includes the understanding of the sound and meaning of cultivating joy in the roots of virtue of oneself or others, combined with the Mahāyāna, is the definition of the path of meditation on rejoicing. In terms of division, there are two: the path of meditation on rejoicing in the roots of virtue of oneself, and the path of meditation on rejoicing in the roots of virtue of others. Its scope extends from the first ground to the end of the continuum. Since the increase of the roots of virtue to be dedicated to unsurpassed awakening depends on rejoicing, the path of meditation on rejoicing is taught first. The meaning of the single verse beginning with "The assemblies of śrāvakas..." is as follows: Even if the assemblies of śrāvakas generate a great hundredfold collection of merit, which is fully endowed with roots of virtue arising from giving, morality, and meditation practiced for their own benefit, they cannot compare to even a fraction of a single moment of a bodhisattva’s mind of rejoicing, which is seized by the wisdom that realizes the roots of virtue of all ordinary and noble beings as unobservable, and by the special skillful means of dedicating them to unsurpassed awakening. This is because śrāvakas do not possess such special skillful means and wisdom.

དཔེར་ན་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་འདི་ན་མུན་པ་སེལ་ཞིང་གཟུགས་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་པའི་འོད་རྒྱུ་སྐར་དང་སྒྲོན་མེ་དང་མེ་ཁྱེར་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྲོག་ཆགས་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་ཀུན་གྱིས་ཕྱོགས་རྣམས་སྣང་བར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འོད་རྣམས་གཅིག་ཆར་དུ་ཕྱུང་བ་པས། ཉི་མའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་གྱི་འོད་ཟེར་གཅིག་པུ་བྱུང་བ་ཆེས་ཁྱད་པར་དུ་འཕགས་ཤིང་མཆོག་ཏུ་གྱུར་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱུ་སྐར་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སྣང་བྱེད་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་འོད་གཞན་རྣམས་ཀུན་གྱི་ཉི་མའི་འོད་ཀྱི་ཆ་ཤས་སུ་གཏོགས་པ་ཙམ་གྱི་ཆར་ཡང་མི་ཕོད་དོ། །དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ཉན་ཐོས་ལ་སོགས་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཆར་མི་ཕོད་དོ། ། དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བསྟོད་བསྔགས་མཛད་པའང་དོན་ལ་གནས་པར་ཤེས་པར་བྱའོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་གྲངས་ཀྱི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་ལྔ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ།། །།

For instance, if in this world realm all the various light-emitting creatures—such as stars, lamps, and fireflies that dispel darkness and make forms visible—were to emit their lights all at once to illuminate the directions, the emergence of a single ray from the sun’s orb would be far more excellent and supreme; indeed, the other lights of the various illuminators, such as stars, would not even be able to compare to a mere fraction of the sun’s light. In the same way, śrāvakas and others cannot compare to the qualities of a bodhisattva. Therefore, one should know that the praise and commendation bestowed upon bodhisattvas by the Buddhas is well-founded. This is the commentary on the fifth chapter, the chapter on the enumeration of merit, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: **བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
source: བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། དགུ་པ་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བ་ཁྱད་པརཅན། །ནས། བསོད་ནམས་ཆེ་འབྱུང་བདག་ཉིད་དོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། རང་གཞན་གང་རུང་གི་དགེ་རྩ་རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་ཏུ་བསྒྱུར་བར་བྱེད་པའི་སྒྲ་དོན་འདྲེས་རུང་དུ་འཛིན་པའི་རྟོགས་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་རྗེས་ལ་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་ན། ཡོངས་སུ་བསྔོ་བ་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གྱི་སྒོམ་ལམ་དང་། མི་དམིག་པའི་རྣམ་པ་ཅན་གྱི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། ཕྱིན་ཅི་མ་ལོག་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་ཅན་གྱི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། དབེན་པའི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བསོད་ནམས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་དྲན་པའི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པའི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། མཚན་མ་མེད་པའི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་རྗེས་སུ་གནང་བའི་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། ཁམས་གསུམ་དུ་མ་གཏོགས་པའིབསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ། བསོད་ནམས་ཆེན་པོ་འབྱུང་བའི་བསྔོ་བ་ཆུང་ངུའི་སྒོམ་ལམ་དང༌། བསོད་ནམས་ཆེན་པོའི་འབྲིང་གི་བསྔ་ོབ་སྒོམ་ལམ། བསོད་ནམས་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆེན་པོའི་བསྔ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ་དང་བཅུ་གཉིས་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་དང་པོ་ནས་བཅུ་པའི་བར་རོ། །སྔར་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་གིས་མི་ཟད་པར་སྤེལ་བའི་དགེ་རྩ་དེའང་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་ཁ་བསྒྱུར་བར་བྱེད་པ་བསྔོ་བ་ལ་རག་ལས་པ་ཡིན་པས་ཡི་རང་སྒོས་ལམ་གྱི་འོག་ཏུ་བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་སྟོན་པར། འདས་དུས་སྔོན་གྱི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་བརྒྱད་ཀྱིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན་ནི། བསྐལ་པ་འདས་པའི་དུས་ན་བྱུང་བའི་སྔོན་གྱི་སངས་རྒྱས་བྱེ་བ་ཁྲག་ཁྲིག་མང་པོ་གང་ཞིག །ཞིང་ཁམས་མང་པོ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་བྱེ་བ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་དག་ན་གང་བཞུགས་པའི་འདས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་རྣམས་དང་། གང་ཡང་སྲིད་ཞིའི་མཐའ་ལས་འདས་པའིའི་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་མགོན་པོ་རྣམས་ད་ལྟར་འཚོ་ཞིང་བཞེས་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྔུག་བསྔལ་ཟད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུ་རིན་ཆེན་ཆོས་ཀྱང་སྟོན་བཞིན་དུ་བཞུགས་པ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་དང་པོར་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་མཆོག་ཏུ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་བརྟན་པོར་བསྐྱེད་པ་ནས་བཟུང་སྟེ་མཐུར་ཐུག་མངོན་པར་རྫོགས་པར་སངས་རྒྱས་ནས་གདུལ་བྱ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་འཁོར་བ་ལས་རྣམ་པར་འདྲེན་པ་མཛད་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ནུབ་པའམ་ཟད་པར་གྱུར་བ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་དུས་དེའི་བར་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་དེ་དག་གི་དང་པོ་ཐུགས་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་གང་ཡིན་པ་དང་། སྤྱོད་པ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་དང་བསྡུ་བའི་དངོས་པོ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པའི་རླབས་པོ་ཆེའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་སྟོབས་བཅུ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་མ་འདྲེས་པ་བཅོ་བརྒྱད་ལ་སོགས་པ་གང་ཞིག་ཐོབ་པ་དང་། གང་དག་གཞན་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྲས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་དང་ནི་ཉན་ཐོས་དང་རང་རྒྱལ་དང་བཅས་པ་མདོར་ན་སློབ་པ་དང་མི་སློབ་པའི་གང་ཟག་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་དགེ་བ་ཟག་བཅས་དང་ཟག་པ་མེད་པ་དེ་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་གི་བློས་གཅིག་ཏུ་བསྡུས་ནས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ཡིས་ཕྲག་དོག་སོགས་མེད་པར་བསམ་པ་ཐག་པ་ནས་ཡིད་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བས་རྗེས་སུ་ཡི་རང་བར་བྱ་ཞིང་། བསམ་པ་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་འཁོར་གསུམ་མི་དམིགས་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པར་བྱས་ནས་ནམ་མཁའི་མཐའ་དང་མཉམ་པའི་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རྒྱུ་རུ་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕྱིར་ནི་རང་གཞན་གྱི་དགེ་རྩ་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་བསྔོ་བར་བྱའོ། །
translation: The Path of Meditation of Dedication. To explain the ninth, the path of meditation of dedication, the *Ornament* states: "The special thorough dedication, / ... / Is the nature of the arising of great merit." The path of realization that follows the Great Vehicle, which includes the realization that holds the meaning of the words as being compatible with transforming the roots of virtue of oneself or others into a limb of perfect enlightenment, is the definition of the path of meditation of dedication. Regarding its divisions, there are twelve: the path of meditation of special thorough dedication, the path of meditation of dedication characterized by non-apprehension, the path of meditation of dedication characterized by being non-erroneous, the path of meditation of dedication of seclusion, the path of meditation of dedication that recollects the nature of the Buddha’s collection of merit, the path of meditation of dedication of skill in means, the path of meditation of dedication of signlessness, the path of meditation of dedication permitted by the Buddhas, the path of meditation of dedication not included in the three realms, the path of meditation of minor dedication from which great merit arises, the path of meditation of intermediate dedication of great merit, and the path of meditation of great dedication of great merit. The levels range from the first to the tenth. Since the roots of virtue that were previously increased inexhaustibly through rejoicing also depend upon dedication to be transformed into unsurpassable enlightenment, the path of meditation of dedication is taught after the path of rejoicing. To explain this, the meaning of the eight verses beginning with "In the past, in times gone by" is as follows: Regarding the many billions of past Buddhas who appeared in the past, those infinite past Buddhas who resided in thousands of billions of boundless realms, and those protectors of the world who have passed beyond the extremes of existence and peace, who are currently living and dwelling and, in order to exhaust the suffering of beings, are teaching the precious Dharma—from the time they first generated the mind for supreme enlightenment and firmly established it in their own continuum, up until they attained complete and perfect buddhahood and led countless beings to be trained out of cyclic existence, the merit of those victors' initial generation of the mind up until the time their holy Dharma disappeared or was exhausted, the roots of virtue of great magnitude such as the six perfections and the four means of gathering, the results such as the ten powers and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha that were attained, and furthermore, all the roots of virtue, both contaminated and uncontaminated, of all the Buddha's sons, the bodhisattvas, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—in short, all individuals, whether learners or non-learners—are to be gathered together by one's own intellect. That bodhisattva should rejoice in them from the depths of their heart with great joy, without jealousy or the like, and having been seized by the wisdom that realizes the mind, the generation of the mind, and the three spheres as non-apprehensible, one should dedicate all those roots of virtue of oneself and others for the sake of attaining unsurpassable great enlightenment as a cause for accomplishing the benefit of beings who are equal to the limits of space.

heading: **བསྔོ་བ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: Having thus explained the method of dedication in detail, it is taught in order to summarize: since the method of pure and impure dedication has been explained previously, one should learn to dedicate correctly by understanding the faults and virtues in this way. How is this done? The Victors, the perfectly complete Buddhas, have realized and understood without error the rejoicing, the virtues to be dedicated, and the methods of dedication, and so forth. Through their wisdom, they understand what the nature or form of dedication is in conventional terms, what the infallible results that arise from it are and what they are like, and what the characteristics of those phenomena are in terms of ultimate non-conceptualization. Having understood the reality of these as it is, they perform rejoicing and dedication. By thinking, "I too shall perform such rejoicing and dedication in accordance with them," one performs a dedication that, even if one is not personally skilled in the method of dedication, is a perfectly pure dedication because it is performed in accordance with the method of dedication of the Victors. This is as stated in the *Bhadracaryāpraṇidhāna*: "Just as the heroic Mañjuśrī realized..." and so forth. To show the result of such dedication: if one dedicates to great enlightenment by being seized by the wisdom that realizes all one's own and others' merit as non-conceptual, it is a perfectly pure dedication, like fine food without poison. Its result is not abandoning the Buddha, or rather, attaining it, and it is the correct expression of the Great Vehicle teachings spoken by the Victors.
