source: སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།བཅུ་བ་སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། དེ་ཡི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མཆོག །ནས། གཏོད་པར་བྱེད་པ་དོན་ཆེན་ཉིད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། ཟག་པ་མེད་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་རྗེས་ལ་མངོན་རྟོགས་གང་ཞིག །རང་གི་ཐོབ་བྱར་གྱུར་པའི་རྟོགས་པ་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་ལག་རྗེས་འཇོག་བྱེད་དེ། སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་དེའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་དང་། ཤེར་ཕྱིན་གྱི་སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་གྱི་མཆོག་ཉིད་དང་། སྒོམ་ལམ་དེས་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཏུ་འདུ་མི་བྱེད་པ་དང་། སྒོམ་ལམ་དེས་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་གྲུབ་ཀྱི་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པར་གཏོད་པ་དང་། སྒོམ་ལམ་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པའི་དོན་ཆེན་པོ་ཉིད་དང་ལྔ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ས་དང་པོ་ནས་བཅུ་པའི་བར་ན་ཡོད། དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་སྟོན་པར། དམུས་ལོང་དམིགས་པུ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིག་བཅད་བཞིས་སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ་ལྔའི་ནང་གི་མཆོག་ཉིད་ཅེས་པ་དེ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། དེའང་དཔེར་ན་མིག་མེད་པའི་དམུས་ལོང་ལམ་དུ་འཁྲིད་མཁན་གྱི་དམིགས་པུའམ་ལོང་ཁྲིད་མེད་པ་བྱེ་བ་ཁྲག་ཁྲིག་རྣམས་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་འདུས་ཀྱང་། གྲོང་ཁྱེར་དུ་འགྲོ་བའི་ལམ་ཡང་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་མི་ཤེས་ན། ལམ་དེར་ཞུགས་ནས་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་འཇུག་པར་ག་ལ་འགྱུར་ཏེ་དེ་ནི་གནས་མེད་དོ། །
translation: Regarding the path of meditation of accomplishment: to demonstrate the path of meditation of accomplishment, the *Ornament* states, "Its supreme essence," through to "the great purpose of establishing." The definition of the path of meditation of accomplishment is: any realization of the Mahayana untainted path that leaves a trace of the ultimate realization that is to be attained by oneself. Regarding its divisions, there are five: the essence of that path of meditation of accomplishment; the supremacy of that path of meditation of accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom; that path of meditation not conceptualizing all phenomena as truly established; that path of meditation establishing all phenomena without apprehension of true existence; and the great purpose of attaining the result of that path of meditation, which is buddhahood. Its scope exists from the first ground up to the tenth. To demonstrate such a path of meditation of accomplishment, the four verses beginning with "Like the blind without a guide" teach what is called the supremacy among the five paths of meditation of accomplishment. For example, even if tens of millions of blind people who lack a guide or leader to lead them on the path gather together, if they neither see nor know the path leading to the city, how could they possibly enter that path and reach the city? That is an impossibility.

heading: **སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: In the same way, if one lacks this perfection of wisdom—which is like an eye that realizes the nature of reality—then the five perfections, such as generosity, are like the blind; they are not embraced by the wisdom that constitutes the essence of the accomplishment that acts as a guide to lead one to the higher grounds, such as Pramuditā, and because they lack that companion, they are unable to reach the city of perfect enlightenment. At the time when the paths of generosity and so forth are well-embraced by the wisdom that realizes the three spheres are devoid of true existence, then those practices of generosity and the rest find their eyes, receive the name "perfection," and easily proceed to or attain the city of omniscience.

[3-136] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the path of meditation of accomplishment: to demonstrate the path of meditation of accomplishment, the *Ornament* states, "Its supreme essence," through to "the great purpose of establishing." The definition of the path of meditation of accomplishment is: any realization of the Mahayana untainted path that leaves a trace of the ultimate realization that is to be attained by oneself. Regarding its divisions, there are five: the essence of that path of meditation of accomplishment; the supremacy of that path of meditation of accomplishment of the perfection of wisdom; that path of meditation not conceptualizing all phenomena as truly established; that path of meditation establishing all phenomena without apprehension of true existence; and the great purpose of attaining the result of that path of meditation, which is buddhahood. Its scope exists from the first ground up to the tenth. To demonstrate such a path of meditation of accomplishment, the four verses beginning with "Like the blind without a guide" teach what is called the supremacy among the five paths of meditation of accomplishment. For example, even if tens of millions of blind people who lack a guide or leader to lead them on the path gather together, if they neither see nor know the path leading to the city, how could they possibly enter that path and reach the city? That is an impossibility.

heading: **སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: As for the analogy for these, it is like a painting of a king or similar figure: even if all other parts are completely finished, if it lacks just one eye—if that is missing—then as long as the eye has not been painted, the painting is not complete, and one does not receive the wages or reward. Therefore, once one has gained certainty in the way that this very wisdom, which realizes emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, is the supreme essence of the path of the Great Vehicle, those of the lineage of the supreme vehicle should make that excellent path manifest in their own continuums through study, reflection, and meditation. At the time when one examines and investigates the conditioned phenomena of the three realms, the unconditioned phenomena of emptiness, the virtues embraced by the white aspiration for enlightenment, and the virtues of the Hearer continuum down to the lesser phenomena, using the wisdom that investigates the nature of reality, and thereby dismantles the objects of apprehension of grasping at characteristics, realizing that not even an atom of them is observed or exists as established from its own side—at that time, one is counted as having what is called the perfection of wisdom. This is similar to how space is merely the negation of obstruction and, because it lacks any form that constitutes its own essence, it does not depend on anything at all.

[3-137] translation already produced for this document:
In the same way, if one lacks this perfection of wisdom—which is like an eye that realizes the nature of reality—then the five perfections, such as generosity, are like the blind; they are not embraced by the wisdom that constitutes the essence of the accomplishment that acts as a guide to lead one to the higher grounds, such as Pramuditā, and because they lack that companion, they are unable to reach the city of perfect enlightenment. At the time when the paths of generosity and so forth are well-embraced by the wisdom that realizes the three spheres are devoid of true existence, then those practices of generosity and the rest find their eyes, receive the name "perfection," and easily proceed to or attain the city of omniscience.

heading: **སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: At that time, because it is taught that even the mental attachment to the reality of the dharma-dhātu is erroneous, it is said: If, even though one is seized by skillful means, one is bound by the grasping of characteristics and wanders, thinking, "I shall practice this perfection of wisdom, the mother of the victorious ones," while being attached to the object of emptiness as real; and if one has a mind that is attached to the reality of "liberating many millions of beings who are touched by suffering or tormented by suffering," then that bodhisattva, who fully conceptualizes self and others as truly existing as sentient beings, is called one who has an object of apprehension. Such a practice is not the supreme or authentic practice of the perfection of wisdom. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states, "The perfection of wisdom is to be made manifest," and so forth. Although the perfectly pure path of meditation must be taught after this, as the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states, "Attending to the Buddha, giving, and so forth," one must know the two causes for the arising and non-arising of the perfectly pure path of meditation. Therefore, to teach the cause for its arising first, the meaning of the single verse concerning the bodhisattva and so forth is as follows: Any bodhisattva who, in previous lifetimes, has pleased the Tathāgatas and, while practicing the conduct of a child of the victorious ones, has listened to this profound sūtra of the perfection of wisdom with respect, held it, and practiced it through reflection and so forth—such beings, having been born in this world now, due to the power of their previous imprints and good causes, become expert in the meaning of the perfection of wisdom and free from hesitation or doubt regarding its profound meaning. Upon hearing this sūtra, that person generates the perception of the Teacher, thinking, "I have seen the Teacher," and by that cause, they will quickly realize the perfectly pure path of meditation, the great peaceful enlightenment.

heading: **སྒྲུབ་པ་སྒོམ་ལམ།**
translation: To demonstrate the causes for not arising, two verses are spoken, beginning with "In former lives..." The meaning is: If a bodhisattva, while previously practicing the conduct of the heirs of the Victors, has accumulated merit by honoring billions of Buddhas and offering vast provisions, but has not engaged in listening, reflecting, and so forth upon the Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, and lacks faith in it, and has not made the aspiration to realize its meaning, then even if they obtain a human body in the present, upon hearing this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, they are unable to immediately realize its profound meaning. Because of that small-mindedness, they abandon this sutra of the perfection of wisdom and do not uphold it. By abandoning it, they also abandon the Buddha, the Jewel, and, lacking the refuge of the holy Dharma and the companionship of the noble Sangha, they go to the Avīci hell and experience suffering for eons; thus, it is said that the disadvantages are immeasurable. This is what is meant.

translation: Summarizing the meaning of arising and not arising, and providing instruction with examples on how one should train with faith and respect in the Perfection of Wisdom sutra, the author, out of compassion for future disciples, gives this advice: "Because the benefits and disadvantages of having or lacking faith in the Perfection of Wisdom are such, if you desire to touch or attain the supreme wisdom of the Buddhas, you should have faith in this Mother of the Victors and engage in it through listening, reflecting, and meditating." The reason why this is necessary is that, at this time when we have encountered the Buddha’s teachings, which are like an island of precious jewels, and possess the protection of a virtuous friend, we must make our lives meaningful. For example, it would not be right to go to an island of jewels, only to have one's previous trade goods exhausted and, having found no jewels at all, return empty-handed; for there is no greater loss or more wretched method than that. Therefore, those who are fortunate should, upon this basis of leisure, apply themselves with the perseverance of a flowing river to accomplish the two purposes. This concludes the commentary on the seventh chapter, the chapter on the hells, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: **སྤྱིར་བསྟན་པ།**
translation: General Exposition. The first, the general exposition, consists of one line of verse, "The purity of form, and so forth..." The meaning is this: because stains have not entered into the nature of reality, all phenomena included within the aggregates, elements, and sense-sources, such as form, are primordially pure and luminous by nature. However, because they are grasped in a distorted way by the ignorance of grasping at true existence, afflictions such as attachment arise; thus, these are called adventitious stains. As long as one is obscured by grasping at true existence and does not clearly see the nature of reality, form and so forth are described as impure. When the obscuring stains are purified and the nature of reality is clearly seen, the nature of reality of form and so forth is not tainted by stains, and thus they are primordially pure. That purity, and the fact that one’s own way of seeing has become congruent with it, is the reason why the object—the aggregate of form and so forth—is pure of stains, and the subject—the perfection of wisdom or the fruit of the state of a spiritual practitioner, from the path of seeing and the path of liberation up to buddhahood—are both one in meaning. Therefore, because a "purity of the fruit" cannot be established as something separate from that "purity of form and so forth," one should understand that these two cannot be mentally separated and are of one essence. In dependence upon that manner of the purity of the fruit, it is at that time described as the "purity of the object, form." For example, when a cataract or the like appears as falling hairs upon a form, one says the form is not clear, but when the cause of the delusion, the cataract and so forth, is removed, one says the form is clear.

The eleventh, the path of meditation of complete purity, is stated in the *Ornament* as: "The purified result, form and so forth... up to... the path of such is the purified." It is defined as a Mahayana path of realization that is untainted and that establishes the traces of the ultimate abandonment that has become its own object of attainment. This and the path of meditation of accomplishment are identical in meaning, differing only in their conceptual aspects. Its boundaries exist from the first bhūmi up to the tenth bhūmi. heading: **རྣམ་དག་བྱེ་བྲག་འཆད་པ།**
translation:
Explaining the distinctions of purity. Second, regarding the explanation of the distinctions of purity, three lines are spoken, beginning with "The purity of the result and of form." In this regard, the Ornament states:
"Because of the loss of the three—defilements, knowables, and the path—
The purity of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas,
And the bodhisattvas is partial;
The buddha’s is entirely pure."
As stated, the śrāvaka arhat has abandoned only the defilement-obscurations, and the pratyekabuddha arhat, who is like a rhinoceros, has abandoned the defilement-obscurations and a portion of the cognitive-obscurations, namely the conceptualization of grasping; thus, their purity is partial and not absolute purity. However, because the buddha, the noble one, has abandoned the two obscurations without remainder through the path of cessation in his mental continuum, this is absolute purity or ultimate purity. Just as previously explained, the purity of form and the purity of the result are of one essence; likewise, when the stains to be abandoned—which are the share of the uninterrupted path that brings about the attainment of the result, the path of liberation—are purified, the objects thereof, such as form, must also be posited as purified by those very stains of one's own continuum. This is because the perfection of wisdom, which is the subject devoid of the single stain to be negated, or the purity of the result, and the purity of the objects such as form, are inseparable in essence and cannot be conceptually divided as distinct. Similarly, when the nine cycles of the Mahāyāna path of meditation, from the second to the tenth bhūmi, have served as the direct antidote to their respective stains to be abandoned—from the great conceptualization of grasping and fixation down to the subtle—and have abandoned the two obscurations without remainder, the result, which is included by the path of cessation in the buddha’s mental continuum, becomes the entirely pure omniscience. Thus, these three—the ultimate purity of omniscience, the purity of the path of cessation attained as the respective result by the path of learning, and the purity of the phenomena of the basis, such as form, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—merely appear as distinct in conventional reality. In ultimate reality, this is like the space element having no distinctions of different essences; because the naturally pure dharmadhātu is inseparable and cannot be conceptually divided into different essences, for all dharmadhātu is of a single nature. Having thus finished explaining the eleven phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the path, the conclusion of the section is: this is the commentary on the second chapter from the work titled "The Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Reality of Dependent Arising, a Profound Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities."

translation: Knowledge of the Bases. Having thus explained the knowledge of the paths, in order to teach the knowledge of the bases which purifies the knowledge of the paths, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states: "By means of knowledge, [one does not remain] in existence," and so forth, ending with, "Thus, it is asserted as the knowledge of all." The definition of the knowledge of the bases is: a cognition that is conjoined with the wisdom directly realizing selflessness within the continuum of a person possessing their own continuum, and which resides in the lineage of realization of the Lesser Vehicle. There are nine [types of] phenomena that characterize the knowledge of the bases: the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in existence due to knowledge, the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in peace due to compassion, the knowledge of the bases distant from the resultant Mother, the knowledge of the bases near to the resultant Mother, the knowledge of the bases of the discordant side, the application of the knowledge of the bases, the equality of the mode of apprehension of the application, and the path of seeing. Because there are nine, a single verse appears, beginning with "By means of knowledge, [one does not remain] in existence," and so forth, which teaches the first two. The definition of the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in existence due to knowledge is: a cognition of a Great Vehicle Noble Being that resides in the lineage of realization which prevents the extreme of existence in relation to the conventional basis. That and the knowledge of the paths of the Śrāvakas are synonymous. Regarding its divisions, there are three: the Great Vehicle path of seeing, the path of meditation, and the path of no more learning. Its boundaries extend from the Great Vehicle path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. The definition of the knowledge of the paths that does not remain in peace due to compassion is: a cognition of a Noble Being's continuum that resides in the lineage of realization which prevents the extreme of peace in relation to the conventional basis. That and a cognition of a Great Vehicle Noble Being that resides in the lineage of realization of a special method are synonymous. Regarding its divisions, there are three: the Great Vehicle path of seeing, the path of meditation, and the path of no more learning that have become that. Its boundaries are the same as the former.

heading: **ཤེས་པས་སྲིད་ལ་མི་གནས་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས་དང་སྙིང་རྗེའི་ཞིལ་མི་གནས་པའི་ལམ་ཤེས།**
translation: The path of wisdom that does not abide in cyclic existence and the path of compassion that does not abide in peace—in order to explain these two, namely the path of wisdom that does not abide in cyclic existence and the path of compassion that abides in peace, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "How does the hero act?" is as follows: The heroes, the bodhisattvas, who cannot be swayed by the grasping at true existence or the grasping at self-importance, even while acting within the realms of cyclic existence, see the faults of cyclic existence. By abiding in the perfection of wisdom, which is seized by special means and wisdom, they have truly transcended being born into cyclic existence through karma and defilements that are attached to any of the realms of the three worlds of cyclic existence. Yet, even having transcended, they do not abide in the extreme of either cyclic existence or peace, nor do they abide in the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa that is completely liberated from existence like the śrāvakas. Although they have eliminated the karma and defilements that cause one to be born into existence helplessly, they fully demonstrate being born into cyclic existence through the power of compassion and aspiration. As stated in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*: "The noble ones have eradicated the suffering of sickness, aging, and death from the root." Just as this states, although they are free from aging, sickness, and death, they demonstrate the process of passing away for the sake of others, because they are wise ones who possess special means, such as great compassion and the mind of enlightenment, and special wisdom that realizes both existence and peace as empty of true existence. By stating this, it directly teaches the two paths that do not abide in the two extremes of existence and peace, and implicitly teaches the two types of knowledge of the basis: the knowledge of the basis that is far from the resultant Mother [of the Buddhas] due to not being skilled in the means to stop the two extremes of existence and peace, and the knowledge of the basis that is near to the resultant Mother due to being skilled in those means. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* also states: "Bhagavān, the perfection of wisdom does not abide on the near shore, it does not abide on the far shore, and it does not abide in the long space between the two."

translation: The base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother. Fourth, regarding the base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother, it is stated in the Ornament: "Because it is skilled in methods, it is explained as being truly near." That which is a cognition in the continuum of a Great Vehicle Superior residing in the lineage of realization of the Great Vehicle, and which is conjoined with great compassion and the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness, is the definition of the base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother. That and the base-knowledge of the remedy are synonymous. Regarding its boundaries, it exists from the path of seeing of the Great Vehicle up to the stage of a Buddha. The manner in which these two are taught by this sutra is as just explained.

heading: **མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས།**
source: མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས།ལྔ་བ་མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། གཟུགས་སོགས་ཕུང་པོ་སྟེང་ཉིད་དང་།  ནས། མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས།  ཞེས་གསུངས། གཞི་ཤེས་གང་ཞིག །ཐབས་ཤེས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གཉིས་དང་བྲལ་བ་དེ། མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་ཐེག་དམན་འཕགས་པའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱིས་བཅིངས་པའི་གཞི་ཤེས་དོན་གཅིག །ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ནས་ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་མི་སློབ་ལམ་གྱི་བར་ན་ཡོད། དེ་ཉིད་མདོ་འདིས་སྟོན་པར། འགྲོ་བ་འདི་དག་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གསུམ་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། མ་རིགས་པས་རྨོངས་པའི་འགྲོ་བ་འདི་དག་བརྒལ་བར་དཀའ་བའི་མིང་དང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་འདམ་ལ་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་པར་ཆགས་ནས་རྒྱུ་སྐར་འཕུལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གོ་ལའི་རླུང་གི་འཁོར་ལོ་ཡང་དུ་འཁོར་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྲིད་རྩེ་ནས་མནར་མེད་ཀྱི་བར་དུ་འཁོར་བའི་འཁོར་ལོར་འཁྱམས་ཏེ་མ་རིགས་པ་ནས་རྐྱེ་རྒའི་བར་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་ཡན་ལག་བཅུ་གཉིས་འགལ་མེའི་འཁོར་ལོ་ལྟར་ལུ་གུ་རྒྱུད་དུ་འབྱུང་པས་སོ། །འགྲ་ོབ་འཁྲུལ་པར་གྱུར་པ་འདི་དག་འཁོར་བའི་གནས་འདིར་ཚུད་པ་རི་དྭགས་རྣམས་འབྲོས་སུ་མེད་པའི་རྒྱར་ཆུད་པ་དང་འདྲ་བར་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དུ་མས་མནར་ཞིང་ཐར་དཀའ་བར་ཤེས་ནས་བྱང་སེམས་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་འཁོར་བའི་གནས་ལ་ཆགས་པ་མེད་པར་གཞན་དོན་བྱའོ། །
translation: The base-knowledge of the discordant side. Fifth, regarding the base-knowledge of the discordant side, it is stated in the Ornament: "From 'the aggregates such as form' up to 'the discordant side'." What is this base-knowledge? That which is devoid of the two—the special wisdom and the special method—is the definition of the base-knowledge of the discordant side. That and the base-knowledge bound by the apprehension of true existence in the continuum of a Superior of the Lesser Vehicle are synonymous. Regarding its boundaries, it exists from the path of seeing of the Lesser Vehicle up to the path of no-more-learning of the Lesser Vehicle. The meaning of the three lines taught by this sutra to demonstrate this, beginning with "these beings," is as follows: Because these beings, obscured by ignorance, are attached to the true existence of the mire of the five aggregates of name and form, which are difficult to transcend, they wander in the wheel of cyclic existence—from the peak of existence down to the Unrelenting Hell—like a wind-wheel of the spheres that constantly rotates, driven by the stars. Because the twelve links of dependent origination, from ignorance to aging and death, arise in a continuous chain like a wheel of fire. Knowing that these confused beings who have fallen into this place of cyclic existence are like animals caught in an inescapable net, tormented by manifold sufferings and difficult to liberate, Bodhisattvas who are skilled in wisdom and method should work for the benefit of others without attachment to the place of cyclic existence.

The base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother. Fourth, regarding the base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother, it is stated in the Ornament: "Because it is skilled in methods, it is explained as being truly near." That which is a cognition in the continuum of a Great Vehicle Superior residing in the lineage of realization of the Great Vehicle, and which is conjoined with great compassion and the wisdom that directly realizes emptiness, is the definition of the base-knowledge near to the resultant Mother. heading: **གཉེན་པོ་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས།**
source: གཉེན་པོ་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས། དྲུག་པ་མཚན་འཛིན་གྱི་གཉེན་པོས་ཟིན་པ་གཉེན་པོ་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། སྦྱིན་ལ་སོགས་ལ་ངར་འཛིན་མེད། ནས། དེ་ནིབསམ་མི་ཁྱབ་པར་འདོད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། ཐེག་དམན་གྱི་རྟོགས་རིགས་སུ་གནས་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་འཕགས་པའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་མཁྱེན་པ་གང་ཞིག །ཐབས་ཤེས་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པ་དེ། གཉན་པོ་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་ཐེག་ཆེན་འཕགས་པའི་རྒྱུད་ཀྱི་གཞི་ཤེས་དོན་གཅིག །ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། དེ་ཉིད་སྟོན་པར། ཤེས་རབ་ལྡན་པ་མཁའ་ལ་བྱ་བཞིན་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱུ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། དོན་ནི། རྨོངས་པའི་བགྲོ་བ་རི་དྭགས་ཀྱི་རྒྱར་ཆུད་པ་དང་འདྲ་བར་འཁོར་བའི་གནས་འདིར་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཞིང་ཐར་དཀའ་བའི་ཚུལ་ཤེས་པར་བྱས་ནས་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པའི་བརྩེ་བ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་གནས་ལུགས་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཕུད་སོགས་བདེན་པར་འཛིན་པའི་འཁྲུལ་བས་མ་བཅིངས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ནི་བྱ་ནམ་མཁའ་རྒྱུ་ཡང་ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་བྱ་མི་གནས་པ་བཞིན་དུ་འཁོར་བའི་གནས་འདིར་ཆགས་ཞེན་གྱིས་མི་གནས་པར་གཞན་དོན་རྣམ་པར་རྒྱུའོ། །ཞེས་པའོ། །
translation: The remedial class of the knowledge of bases. The sixth, the knowledge of bases of the remedial class, which is seized by the antidote to the grasping at signs, is stated in the Ornament as: "There is no ego-grasping regarding giving and so forth," up to, "That is considered inconceivable." The definition of the knowledge of bases of the remedial class is: a cognition in the continuum of a Mahāyāna noble, which abides in the class of realizations of the Lesser Vehicle, and which is seized by the two special qualities of method and wisdom. That and the knowledge of bases in the continuum of a Mahāyāna noble are synonymous. Its scope exists from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. Regarding the demonstration of that, it is said: "Possessing wisdom, one moves about like a bird in the sky." The meaning is: just as a deer caught in a hunter's net is ignorant, one should understand the manner in which one suffers in this place of cyclic existence and is difficult to liberate. Then, Bodhisattvas who possess the great compassion of non-referential love and the wisdom that realizes the natural state, and who are not bound by the delusion of grasping at "giving and so forth" as truly existent, do not abide in this place of cyclic existence due to attachment, just as a bird, though moving in the sky, does not abide in the sky; rather, they move about for the sake of others. This is what is meant.

heading: **གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ། བདུན་པ་གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས་གཟུགས་སོགས་དེ་མི་རྟག་སོགས་དང་། །ནས། སྣང་བ་རྣམ་བདུན་ཤེས་བྱེད་དོ། །ཅེས་གསུངས། གཞི་ཀུན་རྫོབ་པའི་སྡོད་ལུགས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་དང་ཁྱད་པར་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་ཞེན་པ་དང་དོན་དམ་པའི་སྡོད་ལུགས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ་དང་ཁྱད་པར་ལ་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག་ཏུ་ཞེན་པ་གང་རུང་གི་གཉེན་པར་སྒོམ་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། གཞི་ཤེས་ཀྱི་སྐབས་ནས་བསྟན་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྦྱོང་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། ཁྱད་གཞི་གཟུགས་སོགས་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་བཀག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ཁྱད་ཆོས་མི་རྟག་པ་སོགས་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་བཀག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། གཟུགས་སོགས་དེ་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་རྟེན་དུ་མ་རྫོགས་པ་དང་རྫོགས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་དེ་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་ཆགས་མེད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་སྟེ་ཡུལ་གྱི་ནས་བཞི་དང་། དོན་དམ་པར་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་འཕེལ་འགྲིབ་མི་འགྱུར་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། བྱེད་པ་པོ་བདེན་པར་མེད་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། བྱ་དཀའ་རྣམ་གསུམ་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། དོན་དམ་པར་མེད་ཀྱང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་འབྲས་བུ་ཡོད་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་གཞན་ལ་རག་མ་ལས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ཤེས་བྱེད་དཔེའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྣང་བ་རྣམ་བདུན་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་བཀག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་བཅུ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའ་བར་ན་ཡོད།
translation: The application of the knowledge of bases. The seventh, the application of the knowledge of bases, is stated in the Ornament as: "Form and so forth, that as impermanent and so forth," up to, "the seven types of appearances are the means of knowing." The yoga of a Bodhisattva that meditates as an antidote to either the inverted clinging to the essence and characteristics of the conventional mode of existence, or the inverted clinging to the essence and characteristics of the ultimate mode of existence, is the definition of the training of a Bodhisattva as taught in the context of the knowledge of bases. When divided, there are ten: the application that negates clinging to true existence regarding the subjects, such as form and so forth; the application that negates clinging to true existence regarding the attributes, such as impermanence and so forth; the application regarding whether or not form and so forth are complete as a support for qualities; the application of non-attachment through clinging to the true existence of form and so forth—these are the four regarding the object. Furthermore, there is the application of the perfection of wisdom not increasing or decreasing in the ultimate sense; the application of the non-existence of a true agent; the application of the three types of difficult deeds; the application of the existence of results in conventional terms despite their non-existence in the ultimate sense; the application of enlightenment not being dependent on others; and the application that negates clinging to true existence regarding the seven types of appearances by way of illustrative examples. Its scope exists from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the end of the continuum.

The remedial class of the knowledge of bases. The sixth, the knowledge of bases of the remedial class, which is seized by the antidote to the grasping at signs, is stated in the Ornament as: "There is no ego-grasping regarding giving and so forth," up to, "That is considered inconceivable." The definition of the knowledge of bases of the remedial class is: a cognition in the continuum of a Mahāyāna noble, which abides in the class of realizations of the Lesser Vehicle, and which is seized by the two special qualities of method and wisdom. That and the knowledge of bases in the continuum of a Mahāyāna noble are synonymous. Its scope exists from the Mahāyāna path of seeing up to the level of a Buddha. Regarding the demonstration of that, it is said: "Possessing wisdom, one moves about like a bird in the sky." The meaning is: just as a deer caught in a hunter's net is ignorant, one should understand the manner in which one suffers in this place of cyclic existence and is difficult to liberate. Then, Bodhisattvas who possess the great compassion of non-referential love and the wisdom that realizes the natural state, and who are not bound by the delusion of grasping at "giving and so forth" as truly existent, do not abide in this place of cyclic existence due to attachment, just as a bird, though moving in the sky, does not abide in the sky; rather, they move about for the sake of others. This is what is meant.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ་དེའི་འཛིན་སྟངས་མཉམ་ཉིད།**
translation: The Equality of the Modes of Apprehension of that Application. The eighth, in order to teach the equality of the modes of apprehension of that application, states: "Without conceit regarding form and so forth, / That is the equality of the four aspects." That yoga of a bodhisattva, which is seized by the wisdom that prevents the belief in truth regarding the divisions of the bases, their signs and definitions, and the objects and subjects, is the definition of the equality of the application of the bodhisattva taught in the context of the knowledge of the bases. When divided, there are four: the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding the nature of form and so forth; the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding their signs and definitions; the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding their divisions; and the equality of the application of having no conceit of truth regarding their objects and subjects. The boundaries are the same as those for the application. To summarize and explain these two, one verse is stated, beginning with "Conduct is completely pure." The meaning is: A bodhisattva who realizes that all phenomena, such as the aggregates, are empty of truth and equal, and whose conduct is completely pure, does not engage through a belief in the truth of the nature of form or its characteristics, such as impermanence. Likewise, one does not engage through a belief in truth regarding consciousness, perception, the three feelings of pleasure, pain, and equanimity, or the mental factor of intention. Thus, that conduct of a child of the Victorious One, which does not engage through a belief in truth regarding any object, is what completely abandons all attachment born of belief in truth; and it is the practice of the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas, who are completely liberated from all attachment born of the apprehension of truth. This is what was stated. This is the commentary on the eighth chapter, the chapter on complete purity, from the "Jeweled Lamp that Clarifies the Reality of Dependent Arising," the profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā*.

source: མཐོང་ལམ། དགུ་པ་མཐོང་ལམ་སྟོན་པར། སྡུག་བསྔལ་ལ་སོགས་བདེན་པ་དང་། །ནས། ཀུན་ཤེས་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ། །ཞེས་པའི་བར་བྱུང་། སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་བདེན་པ་མངོན་རྟོགས་དེ། སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་མཐོང་ལམ་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སྐབས་འདིར་དངོས་སུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཤེས་བཟོང་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་བཅུ་དྲུག་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། མཐོང་ལམ་འདི་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དུ་རྟོགས་ཤིང་གོམས་པར་བྱས་ཏེ་ལམ་ལ་རིམ་གྱིས་སློབ་ཅིང་སྤྱོད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གནས་ལུགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ལ་མཁས་ཤིང་བློ་གྲོས་གསལ་བ་དེས་ནི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་མཐོང་ལམ་ཐོབ་ནས་བདེན་འཛིན་གྱི་ཆགས་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་བཅད་ནས་མཐོང་སྤངས་མ་ལུས་པ་ལས་གྲོལ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། མངོན་ཞེན་གྱི་ཆགས་པ་མེད་པར་སྒོམ་ལམ་སོགས་གོང་ནས་གང་དུ་འགྲོ་སྟེ།
translation: The Path of Seeing. The ninth [chapter] teaches the path of seeing, from "the truths such as suffering" up to "the moment of knowing all." In this context, the Mahayana clear realization of the truths that directly realizes the free-from-elaboration [nature] as taught directly here is the definition of the path of seeing as taught directly here. Regarding its divisions, there are sixteen moments of knowledge and forbearance of the Mahayana as taught directly here. Its boundary exists only within the Mahayana path of seeing. In explaining this very path of seeing, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Thus practicing" is as follows: A bodhisattva who, having realized and familiarized themselves with all phenomena as empty of true existence and free from elaboration as previously explained, and who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality and possesses clear intelligence, gradually trains in and practices the path. By attaining the Mahayana path of seeing, they cut through all attachment to true existence, becoming free from all that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing without remainder, and without attachment to manifest grasping, they proceed from the path of meditation and so forth to the higher [stages].

heading: **མཐོང་ལམ།**
translation: Just as the sun, when freed from the planet known as Rāhu, shines with brilliant rays, and just as fire, when kindled, burns all grass, wood, and forests, so too does the non-conceptual timeless awareness, which is the union of method and wisdom, act like the sun’s light and fire to clear away and destroy the darkness and forests of the two obscurations. This is what is said. According to the Master, one must make a chapter break here, for he applies this single verse, "All phenomena," to the summary of the practice of complete realization. According to the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vṛtti* of Jñānapāda, the section from "The Victorious One is the supreme deity" onwards is applied to the practice of complete realization, and by making a chapter break at its beginning, the text of the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* appears to be arranged mostly in that way. However, our own tradition follows the Master’s commentary, as Gungthang Jampai Yang also did in his annotations and so forth, where he makes a chapter conclusion after explaining the nine phenomena that characterize the four knowledges. This is the commentary on the third chapter from the work entitled *The Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Profound Reality of Dependent Arising: A Commentary on the Precious Qualities Collection*.

[3-153] translation already produced for this document:
The Path of Seeing. The ninth [chapter] teaches the path of seeing, from "the truths such as suffering" up to "the moment of knowing all." In this context, the Mahayana clear realization of the truths that directly realizes the free-from-elaboration [nature] as taught directly here is the definition of the path of seeing as taught directly here. Regarding its divisions, there are sixteen moments of knowledge and forbearance of the Mahayana as taught directly here. Its boundary exists only within the Mahayana path of seeing. In explaining this very path of seeing, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Thus practicing" is as follows: A bodhisattva who, having realized and familiarized themselves with all phenomena as empty of true existence and free from elaboration as previously explained, and who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality and possesses clear intelligence, gradually trains in and practices the path. By attaining the Mahayana path of seeing, they cut through all attachment to true existence, becoming free from all that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing without remainder, and without attachment to manifest grasping, they proceed from the path of meditation and so forth to the higher [stages].

heading: ཉམས་ལེན་སྦྱོར་བ་བཞི།
translation: The Four Applications of Practice. Having thus finished explaining the three knowledges, which are the objects of knowledge, the second part is the explanation of the system of the four applications of practice. Regarding these, there are two: the result of mastery over the application, and the cause and effect of stability.

[3-154] translation already produced for this document:
Just as the sun, when freed from the planet known as Rāhu, shines with brilliant rays, and just as fire, when kindled, burns all grass, wood, and forests, so too does the non-conceptual timeless awareness, which is the union of method and wisdom, act like the sun’s light and fire to clear away and destroy the darkness and forests of the two obscurations. This is what is said. According to the Master, one must make a chapter break here, for he applies this single verse, "All phenomena," to the summary of the practice of complete realization. According to the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā-vṛtti* of Jñānapāda, the section from "The Victorious One is the supreme deity" onwards is applied to the practice of complete realization, and by making a chapter break at its beginning, the text of the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* appears to be arranged mostly in that way. However, our own tradition follows the Master’s commentary, as Gungthang Jampai Yang also did in his annotations and so forth, where he makes a chapter conclusion after explaining the nine phenomena that characterize the four knowledges. This is the commentary on the third chapter from the work entitled *The Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Profound Reality of Dependent Arising: A Commentary on the Precious Qualities Collection*.

translation: The result of mastery over the application. The first consists of two: the application of complete aspects, which is the cause of mastery, and the peak application, which is the result.

source: དབང་དུ་བྱེད་པའི་རྒྱུ་རྣམ་རྫོགས་སྦྱོར་བ།དང་པོ་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། རྣམ་པ་སྦྱོར་བ་བཅས་རྣམས་དང་། །ནས། འདི་ནི་ཐབས་མཁས་བཅས་པ་ཡིན། །ཞེས་གསུངས། མཁྱེན་གསུམ་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་བསྡུས་ནས་བསྒོམ་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། རྣམ་རྫོགས་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་མཁྱེན་པ་དོན་གཅིག །དབྱེ་ན་རྣམ་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་བརྒྱ་དོན་གསུམ་དང་། སྦྱོར་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཉི་ཤུ་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། རྣམ་རྫོགས་སྦྱོར་བ་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་དེ་ལ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད་དེ། རྣམ་པ་དང་། སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ཡོན་ཏན་དང་། སྦྱོར་བའི་སྐྱོན་དང༌། མཚན་ཉིད་དང་། ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན་དང་། སློབ་པ་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་དགེ་འདུན་དང་། སྲིད་ཞིའི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཅིག་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར།
translation: The application of complete aspects, the cause of mastery. To explain the first, the Ornament states: "From 'aspects, applications, and so forth' up to 'this includes skill in means.'" A bodhisattva’s yoga, conjoined with the wisdom that meditates by gathering the aspects of the three knowledges, is the definition of the application of complete aspects. This and the bodhisattva’s knowledge are one in meaning. When divided, there are one hundred and seventy-three in terms of aspects, and twenty in terms of applications. Its scope extends from the path of accumulation of the Great Vehicle up to the end of the continuum. There are eleven phenomena that characterize the application of complete aspects: aspects, applications, qualities, faults of application, definitions, the path of liberation, the community of irreversible learners, the application of the equality of cyclic existence and peace, the application of the purification of the field, and the application of skill in means; because there are these eleven.

translation: Aspects. To explain the first, the Ornament states: "From 'the varieties of the knowledge of the basis' up to 'they are explained as thirty-nine.'" Regarding the aspects taught here, there are two: definition and division. The first is: that knowledge which is capable of overcoming its own discordant factors is the definition of the aspects of knowledge of the antidote taught in this context. Regarding the second, when divided, there are twenty-seven aspects of the knowledge of the basis, thirty-six aspects of the knowledge of the path, and one hundred and ten aspects of the knowledge of all aspects, totaling one hundred and seventy-three. Concerning the determination of the nature of these aspects to be meditated upon, the meaning of the verse beginning with "all phenomena" is as follows: all phenomena, from form up to the knowledge of all aspects, are pure because they are not truly established or established by way of their own nature, and they are completely pure because they have not been obscured by defilements in their abiding nature. When a bodhisattva looks upon and abides in the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the application of complete aspects that realizes that suchness of the abiding nature, then the bodhisattva who is practicing the perfection of wisdom also does not apprehend as truly established all the phenomena of the basis, path, and aspects that are to be looked upon as not truly established. Abiding one-pointedly in the realm of the non-conceptual, which is empty of true existence, is to practice the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the nature of the bodhisattva’s path of manifest realization. This explains the one hundred and seventy-three aspects by way of their being the means of attainment. It should be known that the explanation by Buddhasrī in the *Sdug 'grel* (Summary Commentary) that this verse applies to the path of seeing of the third chapter does not accord with the commentary of the Master. This is the commentary on the ninth chapter, the chapter of praise, from the *Precious Qualities Collection* commentary, the *Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Profound Reality of Dependent Arising*.

The application of complete aspects, the cause of mastery. To explain the first, the Ornament states: "From 'aspects, applications, and so forth' up to 'this includes skill in means.'" A bodhisattva’s yoga, conjoined with the wisdom that meditates by gathering the aspects of the three knowledges, is the definition of the application of complete aspects. This and the bodhisattva’s knowledge are one in meaning. When divided, there are one hundred and seventy-three in terms of aspects, and twenty in terms of applications. Its scope extends from the path of accumulation of the Great Vehicle up to the end of the continuum. There are eleven phenomena that characterize the application of complete aspects: aspects, applications, qualities, faults of application, definitions, the path of liberation, the community of irreversible learners, the application of the equality of cyclic existence and peace, the application of the purification of the field, and the application of skill in means; because there are these eleven.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Application. Second, in explaining the application of meditating on those aspects, because it is necessary to first identify the person who is the basis for practicing the application, the text first teaches the vessel for the application by stating the four verses beginning with "To the Victorious One..." The meaning is: The King of Gods, Śakra, asked the Victorious One, the Buddha, the Blessed One, a question. He asked how bodhisattvas, who have performed meritorious deeds for previous Victorious Ones and have cultivated roots of virtue, and who possess the protection of a spiritual friend, should exert themselves in the conduct of the perfection of wisdom and how they should meditate through application. In response, the Buddha taught: To realize that there is not even an atom of truly established existence in phenomena such as the five aggregates and the eighteen constituents, and to not exert oneself through attachment to true existence, but rather to abide in the application of non-apprehension regarding phenomena such as the aggregates and not exert oneself through grasping—this is the unerring diligence of bodhisattvas. Any person who, having heard from the Mother Sutras that all these phenomena, from form up to the omniscience of the Buddha, are explained as being like illusions and magical emanations—even though they are not established by their own nature, all the functions of cause, effect, and dependent origination are validly established in mere conventionality—and who, upon hearing this, is not only not afraid of its meaning but is free of doubt, and who, with faith and joy, diligently practices and applies themselves to learning the perfection of wisdom, that sentient being should be known as having entered the Mahayana path long ago. It should be known that they have previously performed meritorious deeds, such as serving and making offerings to many tens of millions of Buddhas and offering monasteries, because without a special cause having preceded it, one would not attain the faith of conviction in the profound meaning of emptiness and proceed to put it into practice. To teach, by way of a metaphor, the relief of those who have realized the deeds that transcend obstacles, such as listening to the Mahayana, the text states: Just as a person who has entered a vast, many-league-long path through a desolate wilderness, which is frightening due to robbers and the like, sees at some point a pleasant and abundant forest at the border of a wilderness and a village where cowherds of a city reside, and thinks, "These are signs that a village or city is near," thereby finding relief from the fear of robbers and wild beasts, and from then on is free from the fear of robbers and the like; in the same way, when one desires to attain the supreme enlightenment for the sake of others and searches for the path of means to attain it, whoever obtains the good fortune of listening to this Mother of the Victorious Ones, the perfection of wisdom, and engaging in it through hearing, contemplation, and meditation, attains relief from the suffering of cyclic existence and has no fear of falling into the extremes of existence or peace. They do not fall into the level of the śrāvaka arhats, nor do they fall into the level of the pratyekabuddhas, for they are irreversible from the Mahayana path. Thus it is said.

གཟུགས་སོགས་ལ་བདེན་པར་ཞེན་ཅིང་མི་གནས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། དེ་དག་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་གྱིས་གནས་པ་བཀག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་བཞིའི་དེ་ཉིད་རྟོགས་པའི་ཟབ་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ལམ་གྱི་རང་བཞིན་རྟོགས་པའི་གཏིང་དཔག་དཀའ་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་པའི་རང་བཞིན་ཚད་མེད་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་ཚད་མེད་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་ལྔ་ངོ་བོའི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་བ་ཡིན་ལ། ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པ་བརྟན་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། ངེས་པར་འབྱུང་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། བར་ཆད་མེད་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། བྱང་ཆུབ་ལ་ཉེ་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། མྱུར་བར་འཚང་རྒྱ་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཞན་དོན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་བདུན་པོ་འདི་རྟེན་གྱི་གང་ཟག་གི་སྒོས་དབྱེ་བ་དང༌། དོན་དམ་པར་འཕེལ་མེད་འགྲིབ་མེད་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང༌། དོན་དམ་པར་ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་མིན་སོགས་མི་མཐོང་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་བསམ་མི་ཁྱབ་མི་མཐོང་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། གཟུགས་སོགས་མཚན་མཚོན་དུ་བདེན་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་བཞི་ཡུམ་སྒོམ་པ་རྫོགས་པའི་ཐབས་ཀྱི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་བ་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་རིན་ཆེན་སྦྱིན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་གཉིས་འབྲས་བུའི་སྒོ་ནས་དབྱེ་བ་དང་། ས་མཚམས་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་བཅུ་དགུ་ཡོད། ཚེགས་ཆེན་ཡུན་རིང་རྟོགས་དཀའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི་གཙོ་བོ་སྦྱོར་བ་དངོས་མ་ཡིན་ཀྱང་སྦྱོར་བ་ཙམ་ཡིན་པས་བགྲང་ཚེ་སྦྱོར་བ་ཉི་ཤུ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་ནི། ཚེགས་ཆེན་རྟོགས་དཀའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་དང་། གཙོ་བོའི་སྦྱོར་བ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་ན་ཡོད། སྦྱོར་བ་སྔ་མ་གཞན་རྣམས་མདོ་དང་དངོས་སུ་སྦྱོར་རྒྱུ་མེད་ལ་བར་ཆད་མེད་པའི་སྦྱར་བའི་ངོ་བོ་དཔེ་སྔོན་དུ་འགྲོ་བས་སྟོན་པ་ནི། མི་ཞིག་རྒྱ་མཆོའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཉིས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། དཔེར་ན་མི་ཞིག་རྒྱ་མཚོའི་ཆུ་ནི་བལྟ་བའི་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་ན་མི་དེ་ཡིས་གལ་ཏེ་ལྗོན་ཤིང་དང་ནགས་ཚལ་རི་བོ་དག་མདུན་གྱི་ཕྱོགས་སུ་མཐོང་ན་ནི། ད་དུང་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་ཐག་རིང་བར་ཤེས་ཤིང་། ཅི་སྟེ་རི་ལ་སོགས་པ་རིང་བའི་རྟགས་དེ་དག་མ་མཐོང་བར་ས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཁད་ཀྱིས་མཉམ་ཞིང་དམའ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ་ཕ་རོལ་གྱི་མཐའ་མི་མཐོང་བར་གྱུར་ན། ད་ནི་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་བདག་དང་ཉེ་བར་གྱུར་ཏོ་སྙམ་སྟེ་དེ་ལ་སོམ་ཉི་མེད་ཅིང་རྒྱང་ནས་ཀྱང་ཤེས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
translation: Having thus indicated the basis, the nature of the application that relies upon it is stated in the *Ornament* as: "Because of not abiding in form and so forth," up to "that is pure and with limits." Regarding the application, there are three: definition, division, and stage. The first is the bodhisattva yoga seized by the wisdom of the union of calm abiding and special insight, which focuses on the emptiness directly taught in this context. This is the definition of the primary application directly taught in this context. Regarding the second, when divided, there are five based on their nature: the application of not abiding while being attached to form and so forth as true; the application of prohibiting the abiding in them through attachment to truth; the profound application of realizing the suchness of the four, such as form; the application of difficult-to-fathom depth that realizes the nature of the path; and the immeasurable application that realizes the nature of the aspects of form and so forth as immeasurable. There are seven based on the person who is the basis: the application of having attained a prophecy; the application of being firm in non-retrogression; the application of definite emergence; the application of being uninterrupted; the application of being near to enlightenment; the application of quickly attaining buddhahood; and the application of the benefit of others. There are four based on the method of completing the meditation on the Mother: the application of realizing that in ultimate reality there is no increase or decrease; the application of not seeing phenomena and non-phenomena and so forth in ultimate reality; the application of not seeing the inconceivable form and so forth; and the application of not conceptualizing form and so forth as signs or characteristics, along with the application of non-conceptualization. There are two based on the result: the application of giving the jewel of the result, and the application of purification. There is also the application of stage, making nineteen. The application of the great difficulty of long-term realization is not the primary application itself, but since it is an application nonetheless, there are twenty applications when counted. The third, the stage, is as follows: the application of the great difficulty of realization is from the Mahayana path of accumulation, and the primary applications are from the heat level of the Mahayana path of preparation up to the end of the continuum. The other previous applications cannot be directly applied to the sutra, but the nature of the uninterrupted application is taught by preceding it with an analogy, as stated in the two verses beginning with "Just as a person [going to see] the ocean..." The meaning of this is: For example, when a person goes to see the water of the ocean, if that person sees trees, forests, and mountains in the direction ahead, they know that the great ocean is still far away. If they do not see those signs of distance, such as mountains, and the ground becomes gradually level and low, and they do not see the far shore, then they think, "Now the great ocean has become near to me," and they have no doubt about it and know it even from afar.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: In this way, for those who have entered perfectly into the supreme enlightenment for the sake of others, the fortune of gradually engaging through hearing, contemplating, and meditating upon this Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, should be understood as being close to the great ocean of the dharmakāya, the wisdom of omniscience, because they have attained the special capacity to accomplish enlightenment. Therefore, even if a person who possesses the application, which is the main part of the Mahāyāna path, has been explicitly prophesied by the Guides that "you shall attain buddhahood," they know that the buddha-enlightenment will be attained or touched by them without long delay. When the conceptualizations of the path of seeing, which are like the signs of mountains and forests, do not appear in the supreme dharma, they are understood as being close to the path of seeing, which is like the ocean; by this, the quality of attaining the dharmakāya is also indicated. Following that, to demonstrate the tenth application, the application close to enlightenment, which transcends the conceptualizations of the path of preparation below the supreme dharma—which is like old foliage—and becomes the basis for new, untainted phenomena—which is like fresh foliage—one verse is spoken, beginning with "In the fine season of spring..." For example, when, in the fine season of spring, the withered leaves fall to the ground from a tree trunk, that tree, without long delay, produces or generates new leaves, fruits, and flowers from its branches. Likewise, whoever obtains this perfection of wisdom in their hands will attain the enlightenment of the Guides without long delay, and through the rūpakāya, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree, they will fulfill the hopes of beings just as they desire. By this, the quality of accomplishing the sambhogakāya is also indicated.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To demonstrate the application for quickly attaining complete enlightenment, the meaning of the one verse beginning with "For example, a woman..." is as follows: Just as a pregnant woman who has conceived a child in her womb is distressed by experiencing the suffering of childbirth, and that state is the measure of the time having arrived for her to give birth to that child, in the same way, any bodhisattva who, through listening to and contemplating this sūtra of the noble perfection of wisdom, generates a longing for the goal of desiring to attain the higher path and a joy of a very clear mind, and then practices it through application, will quickly come to touch upon great enlightenment. As the Lord of Logic (Dharmakīrti) stated: "That which is an inference that an effect arises from the gathering of causes, because it does not depend on another factor, is stated to be nature." By this, the quality of attaining the nirmāṇakāya is also indicated. Although Buddhaśrī explained this differently, it is set forth here according to the commentary of the Master (Haribhadra). The application of preventing increase and decrease is the meaning taught by the two lines beginning with "The perfection of wisdom..." When a yogi who is cultivating the application acts in accordance with listening to, contemplating, and meditating upon the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom, they do not see in the ultimate sense the increase—that is, the arising—of phenomena of the side of defilement and the side of purification, such as form, and the characteristics indicated by that, nor do they see the complete decrease—that is, the cessation and decline—of them, because all phenomena are, in the ultimate sense, without increase or decrease, being empty of true existence and like an illusion.

heading: **སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: In explaining the practice of not perceiving phenomena, non-phenomena, and so forth, the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Whoever, with phenomena..." is as follows: Any bodhisattva who does not perceive, in an ultimate sense, virtuous phenomena, non-virtuous phenomena, or the suchness of phenomena—the dharmadhātu—and who, while abiding in that suchness which is free from proliferation and in which all focal points of grasping at characteristics have been pacified, does not touch upon—that is, does not abide in—a nirvāṇa that is merely one-sided peace, but rather abides in the supreme prajñā that transcends the extremes of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

source: སྦྱོར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། གསུམ་པ་སྦྱོར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། བདུད་ཀྱི་མཐུ་བཅོམ་ལ་སོགས་པ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རྣམ་པ་བཅུ་བཞིའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། རང་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་སུ་གྱུར་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་བསྒོམ་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་ཕན་ཡོན་དེ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སྦྱོར་བ་བསྒོམ་སྟབས་ཀྱིས་བདུད་ཀྱི་མཐུ་བཅོམ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་དགོངས་ཤིང་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། རྫོགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་དང་ཉེ་བར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། དོན་ཆེ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། ཡུལ་སྤྱད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། ཟག་མེད་ཀྱི་ཡོན་ཏན་ཐམས་ཅད་རྫོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སྨྲ་བའི་སྐྱེས་བུ་ཉིད་དུ་འགྱུར་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། མི་མཐུན་ཕྱོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཕྱེད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པ་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན། དམ་བཅས་པའི་དོན་འགྲུབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། འབྲས་བུ་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་གྲུབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན། ཡུམ་ངེས་པར་ཐོབ་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་བཅུ་བཞི་ཡོད། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་སའི་བར་ན་ཡོད། ཡོན་ཏན་དེ་རྣམས་སྤྱིར་སྟོན་པར། གང་ཞིག་འདིར་སྤྱོད་ཅེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། བདག་མེད་གཉིས་བསྒོམ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་ཐེག་ཆེེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་འདིར་ཚུལ་བཞིན་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་ཅིང་སྤྱོད་པ་དེ་ནི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སྟོབས་བཅུ་དང་མི་འཇིགས་པ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་ལ་དེ་དང་དེར་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་ནས་མི་རྟོག་སྟེ། དེ་བཞིན་དུ་ལམ་དང་སོགས་དབང་པོ་ལྔ་དང་སྟོབས་དང་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་རྐང་པ་དང་དྲན་པ་ཉེར་བཞག་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་ཡན་ལག་བདུན་པ་སོགས་དང་། འབྲས་བུ་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཞི་བ་མཆོག་ལ་ཡང་བདེན་པར་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་ལ། ཕུང་ཁམས་སྐྱེ་མཆེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་ལའང་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པར་གཉིས་སྣང་གི་རྟོག་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བའི་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དེ་བཞིིན་ཉིད་ལ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱིན་གྱིས་རླབས་ཀྱིས་བདུད་ཀྱི་མཐུ་བཅོམ་པ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་བསྐྱེད་པའི་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་འདི་ནི་རྣམ་ཀུན་གྱི་ངོ་བོར་གྱུར་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་མཆོག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ་ཞེས་པའོ། །བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་ཚེ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་འདི་སྐད་ཅེས་གསོལ་ཏོ། །བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་འཛིན་པ་དང་། ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་འཛིན་པའི་ཡོནཏན་ཡོངས་སུ་བརྗོད་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་པའིའགྲེལ་པའོ།། translation: Qualities of the Application. Third, regarding the qualities of the application, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states: "The subduing of the power of Māra, and so forth, are the fourteen types of qualities." The definition of the qualities of the Mahāyāna application is the benefit attained through the power of meditating on the Mahāyāna application, which serves as the method for attaining one's own goal. Regarding their classification, there are fourteen: the quality of subduing the power of Māra through the power of meditating on the application; the quality of the Buddha’s intention and knowledge; the quality of the Buddha’s direct realization; the quality of becoming near to perfect enlightenment; the quality of great significance and so forth; the quality of utilizing the domain; the quality of the perfection of all stainless qualities; the quality of becoming a spokesperson; the quality of not being divided by adverse factors; the quality of the arising of unique roots of virtue; the quality of fulfilling one's vows; the quality of fully grasping the vast fruit; the quality of accomplishing the benefit of sentient beings; and the quality of definitely attaining the Mother. Their scope extends from the Mahāyāna path of accumulation up to the Buddha ground. To explain these qualities in general, the meaning of the verses beginning with "Whoever practices here..." is as follows: Any bodhisattva who meditates on the two types of selflessness and who practices and engages in this Mahāyāna application in accordance with the truth does not conceptually construct—by way of grasping at them as truly existent—the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and so forth. Likewise, they do not conceptually construct as truly existent the path and so forth, such as the five faculties, the powers, the bases of miraculous power, the establishments of mindfulness, the seven limbs of enlightenment, and so forth, nor the fruit—the supreme peace of nirvāṇa and enlightenment. Furthermore, they do not conceptually construct the phenomena of the aggregates, elements, and sense spheres. By engaging in the Mahāyāna application, which generates qualities such as the subduing of the power of Māra through the blessings of the Buddha, while abiding in suchness—which is free from proliferation and devoid of all conceptual constructs of dualistic appearance—they are engaging in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the essence of all aspects, and in non-conceptual primordial wisdom. In the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, the venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, holding the perfection of wisdom, and so forth," he stated. This is the commentary on the tenth chapter, which expresses the qualities of holding, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of Fortunate Ones*, the profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the suchness of dependent origination.

།ཆོས་དང་ཆོས་མིན་སོགས་མི་མཐོང་བའི་སྦྱོར་བ་འཆད་པར། གང་ཞིག་ཆོས་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་བྱུང་དོན་ནི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་ཆོས་དགེ་བ་དང་ཆོས་མིན་པ་མི་དགེ་བ་དང་། ཆོས་རྣམས་ཀྱི་གནས་ལུགས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཀྱང་དོན་དམ་པར་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་མཚན་འཛིན་གྱི་དམིགས་གཏད་ཐམས་ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བའི་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ལ་གནས་ན་འང་། ཞི་བ་ཕྱོགས་གཅིག་པའི་མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་ལ་མི་རེག་པ་སྟེ་མི་གནས་ཤིང་བྱང་ཆུབ་དེ་ནི་སྲིད་ཞི་གཉིས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་ལས་འདས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་མཆོག་ལ་གནས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
[3-163] translation already produced for this document:
In explaining the practice of not perceiving phenomena, non-phenomena, and so forth, the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Whoever, with phenomena..." is as follows: Any bodhisattva who does not perceive, in an ultimate sense, virtuous phenomena, non-virtuous phenomena, or the suchness of phenomena—the dharmadhātu—and who, while abiding in that suchness which is free from proliferation and in which all focal points of grasping at characteristics have been pacified, does not touch upon—that is, does not abide in—a nirvāṇa that is merely one-sided peace, but rather abides in the supreme prajñā that transcends the extremes of both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.

heading: **ལན།**
translation:
Furthermore, among the forty-six faults of practice, there are eight that are explicitly taught here. The first is instability, characterized by being conceited due to overly rapid confidence and then turning back midway. Regarding the meaning of the single verse beginning with "By the Victorious One," it is as follows: When one is engaged in reading, holding, reciting, or teaching this Perfection of Wisdom, which is the Mother of the Victorious Ones of the three times, there arise various unfixed and diverse types of confidence regarding objects such as forms and sounds, as well as various states such as agitation, dullness, sleepiness, regret, attachment, and aversion. Due to the power of these, one does not accomplish the benefit of oneself and others, such as realizing the meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom, but instead, while reading, reciting, or teaching, one quickly fades away like a flash of lightning, cuts off one's exertion, and completely falls away from the practice; this should be known as the work of Māra.

To demonstrate the actual cause of abandonment—that is, holding to the reason for turning away and forsaking the Great Vehicle canon—the single verse beginning with "When this is taught" is stated. When this sutra is taught, some develop doubts and hesitation, thinking, "The Guide has not explicitly mentioned or indicated my name in this Mother sutra, nor has he mentioned my lineage, the region where I dwell, or my clan." Thinking that they have not been clearly prophesied, they wonder, "What is the point of listening to this? This is not the speech of the All-Knowing One." By holding to this reason for turning away from the Mother, and with that distorted mind, they do not listen to that profound Dharma but rather forsake it; this is the work of Māra.

For example, just as someone who has found food possessing a hundred flavors, without tasting its flavor, having found the finest food, searches instead for poor food such as sixty-day rice, so too, any beginner bodhisattva who, having found this profound sutra of the perfection of wisdom, does not practice to accomplish the enlightenment of a Buddha, but instead relies on texts that teach the path for attaining the stage of a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha arhat to seek unsurpassed enlightenment, is just like the example given above; this too is the work of Māra.

heading: **ལན།**
translation: The listener having great aspiration but the teacher being diminished by indolence, whereby the listener also becomes faithless and turns away from listening to the Dharma, is the meaning of the one verse beginning with "Those who, at that time." This means that at the time when those listeners, who with great earnestness have gone to listen to this supreme Dharma out of aspiration and faith in the Mother (Prajñāpāramitā), find that the one expounding the Perfection of Wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and the like, those listeners perceive that the Dharma speaker is attached to and obsessed with base activities such as delighting in gain, honor, and fame. Consequently, they find no joy in listening to the Dharma, and, becoming faithless and feeling uneasy with the thought, "I shall not request the Dharma now," they depart; this too is the work of Māra, which becomes an obstacle to listening to the Perfection of Wisdom and so forth.

Savoring the taste of gain, honor, and praise and looking toward them is the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Desiring honor." This means that one comes to desire to savor the taste of one's own fame and the honor and respect shown by others, comes to desire the acquisition of food, wealth, and the like, and, with a mind accompanied by the desire to look at various forms and the arrangements of objects, one becomes involved in associating and becoming intimate with householders and the like; being distracted by many activities and thus declining from listening to the perfection of wisdom and so forth is the work of Māra.

[3-174] translation already produced for this document:
Seeking skill in means from the scriptures taught by Māra that are not the path is the meaning of the two lines beginning with "Having abandoned the Dharma." Having abandoned the practice of the Mahāyāna Dharma, one comes to engage in various worldly activities that are not the Dharma, and having cast aside the excellent path that leads to the attainment of Buddhahood, one wanders off onto the wrong path taught by Māra; this is the work of Māra.

heading: **ལན།**
translation: To summarize their meaning: the meaning of the four verses beginning with "At that time" is that these various works of Māra, which obstruct the preparations such as the gathering of those who teach and listen to the Perfection of Wisdom sutra, will arise at that time. What are they? At the time of listening to and contemplating this Dharma, those Māras who are hostile to the Dharma and are tormented by suffering and pain will agitate the minds of many monks who uphold this sutra. Through various means of obstruction, they will prevent the holding and contemplating of the meaning of this Perfection of Wisdom. Many such obstructive phenomena, not explained here but appearing elsewhere, will occur; one should know that all such obstacles are the work of Māra. As it is said in the *Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra*: "O son of noble family, know that all engagement in non-virtuous phenomena and all abandonment of virtuous phenomena are the work of Māra." The reason for the abundance of obstacles is established by way of an example: just as those who have obtained priceless, invaluable treasures, such as the king of wish-fulfilling gems, find them extremely rare and difficult to obtain, and once obtained, they are constantly subject to harm from enemies, thieves, and the like, in the same way, the Mother of the Victors, the supreme, priceless Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, is extremely rare, and because the Dharma is profound, it is constantly subject to many harms. For those beings of small intelligence who have newly entered the Mahāyāna and have not yet found this rare and profound Dharma—this precious Perfection of Wisdom sutra—Māra will strive to create obstacles and will initiate hindrances.

[3-175] translation already produced for this document:
The listener having great aspiration but the teacher being diminished by indolence, whereby the listener also becomes faithless and turns away from listening to the Dharma, is the meaning of the one verse beginning with "Those who, at that time." This means that at the time when those listeners, who with great earnestness have gone to listen to this supreme Dharma out of aspiration and faith in the Mother (Prajñāpāramitā), find that the one expounding the Perfection of Wisdom sutra has become distracted by gain, honor, and the like, those listeners perceive that the Dharma speaker is attached to and obsessed with base activities such as delighting in gain, honor, and fame. Consequently, they find no joy in listening to the Dharma, and, becoming faithless and feeling uneasy with the thought, "I shall not request the Dharma now," they depart; this too is the work of Māra, which becomes an obstacle to listening to the Perfection of Wisdom and so forth.

heading: **སེལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གཉེན་པོ།**
translation: The Antidote that Dispels. Second, the antidote that dispels is the meaning of the five lines of verse beginning with "The buddhas of the ten directions." Even though there are many such obstructions, they will not be able to find an opportunity. Why is that? Because the buddhas of the ten directions, whose power and might cannot be rivaled even in the slightest by the efforts of such demonic obstructions, protect, guard, and conceal those practitioners, thereby engaging them in fully upholding the perfection of wisdom. From the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Hopes of the Fortunate, an Explanation of the Precious Qualities Collection that Clarifies the Reality of Dependent Arising*, this is the commentary on the eleventh chapter, the chapter on Māra.

heading: **སེལ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་གཉེན་པོ།**
translation: If one asks why all the buddhas attend to and protect that person, this is established by an analogy: just as when a mother falls ill, her many children all become distressed and attend to her by seeking a physician to cure her sickness, in the same way, all those Bhagavan Buddhas of the world systems of the ten directions strive to dispel the influence of Māra and attend to this supreme perfection of wisdom, which is the mother that gives birth to each of them, consisting of the generation of bodhicitta and the realization of emptiness. Thus it is said.

heading: **མཚན་ཉིད།**
translation: Characteristics. The first is: a bodhisattva’s yoga, seized by the union of calm abiding and special insight, which serves as the method for attaining the resultant perfection of wisdom that is its own objective; this is the definition of the yoga of the path of the perfection of wisdom. This is the general definition of application. As for the object to be characterized, when considered generally, it is the yoga of the path of the perfection of wisdom itself; here, the "application" in the phrase "definition of application" is also that very path of the perfection of wisdom, and its definition is what is called the definition of application.

[3-180] translation already produced for this document:
Detailed Explanation. Regarding the detailed explanation, it is stated: "From the arising of the Tathāgata, up to the assertion of four characteristics." Regarding that, there are two parts: the characteristics and the divisions.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Divisions. Second, regarding the divisions of that, there are ninety-one: forty-eight knowledge-characteristics that characterize the application of the three knowledges; sixteen distinctive characteristics that characterize the application that is superior to the application of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; eleven activity-characteristics that characterize the application possessing distinctive functions for accomplishing the benefit of others; and sixteen essence-characteristics. Regarding the first of these, there are three, and the first four knowledge-characteristics—the knowledge-characteristic of knowing the arising of the Tathāgata, and so forth—are taught in the two stanzas beginning with "Those who have passed..." The meaning of these is as follows: If this perfection of wisdom is called the "Mother of the Victors," how does it become a mother? Just as in the world one is called a "mother" because she gives birth to a child and establishes him in his tasks, so too, all the Tathāgatas, the Blessed Buddhas who have already passed away in the past, those who currently reside in the worlds of the ten directions as protectors of the world, and all those who will arise in the future, all emerge from this very perfection of wisdom; therefore, it is the mother of all the Victors of the three times. By this, the knowledge-characteristic of knowing the arising of the Tathāgata is taught. The fact that the Buddhas, having seen the suchness of all phenomena included within the world—that is, the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields—exactly as it is, teach it to other beings to be trained, also arises in dependence upon this very perfection of wisdom, the mother that gives birth to the Victors. This Mother also reveals to her own offspring, the noble Buddhas, the immeasurable and infinite mental activities of other sentient beings—those that are gathered within, those that are distracted outward, those that are accompanied by attachment, those that are free from attachment, and so forth. Furthermore, the suchness of the world’s five aggregates, the suchness of the śrāvaka arhats, the suchness of the pratyekabuddhas, and the suchness of the bodhisattva heirs of the Victors are not established as different in essence, and thus they are one. Since they are not different in terms of the nature of the reality-realm (dharmadhātu) that is devoid of any truly established entity, this suchness is one. One should understand that this suchness, which is the reality-realm, is what the Tathāgata has known and realized exactly as it is, and then taught to others. By these sutra passages, one should understand that the knowledge-characteristics, such as knowing the world and the non-destruction of the world, and knowing the mental activities of sentient beings, are for the most part directly taught in the literal words.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: The manner of subduing opponents and teaching the profound doctrine of emptiness is also like this: just as the lion, king of beasts, dwelling in the ravines of the snowy mountains, causes fear in many predators and small animals—such as tigers, leopards, bears, and wild dogs—by roaring without harming any living creature, so too do the Buddhas, the lions among men, relying upon the profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom, which is emptiness, cause fear in many non-Buddhists who have fallen into the abyss of the view of a self, and they proclaim in the world the marvelous and vast sound of the ultimate dharma. Furthermore, a bodhisattva, having perfected the three gateways to liberation, becomes a Buddha; although they deliver countless sentient beings from the sufferings of the lower realms, they do not have the perception that suffering and sentient beings are truly established, and thus they teach that there is no defilement, no purification, no substantiality, no essence, and no basis.
