འདུ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོའང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་ལ་སེམས་པ་མི་མཐོང་ཞིང་།ཆོས་ཉིད་ལ་བརྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་བཞག་པའི་འཕགས་པའི་མཉམ་བཞག་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པའི་གཟིགས་ངོར་གང་ལ་རྣམ་པར་ཤེས་པ་དང་སེམས་དང་ཡིད་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ཅི་ཡང་མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་འདི་ནི་ཕུང་པོ་ལྔའི་གནས་ལུགས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་ཏེ། དེ་ཡངདཔེ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཞེ་ན། འཇིག་རྟེན་པ་དག་གིས་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་ཡིད་ལ་བསམ་ཞིང་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཚིག་ཏུ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྗོད་པ་ནི་ཡོད་མོད་ཀྱི་འོན་ཀྱང་ནམ་མཁའ་ཇི་ལྟར་མཐོང་བར་ནུས་ཞེས་དོན་འདི་ལ་རང་གིས་བརྟག་པར་བགྱིས་དང་། ནམ་མཁའ་ཐོགས་པའི་རེག་བྱ་བཅད་ཙམ་ཡིན་པས་དགག་བྱ་སྒྲིབ་ཐོགས་ཡོད་ན་དམིགས་སུ་རུང་བ་ལས་དེ་མ་མཐོང་པ་ལ་ནམ་མཁའ་མཐོང་ཞེས་བརྗོད་པ་དེ་ལྟར་གཟུགས་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་ཞེས་པའང་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་བཙལ་བ་ན་གཟུགས་སོགས་མ་རྙེད་པའམ་མ་མཐོང་བ་ནི། དེ་དག་གི་གནས་ལུགས་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་མཐོང་བ་ཡིན་ཞེས་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པས་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ལ། མཉམ་བཞག་རྣམ་པར་མི་རྟོག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཉིད་མཐོང་བའམ་གཟིགས་ཚུལ་དཔེ་གཞན་གྱིས་ནི་བསྙད་པར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་པ་སྟེ། ཊིཀ་ཆེན་དགོངས་པ་རབ་གསལ་ལས། མི་མཐོང་བ་ཕུང་པ་ོལྔ་དང་། མཐོང་བ་ནི་ཆོས་ཞེས་གསུངས་ལ། དེ་ནི་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཀྱི་དོན་ཏེ་སུས་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་མ་མཐོང་བ་དེས་ཆོས་མཐོང་ངོ་ཞེས་གསུངས་པ་བཞིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་དང་། ཇི་ལྟ་བ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་དེས་ཕུང་སོགས་ཀྱི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་རྣམས་གཟིགས་ངོར་མ་གྲུབ་པ་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་དང་། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་དགོས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། རང་འགྲེལ་ལས། དངོས་པོ་བྱས་པ་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་རང་བཞིན་འབའ་ཞིག་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་མཛད་པས། དེ་ཉིད་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པའི་ཕྱིར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཞེས་བརྗོད་དོ། །ཞེས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་དོན་དམ་མཁྱེན་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་ཆོས་ཅན་ལ་མ་རེག་པར་ཆོས་ཉིད་འབབ་ཞིག་ཐུགས་སུ་ཆུད་པར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཕུང་སོགས་མ་གཟིགས་པའི་ཚུལ་གྱིས་དེ་དག་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གཟིགས་པར་གསུངས་པ་དང་དོན་གཅིག་གོ །མཐོང་བ་མེད་པ་ནི་མཐོང་བ་དམ་པའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ཡང༌། ཅི་ཡང་མ་མཐོང་བ་མཐོང་བ་མི་བཞེད་ཀྱི། སྔར་བཤད་པ་ལྟར་སྤྲོས་མ་མཐོང་བ་སྤྲོས་བྲལ་མཐོང་བར་འཇོག་པས། མཐོང་མ་མཐོང་གཞི་གཅིག་ལ་བྱེད་པ་མིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །བུདྡྷ་ཤྲཱིས་གཟུགས་རྣམས་མི་མཐོང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཁྱད་མཚན་ལ་མར་སྦྱར་ཡང༌། སློབ་དཔོན་གྱིས་ཤེས་མཚན་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་ཉི་ཁྲི་དང་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་སོགས་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་འགྲིགས་ཞེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱི་གསུངས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་འཇིག་རྟེན་བསྟན་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་གཉིས་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ༎  །།
translation: The third section, which demonstrates the signs of omniscience such as the Tathāgata’s abiding in happiness within the vision of the Dharma, explains the meaning of the three verses beginning with "Just as one dwelling in the sky." For example, just as the rays of the sun dwelling in the sky possess two functions—drying up the moisture on this earth and, by dispelling darkness, clearly revealing all forms—so too does the Buddha, the Bhagavan, the King of Dharma and Sun of Speech, relying upon the sky-like perfection of wisdom, use the sharp rays of the profound and vast Dharma to dry up the entire river of faults, such as the craving of existence, and truly reveal the Dharmas that increase all qualities. How is the reality (dharmatā) taught? When one searches for the nature of the five aggregates using the analytical wisdom that investigates the ultimate, forms are not seen because they cannot be apprehended; likewise, feelings are not seen, the essence of perceptions is not seen, and volitions are not seen. This is what the Tathāgata taught: that the vision of the reality of the five aggregates—the suchness—is the state in which, within the perspective of the noble one’s meditative equipoise wisdom, which is single-pointedly placed in equipoise upon reality, nothing whatsoever called consciousness, mind, or intellect is seen. What is the example for this? Although worldly beings think in their minds that they see the sky and sentient beings speak of it in words, one should examine for oneself: how is it possible to see the sky? Since the sky is merely the absence of tangible objects that provide resistance, if there were an object of negation—something that obstructs—it would be an appropriate object of apprehension; yet, because that is not seen, it is called "seeing the sky." In the same way, the Tathāgata taught that "seeing the reality of forms and so forth" means that when one searches with analytical wisdom, forms and the like are not found or seen, which is seeing their nature, suchness. The manner in which the reality is seen or viewed by the non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise cannot be explained by other examples. This is what is meant. The Great Commentary, *Dgongs pa rab gsal*, states: "Not seeing is the five aggregates, and seeing is the Dharma," and this is the meaning of reality, just as it is said: "Whoever does not see dependent origination sees the Dharma." Furthermore, because that wisdom of knowing things as they are sees the suchness of the aggregates and so forth directly, and because the aggregates and so forth are not established within the perspective of that vision, and because one must see their suchness by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth, the *Auto-commentary* states: "Because one directly realizes only the nature without touching the constructed entities, one is called a Buddha because one has realized that very thing." This states that the wisdom of the Buddha that knows the ultimate realizes only the reality without touching the phenomena, which is the same meaning as the statement that one sees their suchness by way of not seeing the aggregates and so forth. The statement "Not seeing is the supreme seeing" does not mean that seeing nothing at all is considered seeing; rather, as explained before, it is established as seeing the free-from-proliferations by not seeing the proliferations, so it does not mean that seeing and not seeing are based on the same thing. Although Buddhaśrī applied "not seeing forms" and so forth to the signs of qualities, the master Gung-thang Jamyang said that applying them to the signs of wisdom is perfectly consistent with the *Large* and *Eight Thousand Line* [Perfection of Wisdom] and so forth. This is the commentary on the twelfth chapter, the chapter on the manifestation of the world, from the commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* entitled *The Jewel Lamp that Clarifies the Reality of Profound Dependent Origination and Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*.

The manner of subduing opponents and teaching the profound doctrine of emptiness is also like this: just as the lion, king of beasts, dwelling in the ravines of the snowy mountains, causes fear in many predators and small animals—such as tigers, leopards, bears, and wild dogs—by roaring without harming any living creature, so too do the Buddhas, the lions among men, relying upon the profound meaning of the perfection of wisdom, which is emptiness, cause fear in many non-Buddhists who have fallen into the abyss of the view of a self, and they proclaim in the world the marvelous and vast sound of the ultimate dharma. Furthermore, a bodhisattva, having perfected the three gateways to liberation, becomes a Buddha; although they deliver countless sentient beings from the sufferings of the lower realms, they do not have the perception that suffering and sentient beings are truly established, and thus they teach that there is no defilement, no purification, no substantiality, no essence, and no basis.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Second, in order to explain the distinguishing characteristics marked by being "inconceivable" and so forth, the meaning of the fourteen verses beginning with "By whom it is seen in that way" is as follows: For a bodhisattva, when they see the nature of reality (dharmatā) through the meditative equipoise wisdom of the Mahāyāna path of seeing—such as the forbearance of the truth of suffering—they do not perceive form and the like; seeing the nature of reality of those things, which is thus inconceivable, incomparable, and so forth, is to see the nature of reality of all phenomena. How is it that the function of "knowledge of dharma" and the rest [operates]? Just as a king remains in equanimity without exerting effort in tasks, while the great ministers perform all the king’s duties, so too does the supreme, non-conceptual wisdom of the perfection of wisdom perform all the activities of the Buddha’s enlightened deeds, as well as all the qualities of abandonment and realization of the Solitary Realizers and Hearers. By these [verses], the distinguishing characteristics such as being "inconceivable" are indicated. To clarify this, it is said: Just as a great king does not go into the city or to other regions, but remains comfortably within his own royal palace while gathering in all the revenues and the like, so too the wisdom of the bodhisattva’s continuum that realizes the profound nature of reality—such as the forbearance of the truth of suffering—does not waver or go anywhere else; yet, by gathering all the qualities of the Buddha-ground within their own continuum, it is a quality of extraordinary activity. By this, the distinguishing characteristics of gathering the qualities of abandonment and realization of the three types of noble ones are indicated. This is the commentary on the thirteenth chapter, the chapter on the inconceivable, from the "Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate," a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the suchness of dependent origination.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Furthermore, when are the extraordinary qualities of a Buddha attained? heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Therefore, because unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is not attained through a partial aspect of skillful means and wisdom, the way in which a bodhisattva must train in the path of complete skillful means and wisdom is illustrated by an analogy. For instance, if the boat of people setting out upon the ocean breaks and falls apart, those who do not grasp onto a corpse, grass, a wooden plank, or the like, but remain as they are, will perish in the midst of the water—they will die and will not reach the shore of the ocean. However, one who does grasp onto wood or the like will, by relying upon it, safely reach the other shore of the ocean. Just so, any person who possesses the faith that seeks perfect enlightenment and has attained a joyful, inspired faith, but who, having found faith in the perfection of wisdom—the supreme path for attaining unsurpassed enlightenment and the mother that gives birth to all Victors—does not subsequently engage in practicing it, will not attain the fruit of perfect enlightenment. This is because the great ocean of cyclic existence, which is constantly churning with the waves of various types of suffering and distress, such as birth, aging, sickness, death, and mental unhappiness, will continue to revolve forever. Yet, when an individual is completely seized by the supreme perfection of wisdom that realizes the lack of true existence, they become skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality as it is, and, being free from grasping at characteristics, they will come to demonstrate the ultimate truth without error.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Furthermore, for example, if a potter who is not foolish makes a pot but does not fire it—that is, does not bake it in a fire—and then pours water into it, that pot is easily destroyed; because it is fragile, it will quickly perish. If one pours water into a pot that has been fired, it will not break along the way, nor will it suffer the destruction caused by the conditions of breaking, and it will safely arrive at its own home. Just so, even if a bodhisattva has great and abundant aspiration and faith in seeking perfect enlightenment, if they are completely bereft of the skill in means that accomplishes this and the path of the perfection of wisdom, they will fall into the inferior path, decline from the Great Vehicle, and quickly come to ruin. If that person’s continuum is completely seized by both the perfection of wisdom and the aspects of means—that is, faith and the like—then they will transcend the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and will attain the supreme enlightenment of perfect buddhahood.

If those qualities of means, such as faith and compassion, which seek the perfect enlightenment of those beings, are completely seized by the wisdom that realizes them as non-referential, then the two accumulations of merit and wisdom will be completely perfected; and because they do not fall within the scope of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and the like, one will quickly touch—that is, attain—the enlightenment of the Sugatas, which is supremely marvelous.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: To illustrate this with another example, it is said: For instance, a ship that is leaky, has holes, and has not been well repaired will, while in the middle of the ocean with its cargo and merchants, be destroyed and come to ruin. However, if that ship is well inspected and has been properly repaired, it will not be destroyed or perish in the middle of the waters, and the merchants and their cargo will safely reach the shore on the other side of the ocean. In the same way, even if a bodhisattva has a continuum fully endowed with faith, compassion, and the like, if they do not rely upon the path of the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly decline from perfect enlightenment. If that same person, who possesses such marvelous faith and the like, is also endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom, they will not be harmed by the mindset of the inferior vehicle, and without declining from the path of the Great Vehicle, they will attain the enlightenment of the victorious ones.

[3-191] translation already produced for this document:
Furthermore, for example, if a potter who is not foolish makes a pot but does not fire it—that is, does not bake it in a fire—and then pours water into it, that pot is easily destroyed; because it is fragile, it will quickly perish. If one pours water into a pot that has been fired, it will not break along the way, nor will it suffer the destruction caused by the conditions of breaking, and it will safely arrive at its own home. Just so, even if a bodhisattva has great and abundant aspiration and faith in seeking perfect enlightenment, if they are completely bereft of the skill in means that accomplishes this and the path of the perfection of wisdom, they will fall into the inferior path, decline from the Great Vehicle, and quickly come to ruin. If that person’s continuum is completely seized by both the perfection of wisdom and the aspects of means—that is, faith and the like—then they will transcend the two stages of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas and will attain the supreme enlightenment of perfect buddhahood.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: The importance of practicing the union of means and wisdom without separation is taught as follows: For instance, a person who has reached the age of one hundred and twenty and is at the end of their life, suffering from old age, illness, and the like, may be able to rise from their seat, but they are unable to travel any distance on their own strength because they are aged and decrepit. If that person is supported by two strong individuals, one on each side, they will not face the danger of falling along the way and will easily reach the destination they wish to go. In the same way, a bodhisattva who has only weak wisdom realizing emptiness, even if they have entered the path of the Great Vehicle, will decline before attaining the fruit of unexcelled enlightenment. If that same bodhisattva’s entire path of the continuum is fully seized by the aspects of means, such as faith, and by supreme wisdom realizing non-truth, they will not decline from the path of the supreme vehicle and will quickly attain the enlightenment of the tathāgatas. Therefore, bodhisattvas endowed with intelligence should train in the path that completes both means and wisdom, so as to seize the royal throne of supreme enlightenment. This is the commentary on the fourteenth chapter, the chapter on examples, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

To illustrate this with another example, it is said: For instance, a ship that is leaky, has holes, and has not been well repaired will, while in the middle of the ocean with its cargo and merchants, be destroyed and come to ruin. However, if that ship is well inspected and has been properly repaired, it will not be destroyed or perish in the middle of the waters, and the merchants and their cargo will safely reach the shore on the other side of the ocean. In the same way, even if a bodhisattva has a continuum fully endowed with faith, compassion, and the like, if they do not rely upon the path of the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly decline from perfect enlightenment. If that same person, who possesses such marvelous faith and the like, is also endowed with the supreme perfection of wisdom, they will not be harmed by the mindset of the inferior vehicle, and without declining from the path of the Great Vehicle, they will attain the enlightenment of the victorious ones.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: In order to demonstrate that the practice of the exceptional application of the Great Vehicle and its attainment depend upon relying in the proper manner upon a spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle, three verses beginning with "Bodhisattva" are spoken. In this regard, a bodhisattva who abides in the stage of the initial practitioner—that is, one who abides in the first stage, the Joyous, and so forth—who, with a pure resolute intention to attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening for the sake of others, has entered into the practice of cultivating the exceptional application of the Great Vehicle while seeking the supreme awakening of a Buddha, should, as a good student who possesses faith and respect for the guru and who acts according to whatever is taught, always rely upon learned gurus who possess supreme views and conduct and who are capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom sutras without error.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: If one asks what the reason is for needing to rely [upon a spiritual friend] in that way, it is because all qualities—such as the knowledge of the Mahayana path and its fruition, and the arising of those paths within one’s own continuum—arise from relying in the proper manner upon a spiritual friend. This is because those spiritual friends point out this Mahayana path, the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, the Victorious One, the perfectly awakened Buddha, who possesses the supreme of all qualities, has stated that the qualities of abandonment and realization—such as the Buddha’s powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—are attained by relying upon a Mahayana spiritual friend, for there is no basis for those qualities to arise without relying upon a spiritual friend. Thus, it is out of love that we are instructed to rely upon a spiritual friend in the proper manner through both intention and application. By this, the characteristic of being completely encompassed by the skillful means of a spiritual friend is demonstrated. If one asks what kind of instructions and guidance the spiritual friends provide, they instruct one in the side of skillful means by saying: "The summary of the Mahayana path that you must practice is the six perfections; train properly in the vast practices of the perfection of generosity—giving away your body, enjoyments, and all roots of virtue to others—as well as the perfections of pure ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom, and dedicate all these roots of virtue to unsurpassed awakening without letting them be tainted by the stains of the Lesser Vehicle’s way of thinking." Furthermore, they instruct one in the side of wisdom by saying: "Do not, through a mistaken sense of reality, grasp at or hold as supreme that ultimate great awakening as if it were a truly existent, undefiled aggregate, such as the aggregate of ethical discipline." This is how one should instruct the initial practitioner who is at the first of the seven [stages] of awakening. By this, the characteristic of the distinction of having no taste for grasping at reality is demonstrated.

[3-194] translation already produced for this document:
In order to demonstrate that the practice of the exceptional application of the Great Vehicle and its attainment depend upon relying in the proper manner upon a spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle, three verses beginning with "Bodhisattva" are spoken. In this regard, a bodhisattva who abides in the stage of the initial practitioner—that is, one who abides in the first stage, the Joyous, and so forth—who, with a pure resolute intention to attain unsurpassed, perfect awakening for the sake of others, has entered into the practice of cultivating the exceptional application of the Great Vehicle while seeking the supreme awakening of a Buddha, should, as a good student who possesses faith and respect for the guru and who acts according to whatever is taught, always rely upon learned gurus who possess supreme views and conduct and who are capable of teaching the meaning of the perfection of wisdom sutras without error.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Third, in order to demonstrate the defining characteristics of those who possess the distinct functions of being a protector of benefit and happiness and so forth, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Acting in that way" is explained. By the power of having cultivated the distinct application of the Great Vehicle, the great bodhisattvas who excellently teach the instructions on how to practice the path of the Great Vehicle—acting in that way as previously explained—are like an ocean of qualities of abandonment and realization. These "moons of speech," who possess the rays of the nectar of the profound and extensive Dharma, are: because they teach the Dharma that is the cause of benefit and happiness, they have become a refuge that dispels the suffering of beings; they have become a helper that establishes them in the happiness of liberation; and they have become a place that dispels the obscurations of karma, which are the cause of suffering. Likewise, they have become a support for proceeding to great enlightenment; they have become the wisdom that distinguishes between good and evil; they are an island because they establish those who are drowning in the river of existence upon the dry land of the holy Dharma, the true path; they are like a captain who desires or performs the task of completely guiding them across the ocean of cyclic existence by teaching the meaning of the unborn; they have become a great lamp of Dharma that dispels the darkness of ignorance and makes the path to enlightenment shine brightly; and because they speak of the profound meaning of emptiness, the supreme Dharma, they are "unshaken" in that they cannot be disturbed by opponents, Māra, or non-Buddhists, and they are indestructible in any respect. Since they have attained certainty regarding the profound Dharma through valid cognition, their confidence in victory over all directions in explaining it is fully perfected. This is what is meant. Furthermore, the phrase "refuge of beings" indicates the defining characteristic of the knowledge of the basis, while "helper" and so forth indicate the defining characteristics of the knowledge of the path and so on. Even in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, it is said: "Subhūti, any bodhisattva mahāsattva who has embarked for the sake of benefiting the world, for the sake of the world's happiness, and for the sake of compassion for the world, and who, having fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfectly complete enlightenment, becomes a protector of the world," and so forth. By this, the first nine functions, such as being a protector of benefit and happiness, are briefly indicated together. Then, by the passage beginning with "Subhūti, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva..." it is explained in detail.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: In this way, those bodhisattvas possess such profound and difficult-to-fathom qualities, and having generated within their mental continuum the non-conceptual primordial wisdom—which is attained through the power of cultivating the practice and is devoid of the elaborations of dualistic appearance—they are free from hesitation, doubt, and two-mindedness regarding the teachings of the Great Vehicle. Having attained certainty regarding their own path through valid cognition, they possess the meaning of conviction. By virtue of this, upon hearing the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not let their minds waver from its meaning; rather, because they have attained deep certainty in their own path and have internalized it, they do not rely on others. They do not go wherever others might lead them, and it should be known that they are irreversible from the Great Vehicle.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: This perfection of wisdom, which is the teaching of the Buddhas, the guides, is supremely profound. The way things are—the suchness of phenomena—is difficult to see as it is by a mind that possesses dualistic appearance, and it is not directly realized by anyone whose continuum is tainted by the ordinary person’s grasping at true existence; in the ultimate sense, there is no attainment, nor is there anything that will be attained or that does not exist.

[3-197] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the fourth point, demonstrating the nature and characteristics, the meaning of the six verses beginning with "Those endowed with great renown" is as follows: Those who have entered the path of the Great Vehicle and possess the great renown of being called "bodhisattvas" in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions don the great armor that is extremely difficult to undertake. They generate the mind with the thought, "I alone shall establish all sentient beings, who are as vast as space, in non-abiding nirvāṇa." Furthermore, they do not don this armor by way of apprehending as truly existent the nature of phenomena such as the five aggregates, the eighteen constituents, and the twelve sense spheres, which are the side of the thoroughly afflicted. Rather, because they are free from the notion of attachment to the path of the three vehicles—which are the side of the antidotes and the purified—and because they abide in the perfection of wisdom, in which no phenomenon is apprehended or grasped as truly established, they do not decline from their own perfect welfare, and thus do not turn back from perfect enlightenment. They do not waver from the path of the Great Vehicle, which is the perfect welfare of others, and because no one, including Māra, can afflict their mental continuum, they are of the nature of not declining from or being disturbed by the two perfect welfares.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: In this way, because this profound suchness is deep and difficult to fathom, when the compassionate Buddha, the Blessed One—who works to accomplish the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings—attained the unsurpassed, great enlightenment and became perfectly and fully awakened, he thought, "This profound Dharma that I have realized is difficult for the masses of sentient beings, whose intellects are dull, to understand," and thus he was initially disinclined to teach the Dharma. As it is said in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*: "I have found a Dharma that is profound, peaceful, free from elaborations, luminous, and unconditioned, like nectar. Since whoever I teach it to will not understand, I shall remain silent and hide it in the forest." After he had spoken thus and acted in a way that did not involve teaching the Dharma for a time, he turned the wheel of Dharma in reliance upon the request made by Mahābrahmā.

In this way, those bodhisattvas possess such profound and difficult-to-fathom qualities, and having generated within their mental continuum the non-conceptual primordial wisdom—which is attained through the power of cultivating the practice and is devoid of the elaborations of dualistic appearance—they are free from hesitation, doubt, and two-mindedness regarding the teachings of the Great Vehicle. Having attained certainty regarding their own path through valid cognition, they possess the meaning of conviction. By virtue of this, upon hearing the profound perfection of wisdom, they do not let their minds waver from its meaning; rather, because they have attained deep certainty in their own path and have internalized it, they do not rely on others. They do not go wherever others might lead them, and it should be known that they are irreversible from the Great Vehicle.

[3-199] translation already produced for this document:
This perfection of wisdom, which is the teaching of the Buddhas, the guides, is supremely profound. The way things are—the suchness of phenomena—is difficult to see as it is by a mind that possesses dualistic appearance, and it is not directly realized by anyone whose continuum is tainted by the ordinary person’s grasping at true existence; in the ultimate sense, there is no attainment, nor is there anything that will be attained or that does not exist.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Why is this profound Dharma difficult to understand? It is because sentient beings, due to their familiarity with grasping at true existence since beginningless time, perceive all that appears as truly existent and hold it to be established as such. They delight in the objects of desire—the bases for the arising of attachment and other afflictions—and crave objects such as forms and sounds. They dwell in grasping at these as truly existent, and, being unskilled in the profound meaning of suchness and ignorant of the profound and vast path as it is, they have become foolish and deluded, like those dwelling in the midst of darkness. The phenomena of the path to be attained are devoid of true existence; thus, there is not even the slightest true establishment, nor is there any grasping at true existence by the non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise, because it realizes the meaning of suchness without error.

In this way, because this profound suchness is deep and difficult to fathom, when the compassionate Buddha, the Blessed One—who works to accomplish the benefit and happiness of all sentient beings—attained the unsurpassed, great enlightenment and became perfectly and fully awakened, he thought, "This profound Dharma that I have realized is difficult for the masses of sentient beings, whose intellects are dull, to understand," and thus he was initially disinclined to teach the Dharma. As it is said in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra*: "I have found a Dharma that is profound, peaceful, free from elaborations, luminous, and unconditioned, like nectar. Since whoever I teach it to will not understand, I shall remain silent and hide it in the forest." After he had spoken thus and acted in a way that did not involve teaching the Dharma for a time, he turned the wheel of Dharma in reliance upon the request made by Mahābrahmā.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**
translation:
In this way, those phenomena that transcend the world are inconsistent with worldly beings and are supreme; therefore, conflict arises with worldly beings, because worldly beings hold things to be truly established, while the Buddha teaches that they are not truly established. Worldly beings, not seeing the actual state of phenomena, engage in conflict, whereas the Tathāgata, although teaching that they do not exist in the ultimate sense, accepts phenomena that are like illusions in accordance with worldly convention. The Sutra states: "One should not conflict with worldly beings; whatever they hold to exist in the world, one also holds to exist." This is the commentary on the fifteenth chapter, the chapter on gods, from the *Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the suchness of dependent origination.

To illustrate by analogy that the *dharmadhātu* is without any difference in essence: just as the element of space is not established as having the essence of form and is not limited by directions or boundaries—so that the eastern direction, the southern direction, and likewise the western direction and the northern direction, these four directions are limitless and thus have no end—in the same way, the zenith, the nadir, and the four intermediate directions, in short, the vastness of the ten directions, exist wherever they may be, for there is nowhere that is not pervaded by space. In those spaces, there is no difference in essence, nor is there any distinction such as shape or the like.

Just as in that analogy, the suchness of phenomena of the past, the suchness of those that have not yet come, that is, the future, the suchness of those that are present, the suchness of persons such as arhats, the suchness of all phenomena that are objects of knowledge, the suchness of the fruit of Buddhahood, and the suchness of the phenomena of the path—in all of these, there is no difference or distinction in essence, for they are of one taste in the *dharmadhātu*, which is merely the negation of the object to be negated, true establishment.

Why is this profound Dharma difficult to understand? It is because sentient beings, due to their familiarity with grasping at true existence since beginningless time, perceive all that appears as truly existent and hold it to be established as such. They delight in the objects of desire—the bases for the arising of attachment and other afflictions—and crave objects such as forms and sounds. They dwell in grasping at these as truly existent, and, being unskilled in the profound meaning of suchness and ignorant of the profound and vast path as it is, they have become foolish and deluded, like those dwelling in the midst of darkness. The phenomena of the path to be attained are devoid of true existence; thus, there is not even the slightest true establishment, nor is there any grasping at true existence by the non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise, because it realizes the meaning of suchness without error.

heading: **དབྱེ་བ།**

heading: **ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན།**
translation: Aids to liberation. The sixth, explaining the aids to liberation itself: regarding the meaning of the three verses beginning with "The enlightenment of the Sugatas," the ultimate goal to be attained is the enlightenment of the Sugatas, which is a reality (dharmatā) comparable to space, free from the various distinct phenomena of differing natures. Any bodhisattva who wishes to attain this must, through means such as the aspiration to seek perfect enlightenment for the sake of others, and by possessing special methods, strive in the application to the supreme perfection of wisdom, which realizes that cyclic existence and peace are equal in being empty of inherent existence. This guide, the Mother, the perfection of wisdom of the Victors, is such that without it, that great enlightenment can never be attained, because this perfection of wisdom, which realizes the true nature of all phenomena, is the supreme cause for attaining that very state. For example, if a bird with a massive body of one hundred and fifty-one yojanas were to have its wings worn away and lost, such that it lacked the skill and power to fly in the sky, and if that bird were to think, "I shall travel from the realm of the gods of the Thirty-three to this Jambudvīpa," and then failed to exert itself, there would be no alternative but for that bird to suffer great harm, such as injury to its body, in that situation.

heading: **ཐར་པ་ཆ་མཐུན།**
translation: Similar to that analogy, this path of the five perfections, such as generosity, which serves as the means for the Victors to attain enlightenment, even when practiced for a long duration through the exertion of many billions of eons, and even when one relies constantly in this world upon the Bodhisattva’s countless, vast, and infinite aspirations, such as the ten hundred thousand aspirations, one cannot attain great enlightenment if the method and wisdom are not complete. When one is devoid of such exceptional method and wisdom—namely, the immeasurable skillful means such as dedicating roots of virtue toward omniscience, and the wisdom that realizes all phenomena as being empty of true existence and equal—one falls into the state of a Śrāvaka, just as a large bird without wings, having leaped, falls downward and suffers. Therefore, one who desires to attain great enlightenment must become skilled in the five areas, such as faith, and must train in the path where method and wisdom are complete. This is what is meant.

translation: The seventh [topic], the factors of definite discrimination, is stated in the *Ornament* as: "Faith in the Buddha and so forth," up to "should be known through the ripening factors and so forth." There are three parts: the definition, the divisions, and the boundaries. Regarding the first, this refers to the realization of the Mahāyāna meaning directly taught in this context, which is characterized primarily by the method; it is the definition of the Mahāyāna path of preparation directly taught in this context. As for the divisions, there are the four, such as heat, of the Mahāyāna path of preparation as taught here. The boundaries are only within the Mahāyāna path of preparation. Regarding the meaning of the single verse taught to demonstrate such factors of definite discrimination, beginning with "the Buddha vehicle," if one asks how a Bodhisattva who wishes to definitely emerge—that is, to attain—great enlightenment by relying on this perfection of wisdom, which is the path of definite discrimination of the unsurpassed Buddha vehicle, the great path that is the single journey of all Victors, should enter the Mahāyāna path: one must generate great love and great compassion focused on all sentient beings and train in the six perfections and so forth. Therefore, one must first cultivate an even mind—a mind of equanimity—free from the limitations of attachment and aversion toward all infinite beings. One must abide in perceptions such as: the perception of parents toward elderly men and women; the perception of siblings toward those of equal age; the perception of sons and daughters toward the young; and the perception of friends, companions, and close relatives toward others. One must abide in a mind that is permanently beneficial, such as the desire to establish them in enlightenment, and a mind that is temporarily beneficial, such as the desire for their happiness in the present. One must exert oneself—that is, strive—for the benefit of sentient beings with a loving mind. One should be free from the faults of anger and harm, be without deceit, have a straightforward mental continuum, teach the Dharma through speech, speak gentle words that are agreeable to the mind, and perform physical actions of love that benefit others, thereby abandoning self-interest and engaging in the accomplishment of the entire benefit and happiness of others. This directly teaches most of the objects of focus for the small, medium, and great [levels of] heat of the Mahāyāna path of preparation, and implicitly suggests the aspects of the peak and so forth. This is the commentary on the sixteenth chapter, the chapter on suchness, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

Similar to that analogy, this path of the five perfections, such as generosity, which serves as the means for the Victors to attain enlightenment, even when practiced for a long duration through the exertion of many billions of eons, and even when one relies constantly in this world upon the Bodhisattva’s countless, vast, and infinite aspirations, such as the ten hundred thousand aspirations, one cannot attain great enlightenment if the method and wisdom are not complete. When one is devoid of such exceptional method and wisdom—namely, the immeasurable skillful means such as dedicating roots of virtue toward omniscience, and the wisdom that realizes all phenomena as being empty of true existence and equal—one falls into the state of a Śrāvaka, just as a large bird without wings, having leaped, falls downward and suffers. Therefore, one who desires to attain great enlightenment must become skilled in the five areas, such as faith, and must train in the path where method and wisdom are complete. This is what is meant.

source: ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།བརྒྱད་པ་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། ངེས་བྱེད་ཡན་ལག་ནས་བཟུང་སྟེ། །ནས། དེ་རིང་འདིར་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་ཆོགས། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། གཟུགས་སོགས་ལ་བདེན་ཞེན་མངོན་འགྱུར་བ་ལྡོག་པ་སོགས་རྟགས་ཞེ་བཞི་པོ་གང་རུང་ཐོབ་པའི་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་བདུན་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། དབང་རྣོན་སྦྱོར་ལམ་ནས་རྟག་ཐོབ་པ་དང་། དབང་འབྲིང་མཐོང་ལམ་ནས་ཐོབ་བ་དང་། དབང་རྟུལ་སྒོམ་ལམ་ནས་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན་དང་གསུམ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། དེ་ལ་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་བའི་སྤྱིའི་མཚན་ཉིད་དམ་རྟགས་ཞུ་བ་ནི། འཇིག་རྟེན་མགོན་ལ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གིས་བསྟན་པའི་དོན། ས་འོག་ས་སྟེང་ས་བླའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གསུམ་གྱི་མགོན་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལ་གནས་བརྟན་རབ་འབྱོར་གྱིས་དྲི་བ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཞུས་པ། ཡོན་ཏན་རྒྱ་མཚོ་ལྟ་བུ་ཚད་མེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་དག་གིས་ཉོན་མོངས་མ་མཆིས་པ་སྟེ་ཉོན་མོངས་སྤངས་པ་ལས་མི་ཉམས་པའི་རྟགས་དང་མཚན་མ་ཇི་ལྟ་བུ་ཡིན་པ་དེ་བདག་ལ་བསྟན་དུ་གསོལ། དོན་གཉིས་སྒྲུབ་པའི་མཐུ་ཆེ་བ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་ཇི་ལྟར་རྫོགས་བྱང་ལས་སླར་ལྡོག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་བ་སྟེ་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཡིན་པར་ཤེས་པར་འགྱུར་བ་དེ་ལྟར་དེ་དག་གི་རྟགས་དང་ཡོན་ཏན་ཚད་མེད་པ་ལས་ཕྱོགས་ཙམ་རྒྱལ་བས་བདག་ལ་ལུང་བསྟན་དུ་གསོལ་ཞེས་ཞུས་པའོ། །
translation: The Sangha of Irreversible Bodhisattvas. To demonstrate the eighth, the Sangha of irreversible bodhisattvas, the Ornament states: "Starting from the limbs of definite discrimination, up to... today, here, the assembly of the irreversible." Regarding this, there are three: the definition, the classification, and the boundaries. The first: that bodhisattva who has attained any one of the forty-four signs, such as the reversal of the manifest grasping at the truth of forms and so forth, is the definition of the Sangha of bodhisattvas who have attained the signs of irreversibility. The second, regarding their classification: there are three, namely the Sangha of bodhisattvas who attain the signs from the path of preparation (for those of sharp faculties), those who attain them from the path of seeing (for those of medium faculties), and those who attain the signs from the path of meditation (for those of dull faculties). The third, the boundaries: they exist from the heat level of the path of preparation up to the end of the continuum. Regarding the request for the general definition or signs of irreversibility, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "To the protector of the world" is as follows: The elder Subhūti makes a full inquiry to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the protector of the three worlds—the subterranean, the terrestrial, and the celestial. He asks: "Please reveal to me what the signs and marks are by which those powerful bodhisattvas, who possess immeasurable qualities like an ocean, do not degenerate from the state of having abandoned the afflictions—that is, having no afflictions. Please reveal to me, from among the immeasurable signs and qualities of those powerful bodhisattvas who accomplish the two goals, a portion of how they do not turn back from perfect enlightenment, so that it may be known that they are irreversible bodhisattvas."

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: Regarding the explanation of the actual signs of non-retrogression, these are the signs of non-retrogression for those on the path of preparation, the path of seeing, and the path of meditation. As for the essence, the meaning taught by the three verses beginning with "the perception of difference" is the response given by the Blessed One to the question posed by Subhūti: A bodhisattva on the path of preparation who has realized the profound reality as it is, is free from the perception that grasps the essence of the dharmadhātu of all phenomena—such as the two, cyclic existence and nirvana—as being different. Because they have realized that all things, such as form, are of one taste in being empty of true existence, they have the sign of non-retrogression, which is called the turning away from the manifestation of grasping at the truth of phenomena. They speak words that are perfectly true, possessing both scripture and reasoning that correctly reveal the profound nature of reality, which is emptiness. Having known the qualities of the Three Jewels and attained faith of conviction, they do not go for refuge to other sectarian ascetics or brahmins, nor do they teach them. Being skilled in and convinced of the law of cause and effect and dependent origination, they abandon the manifestation of the ten non-virtues and so forth, and thus at all times they have abandoned the three lower realms and the eight states of non-freedom represented by them. Those wise ones always remain on the path of the ten virtues themselves and are intent on establishing other beings to be trained upon that path. Without a mind that looks toward material gain, such as offerings, honors, or wealth, they correctly instruct other beings in the six perfections, the four means of gathering, and so forth. Having attained certainty regarding the profound Dharma, they take delight in the profound reality and, without doubt, focus their minds one-pointedly. Since they have entered into the conduct of the three doors as being solely for the benefit of others, they always speak gentle words and possess the three—body, speech, and mind—of loving-kindness. Through familiarity with mindfulness, alertness, and conscientiousness, they have abandoned heedlessness in all situations of the four modes of deportment—whether going to another place, walking nearby, lying down, or sitting. Thus, even when walking on a path, they look only as far as a yoke’s length, and because they do not turn back from the path or tread upon black snakes and the like, their minds are without confusion. Because their moral discipline is perfectly pure and they do not engage in actions disparaged by the noble ones, all their internal and external conduct is purified; having abandoned wrong livelihood, they wear clean robes and so forth, making their three doors of body, speech, and mind beautiful and pleasing, being devoid of the stains of faults. No types of vermin appear on their bodies, and they do not desire gains and the like, as they adopt the qualities of asceticism. Just as one who follows a great bull does not encounter harm or injury on the path but meets with prosperity, they become the foremost among noble beings who walk straight on the middle path, which is free from the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism. Not only do they not harm others at any time, but they also remove the suffering of others and establish them in benefit and happiness; wishing to practice the Great Vehicle, they are not afraid to dwell even in the fire of hell for the sake of others due to the power of their compassion. Because they have deep conviction in the view that realizes the nature of reality, they cannot be led astray by others who teach a different path, and they recognize the demons who teach a false path disguised as the true path as being demons; thus, they are not harmed by the deeds of demons, are beyond the domain of demons, and, having attained certainty in method and wisdom through their own power, they do not rely on others. They enter into the four meditative absorptions, or even if they practice meditation, they do not dwell in the actual meditative absorption by relishing its taste; rather, all the activities of their three doors become conduct that pleases the Buddhas. These should be understood as the signs of non-retrogression from the Great Vehicle. These signs are also as stated in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*: Then, the venerable Subhūti said this to the Blessed One.

translation: "What are the aspects, what are the tokens, and what are the signs of an irreversible Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, O Blessed One?" By such questions, the text teaches the reversal of the perception of form and so forth; and by statements such as "entering into that reality, that nature, and abiding in that reality," it teaches the state of being free from doubt and so forth. The second section, explaining the tokens of one who is irreversible on the path of seeing, is taught by three verses beginning with "desiring fame." Although it appears to align with the explanation of Ye shes zhabs that a single line beginning with "meditative stabilization" teaches the token of the irreversible one on the path of seeing as the exhaustion of the limbs, the Master explains it as being taught from the phrase "not desiring fame" onwards. In this regard, a Bodhisattva abiding on the path of seeing knows all phenomena as empty of truth and like an illusion, and because they have reversed the conceptualized grasping at truth—which is the grasping at form and so forth as true—they do not desire their own good reputation. Because they have given rise to exceptional love and compassion in their hearts, they are free from the mental agitation or the mental afflictions caused by anger. Because they are skilled in the means of taming the mind, even if they become householders for the sake of others, they are never attached to any objects of desire and give away all their possessions to others. Realizing selflessness and having become subject to compassion, they follow the conduct of a noble being, abandoning wrong livelihood and the extremes of karma. For the sake of their own livelihood, they do not seek wealth through terrifying karmic results such as taking life, or through deceitful speech, flattery, or manipulation. They do not engage in violent, magical, or coercive rites to harm others for their own sake. They do not perform mantras to control women or to force them into submission due to attachment. They do not make predictions for those in the womb, saying, "This one will be a boy, this one will be a girl," for the sake of fame and the like. By thus purifying wrong livelihood and the extremes of wrong karma, they possess the tokens of one who is irreversible. They are diligent in practicing the supreme perfection of wisdom by being completely secluded from the distractions and worldly busyness that agitate body, speech, and mind. Because their mental continuum is tamed by love and compassion, wherever they dwell, they are free from mutual conflict and strife, and their loving heart—which wishes to establish others in happiness—is completely stable and cannot be stolen by adverse conditions. Wishing to attain for themselves the rank of a Buddha who knows all aspects of knowable things for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of others, they possess a mind that is constantly devoted to the holy Dharma—the Buddha's teachings—and is diligent in practicing it. Having abandoned birth in borderlands, among barbarians, or in lands where the Dharma does not flourish—where one is not free from the power of karma and afflictions—they obtain a body that is entirely virtuous. Because they have attained certainty and confidence in the realizations or levels they have reached, they are unshakable and undiminished, always remaining like Mount Meru, free from hesitation or doubt. They are diligent in the yoga of practicing the Great Vehicle, even abandoning their own lives for the sake of the Dharma. These are the marvelous qualities; one should know that these are the tokens of a Bodhisattva abiding in the path of seeing who is irreversible from complete enlightenment. In this regard, one should also understand the tokens taught here through the logic of the *Pramāṇavārttika*, such as "the result arises from the gathering of causes." These tokens are also taught in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* through passages such as, "Furthermore, Subhūti, if one desires, one enters into the first meditative stabilization." This is the commentary on the seventeenth chapter, the chapter on the aspects of the irreversible, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

translation: Following this, although it is necessary to teach the characteristics of a non-returning bodhisattva on the path of meditation, because the basis of the quality—the path of meditation—must be established first in order to ascertain the signs of a non-returning bodhisattva, there are two parts: an explanation of the path of meditation and an explanation of the signs of a non-returning bodhisattva on the path of meditation. The first of these also has two parts: the profundity of the path of meditation and an explanation of the path of meditation as the basis of the quality. Regarding the first, the meaning of the three verses beginning with "Form, feeling, and..." is taught here in accordance with the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra*, which states, "The path of meditation is profound." Phenomena such as form appear to exist to the innate mind that has not examined or analyzed them, but when the wisdom of reasoning that investigates the ultimate is used to analyze the individual parts of those that have form, and to analyze the individual momentary parts of those that do not have form, one cannot find an intrinsic nature remaining; thus, one is freed from the extreme of permanence. Because all actions and functions are possible within that which appears like an illusion while being empty, one is freed from the extreme of nihilism. Since appearance and emptiness assist one another, emptiness is profound. Likewise, form is also profound because it is not produced in the ultimate sense. Similarly, feeling, perception, volition, and consciousness are also profound, because they are empty of intrinsic nature and are merely imputed by conceptual thought. Because they are naturally isolated, there are no signs such as "form" in the ultimate sense, and because the aspiration that is intensely attached to the result is completely pacified, the meaning of the actual mode of existence is difficult to fathom. For example, when one seeks the depth of the ocean with an arrow, one cannot find the bottom or the limit by saying, "It is like this." In the same way, when one investigates and analyzes with the wisdom that examines suchness, one cannot find the depth of the aggregates such as form. Since the object, emptiness, is profound, one should know that the subject that realizes it—the Mahayana path of meditation—is also profound.

The question, "What greater fruit could there be for such a profound path of meditation?" is posed with the thought: "For a bodhisattva who has realized this profound Dharma—in which, from the perspective of the non-conceptual wisdom of meditative equipoise that is the subject of the ultimate, the path of meditation of the supreme Great Vehicle, there is no conventional proliferation of the aggregates, elements, or sense-fields, because one is free from attachment through intense realization—what could be greater or more supreme than the immeasurable merit that is perfectly accomplished through realizing the emptiness of the natural state of phenomena, as previously explained, given that it is immeasurable?"

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: Secondly, regarding the explanation of the path of meditation as the basis of the distinction: although there are nine antidotes for the nine types of discursive thoughts of grasping at true existence, here they are condensed into three. To explain the first, the minor path of meditation, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "A bodhisattva..." is as follows: Even if a bodhisattva were to practice generosity or maintain perfectly pure ethical discipline for a thousand billion eons while mentally oriented toward seeking the awakening of the Lesser Vehicle, and were to offer these to Śrāvaka Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and so forth, if another son of the Victorious One were to possess the practice of the nature of the minor path of meditation, and upon arising from that in the subsequent attainment, were to explain or express even a single reality of the perfection of wisdom—which is the supreme object of expression—then that previous generosity and ethical discipline would not even be a fraction of the merit of that. This is what is meant.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: To explain the great path of meditation, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "That merit also..." is as follows: Although there is immeasurable merit in terms of conventional reality when explaining the profound dharma in accordance with what one has personally meditated upon, in terms of ultimate reality, there is not the slightest thing established. This is because that merit arising from explaining the dharma is also, due to being established by characteristics, something that is accumulated; likewise, it is something that is cultivated because it is empty of intrinsic nature and empty of the object of negation, truly established existence. Furthermore, because it is not established from its own side and arises from the gathering of causes, conditions, and dependent relationships, it is illusory; and because it is of the nature of being empty of truth and like an illusion, one should thoroughly understand it as lacking any essence. When one practices the profound perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas—which is the nature of the great path of meditation—in this way, then at the time of engaging in such practice, one takes hold of, or generates, immeasurable and boundless merit. Thus it is said. Regarding the objection raised in the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* with the words, "In that which is inexpressible, / Decrease and increase are not tenable," and so forth: because all phenomena are equal in the expanse of reality as being without intrinsic nature, one might wonder if it is unreasonable to speak of the exhaustion of what is to be abandoned and the arising of the antidote, and therefore unreasonable to speak of a sequence of superior and inferior realizations for the heirs of the Conqueror. To address this doubt, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "The Buddha explained..." is as follows: All the various dharmas that the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, have taught—whether they have taught the meaning in brief, explained it in great detail by connecting the meaning to examples, or elaborated upon it through endless logic of refutation and proof—are all, in ultimate reality, such that neither the expressed nor the expression can be found, and one should understand that they are merely names used conventionally. Even if one were to express the profound reality of emptiness for many tens of millions of eons using countless logics of refutation and proof, there is no decrease or exhaustion in the expanse of reality of the dharmas of the path of meditation and so forth, nor is there the slightest increase or growth; thus, the objection that the exhaustion of what is to be abandoned and the arising of the antidote are untenable is addressed. In response, if one establishes that there is no increase or decrease in ultimate reality, then since that is exactly what we ourselves assert, it results in establishing what is already established.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: In order to demonstrate that, conventionally, the phenomena of cyclic existence and nirvana are like illusions because they lack permanence, and thus are subject to increase and decrease, one verse is spoken beginning with the words "Of the Victors." The meaning of this is that those phenomena which are the path of the Great Vehicle—such as what is called the "six perfections," which is the single path traversed by the Victors—are indeed proclaimed and spoken of as existing merely by name, in terms of their own essence. However, a bodhisattva who, in conventional reality, dedicates all roots of virtue to unsurpassed enlightenment, and who is free from the arrogance of grasping at a superior self and the conceit of being attached to the fruition to be attained as truly existent, is not without the path of the union of method and wisdom, as they do not fail in the Great Vehicle by practicing the path where dependent origination, cause, and effect are unerring, and they are merely illusory in conventional terms. It is not only not contradictory that they will attain the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha, but it is entirely logical and possesses the valid cognition of proof. This is the commentary on the eighteenth chapter, on emptiness, from the "Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate," a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the true nature of dependent origination.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: If someone were to argue, "Even conventionally, it is not logical for enlightenment to occur through the progression of realization, because each individual mind that arises earlier or later lacks the capacity for enlightenment, and it is not the case that all earlier and later minds gather simultaneously, as it is impossible for all earlier and later moments to occur at the same time; nor is it dependent upon the former, because the latter does not arise without the former," then, having addressed this objection from within, the text demonstrates the answer by way of an analogy. The meaning of the five verses beginning with "The wick of an oil lamp" is as follows: For example, when the wick of an oil lamp and the burning flame meet, the wick is not consumed by the first moment of the flame alone, yet without that first moment of the flame, the wick is not consumed; nor is the wick consumed by the final contact of the flame alone, yet without the final flame, the wick is not consumed. Nevertheless, one should understand that the wick is consumed in its entirety through the continuum of all the earlier and later moments of the flame.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: Connecting that aforementioned analogy to the meaning of the present context regarding the manner of attaining enlightenment: just as in that analogy, it is not the case that the first moment of generating the mind alone touches supreme enlightenment, nor is it possible to touch that enlightenment without that first moment of mind; and it is not the case that the final moment of mind in that continuum alone attains great enlightenment, which is the pacification of all that is to be abandoned, nor is it possible to attain that enlightenment without that final moment. However, it is through the sequential continuum of the earlier and later generation of the mind that enlightenment is attained by way of the nature of dependent origination. Having thus generally shown that the collection of earlier and later moments of the path of enlightenment is the cause of enlightenment, it is now taught that, in particular, the first moment of the path of enlightenment is also a primary cause, similar to a seed. It is stated: just as from a seed, a sprout arises, and from that, the stalk, flowers, and fruits emerge, yet at the time when its own fruit is established, that seed is also exhausted—it is not the case that the fruit, the tree, does not exist—so too, in this context of the path, the first moment of initially generating the mind is also a cause of enlightenment; at the time of attaining enlightenment, it is also exhausted, yet it is not the case that the fruit, enlightenment, does not exist; rather, one becomes perfectly and fully awakened.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: To demonstrate that the second moment is also a cause, the manner in which a result arises in dependence upon a cause is as follows: having attained the seed itself, which possesses the capacity to produce its own result, the result—various grains, rice, and so forth—comes into being. At the time when that seed’s result ripens—that is, at that time—the seed itself does not exist, yet it is not the case that its own continuum is absent. In the same way, this enlightenment of the Victors also arises from the completion of the components of the path, such as the generation of bodhicitta. Furthermore, when one searches for the object designated by such conventional labels, it is devoid of an intrinsic nature; therefore, one should understand that it arises as a mere illusion, existing only as a convention that has not been analyzed or examined.

Thus it is said. Having thus explained in detail the basis of the meditation path, along with its incidental and related topics, [the text continues].

To demonstrate that the second moment is also a cause, the manner in which a result arises in dependence upon a cause is as follows: having attained the seed itself, which possesses the capacity to produce its own result, the result—various grains, rice, and so forth—comes into being. At the time when that seed’s result ripens—that is, at that time—the seed itself does not exist, yet it is not the case that its own continuum is absent. In the same way, this enlightenment of the Victors also arises from the completion of the components of the path, such as the generation of bodhicitta. Furthermore, when one searches for the object designated by such conventional labels, it is devoid of an intrinsic nature; therefore, one should understand that it arises as a mere illusion, existing only as a convention that has not been analyzed or examined.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་བྱང་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགེ་འདུན།**
translation: The second point, in order to demonstrate the actual signs of non-retrogression for one who abides on the path of cultivating the special qualities that are the subject of the current context, is the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Empty, signless..." This is as follows: A bodhisattva who engages in the meaning of realizing the profound phenomena—the three doors of liberation, such as emptiness because all phenomena are empty of being established by their own essence, signlessness because there are no signs of causes being truly established, and wishlessness because of the way one clings to results as being truly established—and who possesses special methods such as great compassion, does not touch upon the nirvana that is merely a one-sided peace. Furthermore, although they take birth in cyclic existence for the sake of others, because they directly realize that existence is empty of true existence and do not engage in the signs of manifest clinging, they do not abide in either of the extremes of existence or peace. This is like a skilled boatman who travels back and forth across the ocean with cargo, yet does not abide in the two extremes of the far shore or the near shore, nor does he abide in the ocean itself. Thus it is said.

Having explained the manner of enlightenment in detail, to summarize the meaning: just as a water jar is filled by the accumulation of many drops of water—filling that jar completely, little by little, in sequence from the first drop to the last—in the same way, the initial generation of bodhicitta at the stage of the path of accumulation is also a cause of supreme enlightenment. However, it is not that alone; rather, it is through the subsequent generation of the pure altruistic intention and so forth, and by traversing the sequence of the ten stages starting from the path of application, that one relies upon the qualities of the stages and paths increasing progressively, and thereby, through the completion of all pure qualities, one becomes a Buddha. Thus it is said. Having thus explained in detail the basis of the meditation path, along with its incidental and related topics, [the text continues].

heading: **སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ། དགུ་པ་སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། ཆོས་རྣམས་རྨི་ལམ་འདྲ་བའི་ཕྱིར། ནས། ལན་ནི་ཇི་སྐད་བཤད་པར་ཟད། ཅེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་རྗེས་ཐོབ་ཀྱི་གནས་སྐབས་སུ་བདེན་འཛིན་མངོན་འགྱུར་བ་བ་སྐྱེ་བའི་གོ་སྐབས་ཟད་པར་བཅོམ་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་གྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་གསུམ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་ས་མཚམས་དག་པས་ས་གསུམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། སྐུ་གསུམ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་གསུམ་ལས་ཆོས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་སྲིད་ཞི་མཉམ་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྦྱོར་བ་འཆད་པར། དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། དེ་ལྟར་སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་མཉམ་པ་ཉིད་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་རྟོགས་ཤིང་གོམས་པའི་ལམ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྣམས་ནི་འདི་སྙམ་དུ་བདག་སྟོབས་བཅུ་མངའ་བ་རྒྱལ་བས་བླ་མེད་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཏུ་ལུང་བསྟན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་དུ་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པ་དང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་ལ་རེག་པར་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་པའི་བདེན་བཞེན་གྱི་རློམ་སེམས་མེད་ཅིང་། དོན་དམ་དཔྱོད་བྱེད་ཀྱི་རིགས་ཤེས་ཀྱིས་དཔྱད་ཅིང་བཙལ་ན་སྲིད་ཞི་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བསྡུས་པའི་ཆོས་འདི་དག་ལ་བསལ་བྱ་དང་སྤང་བྱ་སོགས་ཅིི་ཡང་མེད་དོ་ཅེས་ཁོང་དུ་ཆུད་ནས་སྤངས་བྱ་འཁོར་བ་དང་ཐོབ་བྱ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་གནས་པ་ལ་བློས་མི་བཟོད་པའི་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་པར་གདེངས་དང་ལྡན་པར་དེ་ལྟར་སྤྱོད་པ་ནི་བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཟབ་མོ་སྲིད་ཞི་བདེན་སྟོང་དུ་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་ལ་སྤྱོད་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །
translation:
The Application of the Equality of Existence and Peace. Ninth, in order to demonstrate the application of the equality of existence and peace, the Ornament states: "Because phenomena are like a dream," up to, "The answer is just as has been explained." Regarding this, there are three points: the definition, the classification, and the levels. The first is: The yoga of the pure levels, which has completely destroyed the opportunity for the manifest grasping of true existence to arise during the state of subsequent attainment, by being seized by the wisdom that directly realizes existence and peace as empty of true existence, is the definition of the application of the equality of existence and peace. The second, when classified, consists of the three wisdoms of the three pure levels. The third, the levels, is that it exists only on the three pure levels.

In order to explain the application of the equality of existence and peace, which is one of the three applications that accomplish the three bodies, and which accomplishes the dharmakāya, the meaning of the single verse beginning with, "A bodhisattva who engages in this way," is as follows: Bodhisattvas who engage in the path of directly realizing and familiarizing themselves with the equality of existence and peace as empty of true existence do not have the pride of true grasping, thinking, "I will be prophesied by the Victor, who possesses the ten powers, to attain unsurpassed enlightenment," nor do they think, "I will touch upon supreme enlightenment." Having understood that if one investigates and searches with the analytical wisdom that examines the ultimate, there is nothing at all to be eliminated or abandoned among these phenomena included within existence and peace, they abide in the illusion-like nature of the cyclic existence to be abandoned and the enlightenment to be attained. Without the unbearable fear of the mind, and possessing confidence, engaging in this way is the practice of the path of the profound wisdom of the Sugatas, which realizes existence and peace as empty of true existence. Thus it is said.

[3-221] translation already produced for this document:
The second point, in order to demonstrate the actual signs of non-retrogression for one who abides on the path of cultivating the special qualities that are the subject of the current context, is the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Empty, signless..." This is as follows: A bodhisattva who engages in the meaning of realizing the profound phenomena—the three doors of liberation, such as emptiness because all phenomena are empty of being established by their own essence, signlessness because there are no signs of causes being truly established, and wishlessness because of the way one clings to results as being truly established—and who possesses special methods such as great compassion, does not touch upon the nirvana that is merely a one-sided peace. Furthermore, although they take birth in cyclic existence for the sake of others, because they directly realize that existence is empty of true existence and do not engage in the signs of manifest clinging, they do not abide in either of the extremes of existence or peace. This is like a skilled boatman who travels back and forth across the ocean with cargo, yet does not abide in the two extremes of the far shore or the near shore, nor does he abide in the ocean itself. Thus it is said.

heading: **ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ།བཅུ་པ་ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། སེམས་ཅན་འཇིག་རྟེན་དེ་བཞིན་དུ། ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཞིང་ནི་དག་པ་ཡིན། ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད་དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། རང་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་འགྱུར་གྱི་ཞིང་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་འགྲུབ་པའི་སྨོན་ལམ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་རང་རྒྱུད་ལ་ནུས་པ་མཐུ་ཅན་དུ་འགྱུར་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད་། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་གི་སྣོད་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་། བཅུད་དག་པའི་སྦྱོར་བ་གཉིས་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་ན་ཡོད། ལོངས་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཞིང་དག་སྦྱོར་བ་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། འཇིག་རྟེན་དགོན་པའི་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཕྱོགས་བཅུའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་འདི་ན་གྲོང་ལས་རིང་དུ་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཆུ་དང་ཟས་ཀྱིས་དབེན་པའི་འབྲོག་དགོན་པའི་ལམ་ཉམ་ང་བ་གཅན་གཟན་གཏུམ་པོས་གང་བ་སོགས་སྣོད་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་དང་བཅུད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་རྣམས་ཀྱང་ཟས་གོས་ལོངས་སྤྱོད་ཀྱིས་དབུལ་ཞིང་ཕོངས་པའི་མུ་གེའི་དགོན་པ་དང་། ནང་གི་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་དང་རླུང་ཁྲིས་བད་རྐན་སོགས་ཕྱིའི་ནད་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་མཐོང་ནས་ཀྱང་དེ་ཐམས་ཅད་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་ཤེས་ནས་སྐྲག་པ་མེད་ཅིང་དེ་ནས་འདི་ལྟར་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་སྦྱང་པའི་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་ཆེན་པོ་གྱོན་ཏེ། ཀྱཻ་མ་སེམས་ཅན་འདི་དག་ནི་ལས་ངན་པ་བསོད་ནམས་མ་བསགས་པས་ནད་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པས་མནར་བ་སྙིང་རེ་རྫེ་བདག་གིས་འདི་དག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་དོན་དུ་རང་གང་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཁྱད་པར་ཅན་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་དང་མ་དག་པའི་སྣོད་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་གང་ཡང་མེད་པར་སྣོད་བཅུད་ཀྱི་འབྱོར་བ་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཞིག་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་དེའི་ཆེད་དུ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་སོགས་པའི་བསོད་ནམས་དང་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ཚོགས་བསོགས་པ་ལ་བསྐལ་པ་ཕྱི་མིའི་མུ་མཐར་ཐུག་གི་བར་དུ་རྟག་ཏུ་བརྩོན་པར་བྱ་ཞིང་དེ་དག་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་རབ་ཏུ་ཤེས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་ལ་སྲིང་མོ་གང་གཱའི་ལྷ་མོ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་སྐྱོ་བའི་ཡིད་ནི་རྡུལ་ཙམ་ཡང་སྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱེད་དོ་ཅེས་བསམ་པའི་གོ་ཆ་གྱོན་ཅིང་སྦྱོར་བས་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །ཞེས་སོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟམ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་གང་གཱའི་ལྷ་མོའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་བཅུ་དགུ་པའི་འགྲེལ་པའོ།།  །།
translation:
The Application of Purifying the Realm. The tenth, the application of purifying the realm, is stated in the *Ornament* as: "Just as for the world of sentient beings, [up to] the Buddha realm is pure." Regarding this, there are three parts: defining the characteristics, the divisions, and the scope. The first is: the yoga of the pure realm, which is the root of virtue—such as the aspiration to accomplish a special realm where one will attain buddhahood—becoming powerful and effective in one's own continuum; this is the definition of the application of purifying the realm. The second, its divisions, are two: the application of purifying the environment of the Buddha realm, and the application of purifying the inhabitants. The third, the scope, exists in the three pure grounds.

To explain that very application of purifying the realm which accomplishes the enjoyment body, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "The world is a wilderness" is stated. Seeing that in this world-system of the ten directions, there are wildernesses of famine where, far from villages and devoid of food and water, the paths are perilous and filled with fierce wild beasts—which are defects of the environment—and the sentient beings who are the inhabitants are also poor and destitute, lacking food, clothing, and resources, and seeing that they are accompanied by internal afflictions and various external illnesses such as wind, bile, and phlegm, one knows all of these to be empty of true existence and like an illusion. Without fear, one then dons the great armor of the intention to purify the Buddha realm in this way: "Alas, these sentient beings are tormented by immeasurable illness and suffering because they have accumulated bad karma and have not gathered merit. How pitiful! I shall accomplish a special Buddha realm for the sake of all these sentient beings, a realm that is perfect in the excellence of its environment and inhabitants, without any defects of suffering or impure environments. For that purpose, I shall strive constantly until the end of future eons to gather the accumulations of merit and wisdom, such as the six perfections. Through knowing that these are devoid of intrinsic nature, I shall train in such a path, and like the sister, the goddess Gangā, I shall not generate even a particle of a weary mind." Thus, one dons the armor of intention and practices through application.

This is the commentary on the nineteenth chapter, the chapter of the goddess Gangā, from the *Lamp of Jewels that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.
