source: ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།བཅུ་གཅིག་པ་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་ནི། རྒྱན་ལས། ཡུལ་དང་སྦྱོར་བ་ཅན་འདི་ནི། ནས། ཐབས་ལ་མཁས་པ་རྣམ་པར་བཅུ། །ཞེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས་གསུམ། དང་པོ་ནི། འབད་རྩོལ་རགས་པ་ཞི་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་འཕྲིན་ལས་ལྷུན་གྱིས་གྲུབ་པའི་དག་སའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བའི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། བདུད་བཞི་ལས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ། དོན་དམ་པར་མི་གནས་ཤིང་ཐ་སྙད་དུ་གནས་པའི་དེ་དང་། གཞན་དོན་སྔོན་གྱི་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་འཕང་བའི་དེ་དང༌། ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་བའི་དེ་དང་། མ་ཆགས་པའི་དེ་དང་། མི་དམིགས་པའི་དེ་དང༌། མཚན་མ་མེད་པའི་དེ་དང་། སྨོན་པ་མེད་པའི་དེ་དང་། ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཀྱི་དེ་དང་། ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་བཅུ་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ས་མཚམས་དག་པ་ས་གསུམ་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། སྤྲུལ་སྐུ་འགྲུབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། མཁས་བྱའི་ཡུལ་བསྟན་བའི་སྒོ་ནས་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ་སྤྱིར་སྟོན་པར། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་བདག་ཉིད་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་ནི་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡུམ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ལ་ཐོས་བསམ་བསྒོམ་པས་སྤྱོད་ཅིང་གནས་པར་བྱེད་ལ། དེ་ཡང་ཚུལ་ཇི་ལྟར་ན་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་ཕུང་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པའི་ཆོས་འདི་དག་ཐམས་ཅད་གདོད་མ་ནས་རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་འགྲུབ་པས་སྟོང་ཞིང་བདེན་པའི་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད་པར་མངོན་སུམ་དུ་ཤེས་ནས་ཆོས་ཉིད་དེ་བཞིན་ཉིད་ལ་རྩེ་གཅིག་ཏུ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་ཀྱང་སྙིང་རྗེའི་དབང་གིས་བར་དེར། འདིར་བསྟན་ཡང་དག་མཐའ་མངོན་དུ་བྱས་ནས་གཞན་དོན་རྒྱུན་ཆད་པ་མེད་དེ། མཉམ་བཞག་ལས་བཞེངས་ནས་རྗེས་ཐོབ་མཉམ་པར་མ་བཞག་པའི་སྐབས་སུ་གདུལ་བྱའི་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་ཁམས་ཚད་མེད་པའི་དོན་སྒྲུབ་པར་མཛད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་དག་ལ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་རྒྱུན་ཆགས་སུ་འཇུག་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཞི་བའི་དབྱིངས་ལ་མི་གནས་པར་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་དཔག་མེད་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་འཇུག་པའི་བར་སྐབས་དེར་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་སྟོབས་བཅུ་མི་འཇིག་པ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་མི་ཉམས་ཏེ། ཤེས་རབ་དང་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཟུང་དུ་འཇུག་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྟབས་ཀྱིས་སངས་ཀྱི་ཆོས་རྣམས་ཐོབ་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །ཞེས་བའོ། །
translation:
The eleventh, the application of skill in means, is as the Ornament states: "From 'This one who possesses the object and the application' up to 'the ten types of skill in means.'" Regarding this, there are three sections: the definition, the classification, and the scope.

The first: The definition of the application of skill in means is that yoga of the pure stages in which, through the pacification of coarse effort, enlightened activity is spontaneously accomplished.

The second: As for its classification, there are ten: the application of skill in means that overcomes the four māras; that which does not abide in the ultimate yet abides in conventional reality; that which is propelled by the force of previous prayers for the sake of others; that which is unique; that which is free from attachment; that which is non-conceptual; that which is without characteristics; that which is without aspiration; that which is the sign of non-retrogression; and the application of skill in means of the immeasurables.

The third: The scope exists only in the three pure stages.

To explain that very application of skill in means which accomplishes the nirmāṇakāya, and to generally demonstrate the application of skill in means by way of showing the object to be mastered, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "The bodhisattva..." is as follows: Bodhisattvas, the great beings, practice and abide in the Mother of the Victors, the perfection of wisdom, through hearing, reflecting, and meditating. How is this so? Having realized through direct perception that all these phenomena, such as the aggregates of form, are empty from the beginning because they are naturally accomplished and lack true birth, they rest in one-pointed equanimity upon the suchness of the nature of phenomena. Yet, due to the power of compassion, in that interval—having realized the true limit taught here—they do not cease to work for the sake of others. Rising from meditative equipoise, during the subsequent attainment when they are not in meditative equipoise, they accomplish the benefit of the immeasurable realms of sentient beings to be tamed, for the sake of causing great compassion to enter into them continuously. In that interval of engaging in accomplishing the immeasurable benefit of sentient beings without abiding in the peaceful expanse, they do not fall away from the Buddha-qualities, such as the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses. By means of the skill in means that unites wisdom and compassion, the qualities of the Buddha are attained.

heading: **བདུད་བཞི་ལས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The skillful means of overcoming the four māras: Regarding the explanation of the skillful means of overcoming the four māras, the meaning of the three verses beginning with "For example, a person..." is that it explains, through many examples, the way to train in the skillful means of uniting compassion and wisdom. As for the first: for example, a person who is skilled in the methods of subduing enemies and protecting their own side, who possesses all the qualities such as great courage, and who possesses the strength and power to accomplish great tasks, is one who strives in tasks that others cannot perform. What is that like? It is like this: one who has become skilled in the arts or rituals such as agility and leaping, who has gone beyond many worldly crafts such as archery, and who knows how to manifest or perform various magical illusions, wishing to greatly accomplish the welfare of beings—such as protecting kin—gathers all their relatives, including their father, mother, and spouse, and leads them onto a path through a desolate wilderness where there are many enemies, robbers, and others who cause harm. When enemies and the like arrive there, rather than abandoning their relatives, that person, through great courage, manifests many people who are extremely brave and possess the valor to fight the enemy, thereby ensuring that the harm from the enemies and others does not occur. Having done so, they travel happily in the direction they wish to go and return safely to their own home. Just like that example, when practicing the path and accomplishing the welfare of beings, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means also generates great compassion at all times for the realms of sentient beings. Having accomplished immeasurable benefit and happiness, both temporary and ultimate, they abide in the supreme meditative concentration that causes one to attain buddhahood, having completely transcended the four māras—such as the māra of the god-son, which is an obstacle on the path—as well as the two [types of] listeners and solitary realizers. By abiding in equipoise in a manner that does not cause them to prematurely rise into the expanse of peace, they do not touch enlightenment. Thus, the noble bodhisattva, without having completed the three [processes of] perfecting, ripening, and purifying, is shown here as not directly realizing the true end, while it is implicitly suggested that they realize it after having completed the three [processes of] perfecting, ripening, and purifying.

Regarding the ten actual applications of skillful means:

heading: **མི་གནས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The Application of Skill in Means of Non-Abiding. To explain the second, the application of skill in means of non-abiding, two verses are spoken, beginning with "Relying on the wind in the sky." This is as follows: at the time the world is formed, initially, the mandala of wind relies upon the sky and forms; upon that wind, the mass of water relies; upon the water, the foundation of gold; upon that, this great earth relies; and upon that earth, the sentient beings of the essence—the four continents, the eight sub-continents, and so forth—rely and abide. The cause or basis for experiencing the results of the collective karma accumulated by sentient beings is just like that. Although the other mandalas of the four elements are established by relying upon one another, if one contemplates, "Upon what does the sky rely to abide?" and reflects on this meaning, one will come to understand the manner in which it does not rely upon anything, as it is not established as a substantial entity of form. In that same way, when a bodhisattva abides one-pointedly in emptiness like the sky, even at that time, without their mind inclining toward peaceful bliss, they possess the great compassion that is devoid of the grasping of sentient beings as truly existent, and they possess the support of having attained immeasurable previous aspirations and prayers. Through the power of those prayers, they manifest immeasurable emanated displays, accomplishing numerous and varied activities that increase the benefit, happiness, and excellence of beings. By being skilled in the means as explained, they do not touch the one-sided peace of nirvāṇa, nor do they abide in emptiness as if it were a truth. Thus it is said.

heading: **གཞན་དོན་སྨོན་ལམ་ཤུགས་ཀྱིས་འཕངས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The skillful means of engagement propelled by the force of the aspiration for the benefit of others. To explain the third, the skillful means of engagement propelled by the force of the aspiration for the benefit of others, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "At the time when..." is stated. At the time when one is training in the path of the Great Vehicle, a bodhisattva is skilled in the meaning of the profound reality of emptiness. Those who dispel the darkness of ignorance for other beings to be trained and illuminate the excellent path of the Great Vehicle are those who, having directly realized that all phenomena are by nature empty, abide in this supreme meditative stabilization—the heroic path that pacifies all elaborations of dualistic appearance without exception. By way of being equipoised in this, during the interval of meditating on the path, they do not meditate even slightly on the signs of conventional, elaborate phenomena. They abide in the meaning of the absence of the signs of truly established objects of negation, and they act while pacifying the conceptual thoughts that cling to nirvana as something truly to be attained and while completely pacifying the conceptual thoughts that grasp at samsara as something truly to be abandoned. Not abiding in either of the extremes of existence or peace is something that arises from the power of meditating on the path of the special skillful means of engagement. Thus it is said.

heading: **ཐུན་མོང་མ་ཡིན་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The skillful means of engagement that is uncommon. To explain the fourth, the skillful means of engagement that is uncommon, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "Flying in the sky..." is stated. For example, for a bird flying in the sky, there is no place or foundation upon which to rely; although it does not abide in the sky, by the power of its two wings it does not fall to the ground. In that same way, a bodhisattva, while abiding in the practice of the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—does not touch the extreme of nirvana due to skillful means, and due to the wisdom that realizes the nature of reality, does not engage in the path of grasping at signs in samsara. That they do not abide in the two extremes is due to the power of skillful means.

The skillful means of engagement propelled by the force of the aspiration for the benefit of others. To explain the third, the skillful means of engagement propelled by the force of the aspiration for the benefit of others, the meaning of the single verse beginning with "At the time when..." is stated. At the time when one is training in the path of the Great Vehicle, a bodhisattva is skilled in the meaning of the profound reality of emptiness. Those who dispel the darkness of ignorance for other beings to be trained and illuminate the excellent path of the Great Vehicle are those who, having directly realized that all phenomena are by nature empty, abide in this supreme meditative stabilization—the heroic path that pacifies all elaborations of dualistic appearance without exception. By way of being equipoised in this, during the interval of meditating on the path, they do not meditate even slightly on the signs of conventional, elaborate phenomena. They abide in the meaning of the absence of the signs of truly established objects of negation, and they act while pacifying the conceptual thoughts that cling to nirvana as something truly to be attained and while completely pacifying the conceptual thoughts that grasp at samsara as something truly to be abandoned. Not abiding in either of the extremes of existence or peace is something that arises from the power of meditating on the path of the special skillful means of engagement. Thus it is said.

heading: **མ་ཆགས་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The fifth, the skillful means of engagement through non-attachment, is explained by two verses beginning with "Having trained in archery..." according to the tradition of the master, although it differs slightly from that of Buddhashri. For example, a person who has well-trained and become skilled in the art of archery shoots an arrow into the sky along with a wooden board. Then, by shooting other arrows in succession after it, he catches the previous arrow continuously without interruption, so that the first arrow finds no opportunity to fall to the ground. If that person, wishing for it to fall to the ground, were to stop shooting arrows, then that arrow would fall to the ground.

In the same way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the supreme perfection of wisdom, while training on the path of the Great Vehicle, does not actualize that sublime limit of reality—the emptiness—in the interim, for as long as those roots of virtue, which have perfected the three processes of perfecting, ripening, and purifying, have not yet been completed. This is due to the skillful means of wisdom that realizes emptiness, great compassion, and the dedication of aspirations, as well as the vast intelligence that analyzes and examines through the powers of faith and so forth, and through clairvoyance and miraculous abilities.

heading: **མཚན་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The seventh, the skillful means of engagement through signlessness, is explained by two verses beginning with "For example, a person..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: For example, if a person were to sit on the edge of a great precipice, hold two parasols in both hands, and leap into the sky above the precipice, letting their body fall into the great abyss, the power of the wind lifting those two parasols would prevent them from immediately falling to the ground and would prevent their body from being injured. Furthermore, they would safely arrive at that place and be able to go to whatever destination they desired. In the same way, a bodhisattva who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality and who dwells in love and compassion, having taken hold of the two parasols of skillful means and wisdom, dwells thus: through the power of wisdom, they realize that all phenomena are by nature empty, signless, and wishless; and through the power of their special skillful means, they do not touch the extreme of peace—nirvana—and yet they come to see all the knowable phenomena as they have been described.

heading: **སྨོན་པ་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The skillful means of engagement through wishlessness. The eighth, the skillful means of engagement through wishlessness, is explained by two verses beginning with "For example, a precious..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: For example, if a powerful and noble person, wishing to bring happiness to their own kin, were to travel to an island of jewels, arrive there, find many jewels, and then return to their own home, it would not be the case that the merchant alone finds happiness by living off what they have found, while leaving their kin and friends—to whom they give nothing—in a state of unhappiness. In the same way, when a bodhisattva travels to the island of jewels—the source of all qualities, which is the wisdom realizing profound emptiness—and attains immeasurable qualities such as the joy and bliss of meditative stabilization, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, they do not merely delight in touching the nirvāṇa that pacifies all suffering without remainder, nor do they leave other sentient beings in a state of being tormented by suffering without working to establish their benefit and happiness; rather, through great compassion, they establish all beings in ripening and liberation.

[3-234] translation already produced for this document:
The seventh, the skillful means of engagement through signlessness, is explained by two verses beginning with "For example, a person..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: For example, if a person were to sit on the edge of a great precipice, hold two parasols in both hands, and leap into the sky above the precipice, letting their body fall into the great abyss, the power of the wind lifting those two parasols would prevent them from immediately falling to the ground and would prevent their body from being injured. Furthermore, they would safely arrive at that place and be able to go to whatever destination they desired. In the same way, a bodhisattva who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality and who dwells in love and compassion, having taken hold of the two parasols of skillful means and wisdom, dwells thus: through the power of wisdom, they realize that all phenomena are by nature empty, signless, and wishless; and through the power of their special skillful means, they do not touch the extreme of peace—nirvana—and yet they come to see all the knowable phenomena as they have been described.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མ་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཀྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The skillful means of engagement through the signs of non-retrogression. The ninth, the skillful means of engagement through the signs of non-retrogression, is explained by two verses beginning with "For example, a seeker..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: For example, merchants seeking jewels, in order to understand the value of the goods for trade through knowledge of the path, travel to all the great cities, towns, and small villages between their own land and the island of jewels; they do not remain there for long, nor do they remain permanently on the island of jewels. Having entered the path, they know and understand the path's features, and they do not remain in their own homes either; rather, being skilled in the manner of traveling the path and diligent, they proceed to the place they desire.

[3-235] translation already produced for this document:
The skillful means of engagement through wishlessness. The eighth, the skillful means of engagement through wishlessness, is explained by two verses beginning with "For example, a precious..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: For example, if a powerful and noble person, wishing to bring happiness to their own kin, were to travel to an island of jewels, arrive there, find many jewels, and then return to their own home, it would not be the case that the merchant alone finds happiness by living off what they have found, while leaving their kin and friends—to whom they give nothing—in a state of unhappiness. In the same way, when a bodhisattva travels to the island of jewels—the source of all qualities, which is the wisdom realizing profound emptiness—and attains immeasurable qualities such as the joy and bliss of meditative stabilization, the five faculties such as faith, and the five powers, they do not merely delight in touching the nirvāṇa that pacifies all suffering without remainder, nor do they leave other sentient beings in a state of being tormented by suffering without working to establish their benefit and happiness; rather, through great compassion, they establish all beings in ripening and liberation.

heading: **ཕྱིར་མ་ལྡོག་པའི་རྟགས་ཀྱི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: In the same way, a bodhisattva who is constantly diligent in accomplishing the welfare of others and who is clear-minded—that is, has become skilled—in the path of method and wisdom, does not remain in the path and fruit of the lesser vehicle after having performed the welfare of the sentient beings to be tamed by them; nor do they remain in the Buddha’s wisdom, which is like the island of jewels, without having completed the three [processes of] perfecting, ripening, and purifying. Although they do not remain in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like their own home, due to grasping at it as true, it should be understood that they act for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as those of the three lineages of trainees, having understood the manner of the path of the three vehicles. Such is the sign of non-retrogression, which is the unique characteristic of a bodhisattva.

heading: **ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The tenth [topic], explaining the application of skillful means regarding the immeasurables, is the meaning of the three verses beginning with "When [the bodhisattva] for beings..." As for the meaning of these verses: when a bodhisattva who is training in the conduct of a conqueror’s child generates great love—which desires that all sentient beings, the wanderers, meet with happiness—and thereby connects with them, they engage in supreme meditative absorption, which is by nature empty of intrinsic nature, signless regarding the true existence of causes, and wishless regarding the true existence of results. Such a bodhisattva does not attain the unconditioned element of nirvāṇa for their own sake alone, nor can it be posited that they are a conditioned being of cyclic existence; such a state does not exist. In the same way, a bodhisattva who is constantly diligent in accomplishing the welfare of others and who is clear-minded—that is, has become skilled—in the path of method and wisdom, does not remain in the path and fruit of the lesser vehicle after having performed the welfare of the sentient beings to be tamed by them; nor do they remain in the Buddha’s wisdom, which is like the island of jewels, without having completed the three [processes of] perfecting, ripening, and purifying. Although they do not remain in the unconditioned dharmadhātu, which is like their own home, due to grasping at it as true, it should be understood that they act for the welfare of immeasurable sentient beings, such as those of the three lineages of trainees, having understood the manner of the path of the three vehicles. Such is the sign of non-retrogression, which is the unique characteristic of a bodhisattva.

heading: **ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: For example, just as the body of a magically conjured person is not invisible to anyone, and although it is empty by its own nature, it can still be designated by a name, and there are even those in the world who describe its manner of being; in the same way, a bodhisattva who practices through the gateway of the three liberations does not abide in the extremes of either cyclic existence or peace, yet they appear in the world and can be designated by a name.

As for the meaning of these verses: when a bodhisattva who is training in the conduct of a conqueror’s child generates great love—which desires that all sentient beings, the wanderers, meet with happiness—and thereby connects with them, they engage in supreme meditative absorption, which is by nature empty of intrinsic nature, signless regarding the true existence of causes, and wishless regarding the true existence of results. Such a bodhisattva does not attain the unconditioned element of nirvāṇa for their own sake alone, nor can it be posited that they are a conditioned being of cyclic existence; such a state does not exist. In order to clarify this through an example:

heading: **ཚད་མེད་པའི་ཐབས་མཁས་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The summary and explanation of the infinite skillful means is as follows: If someone were to ask a bodhisattva about the nature of the conduct in which the conqueror’s children should abide, or about the manner in which the dispositions, intentions, and faculties—sharp or dull—of those to be trained exist, [and] that bodhisattva does not know the dispositions and inclinations of those to be trained, does not teach the profound dharma of emptiness and signlessness, and—because they are unable to ascertain that the bodhisattva is irreversible—does not explain the qualities, tokens, or aspects of the irreversible stage, then it should be understood that this [bodhisattva] has not been prophesied as irreversible. Conversely, one who knows these things and is skilled in teaching the dharma in accordance with the intellect of those to be trained should be known as one who has attained the tokens of irreversibility. Having thus explained the eleven qualities that characterize the application of complete realization, the conclusion of the section is: This is the commentary on the fourth chapter from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

The summary and explanation of the infinite skillful means is as follows: If someone were to ask a bodhisattva about the nature of the conduct in which the conqueror’s children should abide, or about the manner in which the dispositions, intentions, and faculties—sharp or dull—of those to be trained exist, [and] that bodhisattva does not know the dispositions and inclinations of those to be trained, does not teach the profound dharma of emptiness and signlessness, and—because they are unable to ascertain that the bodhisattva is irreversible—does not explain the qualities, tokens, or aspects of the irreversible stage, then it should be understood that this [bodhisattva] has not been prophesied as irreversible. Conversely, one who knows these things and is skilled in teaching the dharma in accordance with the intellect of those to be trained should be known as one who has attained the tokens of irreversibility. Having thus explained the eleven qualities that characterize the application of complete realization, the conclusion of the section is: This is the commentary on the fourth chapter from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: **འབྲས་བུ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར།**
source: འབྲས་བུ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར། གཉིས་པ་དབང་དུ་བྱ་བའི་འབྲས་བུ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་འཆད་པར།མངོན་རྟོགས་རྒྱན་ལས། དེ་ཡི་རྟོགས་དང་རྣམ་འཕེལ་དང༌། ནས། རྩེ་མོའི་མངོན་རྟོགས། ཞེས་གསུངས། མཁྱེན་གསུམ་བསྡུས་བསྒོམ་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་ཚོགས་ལམ་ལས་རབ་ཏུ་གྱུར་བའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ཟིན་པའི་སེམས་དཔའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་དེ། རྩེ་སྦྱོར་གྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་འཇུག་སྒྲུབ་དོན་གཅིག །རྩེ་སྦྱོར་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་བརྒྱད་ཡོད་དེ། དྲོད་སོགས་སྦྱོར་ལམ་བཞིའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར་བཞི་དང་། མཐོང་ལམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར། སྒོམ་ལམ་རྩེ་སྦྱོར། བར་ཆད་མེད་པའི་རྩེ་སྦྱོར། བསལ་བྱ་ལོག་སྒྲུབ་དང་བརྒྱད་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར། ས་མཚམས་ཐེག་ཆེན་གྱི་སྦྱོར་ལམ་དྲོད་ནས་རྒྱུན་མཐའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད།
translation: The result, the peak application. Second, in explaining the peak application which is the result of mastery, the *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states: "Its realization and development, and so forth, up to the peak realization." The yoga of a bodhisattva, which is seized by wisdom that has surpassed the path of accumulation of the Great Vehicle through the condensed meditation of the three knowledges, is the definition of the peak application. That and the application of engagement are synonymous. There are eight phenomena that characterize the peak application, because there are the four peak applications of the four paths of preparation such as heat, the peak application of the path of seeing, the peak application of the path of meditation, the uninterrupted peak application, and the mistaken practice to be eliminated. Regarding the levels, it exists from the heat stage of the path of preparation of the Great Vehicle up to the end of the continuum.

translation: The peak application of the heat stage. Among these, explaining the first, the peak application of the heat stage: The *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states, "Even in dreams, all phenomena... up to... are asserted as the twelve aspects." Regarding this, there are three: definition, division, and levels. As for the first, the definition of the peak application of the heat stage is that first part of the Great Vehicle’s path of definite discrimination that has attained any one of the twelve signs of having attained the peak application. Second, regarding its division, there are three: small, medium, and great heat. Third, regarding the levels, it exists only in the heat stage of the Great Vehicle’s path of preparation. In explaining the peak application of the heat stage, which is characterized by twelve signs such as becoming weary of cyclic existence even in dreams, viewing all phenomena as like dreams, and pacifying the harms of beings through truthful speech, there are the explanation of the first eight signs and the two incidental topics.

Regarding the levels, it exists from the heat stage of the path of preparation of the Great Vehicle up to the end of the continuum.

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱི་རབ་ཏུ་དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: The detailed classification of the signs. First, the meaning of the three verses beginning with "Arhats and..." is as follows: Through the power of having long practiced the Great Vehicle path, which is a union of method and wisdom, one does not desire—let alone actually see—the qualities and happiness of the three realms of cyclic existence, even in dreams. This applies to the levels of the śrāvaka arhats and the pratyekabuddha wisdom, which is the "pratyekabuddha" referred to as the "condition-born buddha," and thus the inferior vehicles. Furthermore, any bodhisattva who sees in dreams or similar states the buddhas surrounded by vast oceans of retinues, and who sees those buddhas teaching the Dharma to beings, should be understood as having attained the signs of the peak application, or as having been prophesied by the buddhas that they will not regress from the Great Vehicle’s enlightenment into an inferior path. By this, the first two lines indicate the realization of method, and the subsequent two lines indicate the second sign, which is that of seeing the buddhas and them teaching.

The peak application of the heat stage. Among these, explaining the first, the peak application of the heat stage: The *Abhisamayālaṅkāra* states, "Even in dreams, all phenomena... up to... are asserted as the twelve aspects." Regarding this, there are three: definition, division, and levels. As for the first, the definition of the peak application of the heat stage is that first part of the Great Vehicle’s path of definite discrimination that has attained any one of the twelve signs of having attained the peak application. Second, regarding its division, there are three: small, medium, and great heat. Third, regarding the levels, it exists only in the heat stage of the Great Vehicle’s path of preparation. In explaining the peak application of the heat stage, which is characterized by twelve signs such as becoming weary of cyclic existence even in dreams, viewing all phenomena as like dreams, and pacifying the harms of beings through truthful speech, there are the explanation of the first eight signs and the two incidental topics.

heading: **རྟགས་ཀྱི་རབ་ཏུ་དབྱེ་བ།**
translation: Furthermore, that bodhisattva, having seen in a dream many sentient beings dwelling in the three lower realms, out of compassion, in that very instant, makes a prayer to cut off the continuity of the lower realms, and by the power of that, sees their sufferings pacified. Also, if, upon waking from a dream, they see a village or the like burning with fire, they are not afraid, for they have been prophesied as irreversible; thus, by the blessing of uttering the power of truth—such as saying, "By this truth and by these words of truth, may this fire be pacified"—the power to pacify the mass of fire is achieved. This should be understood as having been prophesied by the victors of the past as irreversible from complete enlightenment. This verse indicates the sign of abandoning the lower realms and the sign of pacifying fire and the like through truth. Likewise, when they see that in the human world sentient beings are harmed by the spirits of demons and tormented by many different kinds of illnesses, that bodhisattva, possessed of compassion and wishing to protect them from suffering both permanently and temporarily, causes those [afflictions] to be pacified through the blessing of uttering words of truth and so forth. However, they do not become arrogant, thinking, "I possess great power," nor does the pride of holding oneself as supreme arise; this should be understood as a sign of having been prophesied as irreversible or having attained the peak application. By this, the sign of the peak application, which pacifies demonic spirits and the like merely by uttering words of truth, is indicated. When explaining the first sign in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, it is explained in detail from the passage, "Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, even in a dream, sees all phenomena as like a dream, and does not make them manifest, Subhūti, this is also..." up to the twentieth chapter, the chapter on skill in means. This is the commentary on the twentieth chapter, the chapter on skill in means, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: Incidental Topic: Regarding the second incidental topic, having branched off from the two signs—the pacification of a burning city through the utterance of a truth-statement and the pacification of harm from non-human spirits—the text explains how Māra acts, not as a sign of irreversibility, but otherwise, by stating the meaning of the eight verses beginning with "If that..." In this way, when a burning city or the harm of non-human spirits and the like are pacified through the power of Māra by means of an utterance of truth, if that bodhisattva thinks, "Because various blessings have been accomplished or attained through my own words of truth, I am a bodhisattva who has received a prophecy, as I possess such qualities and powers," and thus arrogance arises; or if he becomes arrogant, thinking, "Other bodhisattvas will prophesy me and speak of my fame," and thereby disparages other bodhisattvas, then one should know that such a person, dwelling in pride and arrogance, is a person of inferior intellect and immature mental continuum who is fit to be deceived by Māra, because he possesses the arrogance and the pride of hoping for fame. Based on that, one should understand how Māra acts.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: The explanation of the Māra that arises from the basis of names: A Māra that causes conceit and arrogance to arise also emerges from the basis of names. In this way, Māra the Wicked One will approach that bodhisattva in the guise of a Buddha, a monk, or the like, and speak as follows: "These are the names of you, your parents, and your ancestors back through seven generations of your lineage," and while speaking those names, he will also speak in accordance with what you have previously thought in your own mind, saying, "This is the name you will have when you become a Buddha." He will clearly state whatever qualities that person currently possesses, such as the ascetic virtues of begging for alms or wearing rags, the possession of novice or monastic vows, or the possession of the yoga of calm abiding and special insight, and he will further say, "In your past lives as well, your manner of ascetic virtues and the like were just as they are now." When the person hears those words spoken at that time, that bodhisattva, who has developed manifest arrogance and conceit based on that basis or cause—the mere name that describes his own qualities—should be understood as one whose conceit has been fully stirred up by Māra and who is of inferior or low intellect.

Incidental Topic: Regarding the second incidental topic, having branched off from the two signs—the pacification of a burning city through the utterance of a truth-statement and the pacification of harm from non-human spirits—the text explains how Māra acts, not as a sign of irreversibility, but otherwise, by stating the meaning of the eight verses beginning with "If that..." In this way, when a burning city or the harm of non-human spirits and the like are pacified through the power of Māra by means of an utterance of truth, if that bodhisattva thinks, "Because various blessings have been accomplished or attained through my own words of truth, I am a bodhisattva who has received a prophecy, as I possess such qualities and powers," and thus arrogance arises; or if he becomes arrogant, thinking, "Other bodhisattvas will prophesy me and speak of my fame," and thereby disparages other bodhisattvas, then one should know that such a person, dwelling in pride and arrogance, is a person of inferior intellect and immature mental continuum who is fit to be deceived by Māra, because he possesses the arrogance and the pride of hoping for fame. Based on that, one should understand how Māra acts.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: The manner in which Māra enters even when one has practiced seclusion: In general, there are two types of seclusion: external seclusion from busy distractions and internal seclusion from mental distraction. Among these, for a bodhisattva, the primary seclusion is from the inferior mental engagement that causes distraction from the Great Vehicle. Therefore, even if one dwells by relying upon a secluded village, a great city, a mountain cleft, a remote hermitage, or a forest retreat that is physically secluded from busy distractions, free from the movement of people and the clutter of possessions, if one develops the conceit of thinking, "I am one who dwells in seclusion, having been highly praised by the Sugata," and consequently praises oneself while disparaging other bodhisattvas who dwell in cities, it should be understood that such a bodhisattva’s mental continuum has been completely corrupted or stirred up by Māra, and that they are of small intellect and not of good character.

The explanation of the Māra that arises from the basis of names: A Māra that causes conceit and arrogance to arise also emerges from the basis of names. In this way, Māra the Wicked One will approach that bodhisattva in the guise of a Buddha, a monk, or the like, and speak as follows: "These are the names of you, your parents, and your ancestors back through seven generations of your lineage," and while speaking those names, he will also speak in accordance with what you have previously thought in your own mind, saying, "This is the name you will have when you become a Buddha." He will clearly state whatever qualities that person currently possesses, such as the ascetic virtues of begging for alms or wearing rags, the possession of novice or monastic vows, or the possession of the yoga of calm abiding and special insight, and he will further say, "In your past lives as well, your manner of ascetic virtues and the like were just as they are now." When the person hears those words spoken at that time, that bodhisattva, who has developed manifest arrogance and conceit based on that basis or cause—the mere name that describes his own qualities—should be understood as one whose conceit has been fully stirred up by Māra and who is of inferior or low intellect.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation:
In order to define the seclusion of a bodhisattva, to provide an analogy for the meaninglessness of it if that seclusion does not arise, and to demonstrate how one should not search for it merely through outward appearances if it does arise: [The text] explains that [a bodhisattva] may dwell in cities like Luṣapha, in regions like Campaka, or in towns like Pāṭaliputra. While dwelling there, apart from striving to mature sentient beings who are not yet mature, to liberate those who are mature, and to accomplish unsurpassed enlightenment, that bodhisattva never generates the desire for the state of a śrāvaka arhat or a pratyekabuddha. This is what the Sugata has declared to be the true seclusion of the bodhisattva sons; for if one’s own mind is secluded from the mental engagement of the inferior vehicle, then no matter where one dwells—in a village or elsewhere—one is dwelling in the supreme seclusion.

However, a bodhisattva who does not dwell in such seclusion, but instead dwells for many years in a mountain cleft five hundred leagues away, a place completely secluded from the bustle of people and filled with dangerous snakes and the like, yet who does not understand what this internal seclusion is, will develop a superior conceit, thinking, "I am one who dwells in the supreme seclusion." By dwelling in a manner similar to the inferior mental engagement, such a person is not dwelling in the seclusion of a bodhisattva, because they are corrupted by inferior mental engagement.

Due to the power of such conceit, when they see other bodhisattvas who are striving for the benefit of others, who have attained the four dhyānas, the five powers, the five faculties such as faith, the three gateways to liberation, and the heroic-march samādhi, and who are traveling through villages and cities to benefit others and lead sentient beings to maturity and liberation—because they do not understand the intent and conduct of those [bodhisattvas], they disparage them, thinking, "These are not practicing in a hermitage or in seclusion." The Blessed One has declared that such a person is within the domain of Māra, for they have come to dwell in a realm where Māra finds an opportunity.

དབེན་པ་སྒྲུབ་པ་བྱས་ཀྱང་བདུད་འཇུག་ཚུལ་ནི། སྤྱིར་དབེན་པ་ལ་ཕྱིར་འདུ་འཛི་ལས་དབེན་པ། ནང་རྣམ་གཡེང་གི་དབེན་པ་གཉིས་ཡོད་པའི་ནང་ནས་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་ཐེག་ཆེན་ལས་གཡེང་བར་བྱེད་པའི་དམན་པའི་ཡིད་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་དབེན་པ་གཙོ་བོ་ཡིན་པས། དེ་མེད་པར་རང་ཉིད་འདུ་འཛི་ལས་རབ་ཏུ་དབེན་པའི་གྲོང་དང་གྲོང་ཁྱེར་ཆེན་པོ་རི་སུལ་དང་གྲོང་ལས་ཐག་རིང་དུ་གནས་པའི་དགོན་པ་དང་སྐྱེ་བོས་རྒྱུ་འགྲུལ་དང་ཅ་ཅོས་དབེན་པའི་ནགས་ཁྲོད་ལྟ་བུ་རབ་ཏུ་བརྟེན་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་གནས་ཀྱང་། བདག་ནི་བད་ེབར་གཤེགས་པས་མཆོག་ཏུ་བསྔགས་ཤིང་དབེན་པར་གནས་པའོ་སྙམ་དུ་རློམ་སེམས་སྐྱེས་ནས་བདག་ལ་བསྟོད་ཅིང་གཞན་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གྲོང་ན་གནས་པ་ལ་སྨོད་པར་བྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནི་བདུད་ཀྱིས་སེམས་རྒྱུད་ཡོངས་སུ་བསླད་པའམ་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱས་ཤིང་བློ་ཆུང་བ་བཟང་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པར་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །
[3-248] translation already produced for this document:
The manner in which Māra enters even when one has practiced seclusion: In general, there are two types of seclusion: external seclusion from busy distractions and internal seclusion from mental distraction. Among these, for a bodhisattva, the primary seclusion is from the inferior mental engagement that causes distraction from the Great Vehicle. Therefore, even if one dwells by relying upon a secluded village, a great city, a mountain cleft, a remote hermitage, or a forest retreat that is physically secluded from busy distractions, free from the movement of people and the clutter of possessions, if one develops the conceit of thinking, "I am one who dwells in seclusion, having been highly praised by the Sugata," and consequently praises oneself while disparaging other bodhisattvas who dwell in cities, it should be understood that such a bodhisattva’s mental continuum has been completely corrupted or stirred up by Māra, and that they are of small intellect and not of good character.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: If, then, dwelling alone is not what is meant by seclusion, what is seclusion? If a bodhisattva, whether dwelling in a town or in a wilderness, is free from the mind that desires to attain either of the two vehicles—the Śrāvaka or the Pratyekabuddha—and has become solely and definitively committed to the path of supreme enlightenment, this manner of being is the pure seclusion of bodhisattvas who have entered upon the welfare of beings. Not understanding this, if one judges a bodhisattva who dwells in such seclusion by thinking, "He has warmth,"—that is, by measuring his level of spiritual heat—and concludes, "This is not dwelling in seclusion," then that person who makes such a judgment will himself fall away from the qualities of the stages and paths. Therefore, the Sage, the Blessed Buddha, has said, "Except for one like me, a person should not measure another person, for they will fall away," and as stated in the sutra, "A bodhisattva should realize the understanding within his own continuum and should not seek to find fault in others." Thus, to generate the perception of them as teachers and to act with respect toward all sentient beings is the primary training for bodhisattvas. This is the commentary on the twenty-first chapter, the chapter on Māra, from the *Precious Qualities Collection* commentary, the *Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, which clarifies the profound reality of dependent origination.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: The second point is that since the prevention of such occurrences depends upon relying on a spiritual friend, the text instructs one on the necessity of relying on a spiritual friend and, in order to explain the signs of non-retrogression for that reason, it sets forth the meaning of two verses beginning with "Therefore." Because many obstacles arise that obstruct the practice of the Mahāyāna path, one must recognize them and turn them back, and for that reason, one should rely on external and internal spiritual guides. Regarding the one who relies, they possess an intense resolve to seek supreme, unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of others, and they are skilled in the methods to accomplish it; thus, when the method is taught, they will certainly subdue pride and the like, which hold oneself as supreme. To illustrate this, just as in the world a multitude of sick people rely on a skilled physician to cure their own illnesses, one should rely on a spiritual friend who possesses the characteristics in a proper manner, without distraction, through both intention and application—viewing oneself as the patient, the one who speaks the Dharma as the physician, the Dharma as the medicine, the diligent practice as the healing of the illness, the Tathāgata as the holy being, and the teaching of the Dharma as something that will long endure.

source: བསྟེན་པར་བྱ་བའི་གཤེས་གཉེན་དེ་ཡང་གང་ཞེས་ན། ཕྱིའི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྣམས་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པ་ལ་ཞུགས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དག་དང༌། ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ལམ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་སུ་བསྟེན་པར་བྱའོ། །དེ་ཡང་སངས་རྒྱས་བྱང་སེམས་དེ་དག་ནི་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པར་བྱེད་པ་པོ་ཡིན་པས་ཕྱིའི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱ་ལ། ལམ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ནི་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་བྱ་དང་བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་སུ་ཡིན་པས་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །དེ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་དམན་ལམ་སོགས་སུ་མི་ལྟུང་བར་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་པས་ཡོངས་འཛིན་གཉིས་པ་དེ་བསྟེན་པའི་རྒྱུ་རྣམ་པ་གཉིས་ཀྱིས་བླ་ན་མེད་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མྱུར་དུ་རྟོགས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏེ།ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཚང་བ་ལས་རང་གི་འབྲས་བུ་འབྱུང་བ་རྟེན་འབྲེལ་ཆོས་ཉིད་ཡིན་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཞེས་པའོ། །བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ལས་ཀྱང་། དེ་ནས་ཡང་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ཞེས་པ་ནས། དང་པོ་ཉིད་དུ་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་ལ་བརྟེན་པར་བྱ་གུས་པར་བྱ། ཞེས་སོགས་ཀྱིས་བཤད་དོ། །ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་ཤེར་ཕྱིན་ལ་སློབ་པའི་རྟགས་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར་། རྒྱལ་བ་འདས་དང་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན། ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་གིས་ནང་གི་ཡོངས་འཛིན་བྱེད་ཚུལ་ནི། རྒྱལ་བ་ཡང་དག་པར་རྫོགས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་གང་དག་སྔར་འདས་པའི་དུས་སུ་བྱོན་ཟིན་པ་དང་། མ་བྱོན་པ་མ་འོངས་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་དང་། ད་ལྟ་ཕྱོགས་བཅུ་དག་ན་ཆོས་སྟོན་བཞིན་དུ་གང་དག་བཞུགས་པ་སྟེ་དུས་གསུམ་གྱི་རྒྱལ་བ་ཀུན་གྱི་བགྲོད་པ་གཅིག་པའི་ལམ་པོ་ཆེ་ནི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་ཡིན་གྱི་འདི་ལས་གཞན་ནི་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་ལ་མ་བསྟེན་པར་ཚང་རྒྱ་བ་མི་སྲིད་ཅིང་དེ་ལས་གཞན་པའི་ལམ་གྱི་འཚང་མི་ནུས་པའི་ཕྱིར། ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་པོ་འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་མཆོག་གི་ལམ་མམ་ཚུལ་ལ་ཞུགས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ཉོན་མངས་པའི་སྒྲིབ་པའི་མུན་པ་སེལ་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་པའི་ལམ་གསལ་བའི་གསལ་བྱེད་གྱུར་པ་དང་། ཤེས་བྱའི་སྒྲིབ་པའི་མུན་པ་བསལ་བས་ན་སྒྲོན་མ་དང་མཐོང་ལམ་གྱིས་སྣང་བར་བྱེད་པས་ན་སྣང་བར་གྱུར་པ་དང་། །གནས་སོ་ཞེས་སོགས་གསུངས་སོ། །མདོར་བསྡུ་ན་སངས་རྒྱས་ཐོབ་པ་ལ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་རྗེས་སུ་སྟོན་པའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་དང༌། རང་གིས་སྒྲུབ་པའམ་སྤྱོད་པ་སྟེ་རྒྱུ་གཉིས་པོ་དེ་མེད་མི་རུང་བ་ཡིན་ཞིང་།
translation: If one asks who the spiritual friend to be relied upon is: one should rely upon the external spiritual guide, consisting of the Blessed Buddhas and the bodhisattvas who have entered into the practice of the path to supreme enlightenment, and the internal spiritual guide, consisting of the six perfections of the path, as a spiritual friend. Because those Buddhas and bodhisattvas are the ones who point out the path of the Mahāyāna, they are called the external spiritual guide, and because these six perfections of the path are what must be practiced and accomplished, they are called the internal spiritual guide. Since these two prevent one from falling into the lesser paths and the like, by relying on these two types of spiritual guides, one will quickly realize the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddhas through two types of causes; for it is a principle of dependent origination that one’s own result arises from the complete fulfillment of the perfect conditions. This is what is meant. The *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* also explains this, from the passage "Then, Blessed One..." to "First of all, one should rely upon and respect a spiritual friend," and so forth. In order to explain the sign of learning the perfection of wisdom, which is the internal spiritual guide, it sets forth one verse beginning with "The Victors of the past..." The way in which the six perfections act as the internal spiritual guide is as follows: the great path that is the single journey for all the Victors of the three times—those Victors, the perfectly complete Buddhas who have already passed away in the past, those who have not yet come and are future Buddhas, and those who currently reside in the ten directions teaching the Dharma—is none other than these six perfections; there is no other, for it is impossible to attain Buddhahood without relying on the six perfections, and one cannot achieve the path other than through them. These six perfections are what remove the darkness of the obscurations of mental afflictions for those who have entered the path or method of supreme enlightenment, and they act as an illuminator that clarifies the path of realizing selflessness. Because they remove the darkness of the obscurations of knowledge, they are a lamp; because they illuminate through the path of seeing, they are light; and because they bring the path of the supreme vehicle, such as the path of meditation, to complete fulfillment, they are the supreme teacher. This is what the Victors have explained. Thus, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states: "These six perfections are the teacher. The six perfections are the path. The six perfections are the light. The six perfections are the lamp. The six perfections are the radiance. The six perfections are the protector. They are the refuge. They are the foundation," and so forth. In summary, for the attainment of Buddhahood, the spiritual friend who points out the six perfections and one’s own practice or conduct—these two causes—are indispensable.

The second point is that since the prevention of such occurrences depends upon relying on a spiritual friend, the text instructs one on the necessity of relying on a spiritual friend and, in order to explain the signs of non-retrogression for that reason, it sets forth the meaning of two verses beginning with "Therefore." Because many obstacles arise that obstruct the practice of the Mahāyāna path, one must recognize them and turn them back, and for that reason, one should rely on external and internal spiritual guides. Regarding the one who relies, they possess an intense resolve to seek supreme, unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of others, and they are skilled in the methods to accomplish it; thus, when the method is taught, they will certainly subdue pride and the like, which hold oneself as supreme. To illustrate this, just as in the world a multitude of sick people rely on a skilled physician to cure their own illnesses, one should rely on a spiritual friend who possesses the characteristics in a proper manner, without distraction, through both intention and application—viewing oneself as the patient, the one who speaks the Dharma as the physician, the Dharma as the medicine, the diligent practice as the healing of the illness, the Tathāgata as the holy being, and the teaching of the Dharma as something that will long endure.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: To explain that realization which is free from grasping—whereby, even when the signs of having attained the peak training are present, no grasping arises, and one understands how all faults and qualities arise merely as conceptual imputations—the text states the four verses beginning with "How is the perfection of wisdom..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: Just as the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* states, "The perfection of wisdom is characterized by emptiness," so too, how is the essence or characteristic of the perfection of wisdom empty by nature? It is because it is devoid of the nature of being one or many that would be truly established. Likewise, one should know that all these phenomena, such as form, are also empty by nature, just like that perfection of wisdom, in terms of their mode of existence or characteristics. If one thoroughly understands that all phenomena, from form up to omniscience, are empty of their own essence and are devoid of the marks of true establishment, then at the time of practicing the signs of having attained the peak training as previously described—or, in this way, practicing here—one is practicing the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: If all phenomena are empty by nature, how then do sentient beings become defiled or purified? To explain the answer to this: ordinary sentient beings, by superimposing attractiveness or unattractiveness and thoroughly conceptualizing through improper mental engagement, give rise to desire for the food of sensory objects such as forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tactile sensations. Those who possess a mind attached to cyclic existence, such as these desirable qualities, are like a fly circling the scent of filth; because they are constantly revolving from the peak of existence down to the Avīci hell, they become defiled. Furthermore, apart from being established merely as conventional illusions, the two—the self and the virtuous phenomena of the self—are not truly established and are empty by nature, for they are not produced in the ultimate sense. However, childish beings who are unskilled in the meaning of the mode of existence grasp at what is ultimately non-existent as being existent; this is like someone who imagines they have tied a knot in empty space. Because they are bound in their mental continuum by such distorted conceptualization, it is difficult for these beings to be liberated. The way in which they become miserable in cyclic existence due to the power of grasping at truth—even though things are not established in the ultimate sense—is as follows: for example, when a distorted mind, through the perception of suspicion, gives rise to the manifest conceptualization that "poison has been taken" or "poison has entered the body," even though in reality no such poison has entered, the power of that conceptualization causes suffering to arise and leads to fear and fainting. This is just like a person who, though innocent, begins to tremble in fear merely because an enemy or someone else has said to them, "You are going to be killed."

If one thoroughly understands that all phenomena, from form up to omniscience, are empty of their own essence and are devoid of the marks of true establishment, then at the time of practicing the signs of having attained the peak training as previously described—or, in this way, practicing here—one is practicing the perfection of wisdom of the Sugatas.

heading: **འཕྲོས་དོན།**
translation: In the same way, ordinary beings who are childish and have not attained the path of the noble ones, despite the fact that there is no ultimate establishment, grasp at a self as existing by nature and, by focusing on the eyes, nose, and so forth, claim things as "mine." From this habituation to the path, there arises a conceptualization that is not correct, which perceives a self and what belongs to a self as true. By the power of that, they accumulate karma and, in cyclic existence, are repeatedly born and destroyed—that is, they experience a continuous stream of various sufferings such as death, decline, and unhappiness. Just as it has been taught that, due to the power of total ignorance and delusion, one is thoroughly afflicted by grasping at a self and what belongs to a self even though they do not exist in reality, it is also taught that a bodhisattva who realizes the non-existence of a self—that is, who realizes the meaning of selflessness directly—and who knows and habituates to the nature of reality, will attain the state of liberation, which is complete purification. This, however, is in terms of conventional reality; in terms of ultimate reality, it is said that a bodhisattva who correctly knows that for any person whatsoever there is no becoming afflicted or becoming purified, will realize the perfection of wisdom, which understands the equality of cyclic existence and nirvana as being empty of true existence. This is explained in the *Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom* by such passages as: "Subhūti asked, 'Bhagavan, what is the characteristic of the perfection of wisdom?'"

translation:
The Peak Application. The second, the peak application, is stated in the Ornament as: "From the sentient beings of the Jambudvīpa... to the nature of the sixteenfold increase." Regarding this, there are three parts. The first is: the second of the two [types of] concordant factors for definite emergence of the Great Vehicle, which attains the sixteenfold increase of merit superior to worshipping Buddhas equal in number to the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system, is the definition of the peak application. The second, when divided, consists of the small, intermediate, and great peak applications. Its boundary is found solely in the peak of the path of application of the Great Vehicle.

Regarding the sixteenfold increase of merit in the peak application, the first is the peak application of the increase of merit superior to worshipping Buddhas equal to the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system, including Jambudvīpa. The meaning of the two verses beginning with "In Jambudvīpa..." is as follows: Taking the limit of the investigation as an example, if all the sentient beings of the three-thousandfold world system, represented by the sentient beings in Jambudvīpa, were to obtain human bodies, and all of them were to generate the mind for unexcelled, perfectly complete, supreme awakening, and for many millions of thousands of years were to make vast offerings to Buddhas and Bodhisattvas and give immeasurable gifts to sentient beings, and were to dedicate all those roots of virtue for the sake of the benefit of beings as the cause of supreme awakening, there would be immeasurable merit in that. However, if a Bodhisattva were to exert themselves in the supreme perfection of wisdom, which is of the nature of the peak realization, then—let alone for a long time—even if they were to meditate on the path in accordance with that perfection of wisdom and teach it to others for just a single day, the heap of merit from the giving described above would not be able to compete with, that is, would not be capable of matching, that merit. Therefore, one must engage in this meditation on the perfection of wisdom, or the peak application, constantly and without negligence. This is what is meant.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: The manner in which one must exert oneself in that path of the union of means and wisdom, along with an analogy, is explained in three verses beginning with "The bodhisattva..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: Any bodhisattva who abides in the peak-application and so forth, wishing to liberate from the bondage of karma and defilements those sentient beings—comprised of the five classes, including gods, humans, and the three lower realms, who have been connected as fathers, mothers, and so forth since beginningless time in this place of cyclic existence—and wishing to liberate them from the suffering of cyclic existence, relies upon the vast path, the path of the Great Vehicle. Desiring to reveal that very nirvana, which does not abide on the shore of the ocean of cyclic existence, to the realm of sentient beings, they should exert themselves day and night, without distraction, in the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness, accompanied by compassion.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Explaining the signs of keeping the perfection of wisdom in mind by way of clarifying that meaning through an analogy: For example, if a person were to find a supreme jewel—which they had not found before, meaning it is difficult to find—at another time, and were to become extremely joyful, but then, immediately after finding it, were to fall under the sway of carelessness and distraction, causing that jewel to be lost, then, because it was lost, they would constantly long for it, thinking, "When will I find that jewel again?" and would be perpetually miserable. Just like that analogy, a bodhisattva who has entered the path of supreme enlightenment, having found this perfection of wisdom—which is like a supreme jewel that is extremely difficult to find and of great significance—should practice yoga upon it and never abandon it. Just as one who, having found that previously lost jewel again, takes it up with joy, wraps it in cloth and the like with great diligence, and, fearing that it might be lost or snatched away by others, quickly goes to their own home and treasures it, whereby the sorrow of being parted from the jewel and the suffering of poverty are pacified, so too, if a bodhisattva constantly exerts themselves in meditating on the perfection of wisdom, they will quickly attain unsurpassed enlightenment. Thus it is said. This is the commentary on the twenty-second chapter, the chapter on the spiritual friend, from the *Jewel Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

The manner in which one must exert oneself in that path of the union of means and wisdom, along with an analogy, is explained in three verses beginning with "The bodhisattva..." The meaning of these verses is as follows: Any bodhisattva who abides in the peak-application and so forth, wishing to liberate from the bondage of karma and defilements those sentient beings—comprised of the five classes, including gods, humans, and the three lower realms, who have been connected as fathers, mothers, and so forth since beginningless time in this place of cyclic existence—and wishing to liberate them from the suffering of cyclic existence, relies upon the vast path, the path of the Great Vehicle. Desiring to reveal that very nirvana, which does not abide on the shore of the ocean of cyclic existence, to the realm of sentient beings, they should exert themselves day and night, without distraction, in the perfection of wisdom that realizes emptiness, accompanied by compassion.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To demonstrate how the path of the union of method and wisdom suppresses the discordant factors, and to teach the three types of development—such as patience regarding non-arising phenomena—combined together, the meaning of the two verses beginning with "Like the sun and clouds" is explained. For example, when the sun, which is free from clouds and possesses a network of extremely luminous rays that vanquish all dense darkness, rises, it suppresses the light of all sentient beings—such as fireflies, which possess only a tiny amount of light and can only dispel the darkness immediately surrounding their own bodies—as well as the light of the gathering of stars and the light of the moon, and so forth. Likewise, the bodhisattva who practices the supreme perfection of wisdom, which possesses all aspects, is like the sun free from the clouds of obscuration. By radiating the light of the teachings that demonstrate the selflessness of phenomena and persons, the wise one, practicing emptiness and signlessness by nature, completely vanquishes the dense darkness of views, such as the view of the transitory collection. In doing so, they suppress and are superior to all beings who are like fireflies, śrāvaka arhats who are like other creatures, pratyekabuddhas who are like stars, and many other bodhisattvas who are unskilled in method. By the phrase "practicing emptiness and signlessness," the development of patience regarding non-arising phenomena and the non-apprehension of both enlightenment and the agent of enlightenment are taught, and the development of superiority over arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and others is indicated.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: To explain the method of ripening other beings to be trained, and to elaborate on the increase of all the hosts of gods who have approached, two verses are spoken, beginning with "Like a prince." The meaning is this: For example, a prince who wishes to benefit his subjects by giving away wealth, who protects all people from harm, and who desires to accomplish the purpose of benefit and happiness, is skilled in means and possesses a fine character; he becomes the foremost of all the king’s sons. Because he is honored by all the subjects and because each one of them wishes to accomplish their own purpose, it becomes fitting for them to go into his presence. If that prince, even at a time when he has not yet become king, benefits many sentient beings and makes them joyful, then it goes without saying that when he is consecrated as king, has attained the means of governance, and has become a king abiding in the kingdom, he will accomplish the purpose of the subjects and make them joyful. In that same way, a wise Bodhisattva who practices the conduct of a son of the Conqueror with a heart of wisdom and compassion also gives the nectar of Dharma to the assembly of fortunate beings and, by means of leading them onto the path and so forth, makes gods and humans joyful, so that the gods of the desire realm, the six classes, and others come into his presence to listen to the Dharma and pay him homage. If this Bodhisattva, even now while in the stage of the path of learning, strives to accomplish the benefit and happiness of many sentient beings, then it goes without saying—because it is unnecessary to state—that when he becomes a Dharma King, a Buddha, and abides in the wisdom of omniscience, he will perform the benefit of all wandering beings. This is the commentary on the twenty-third chapter, the chapter on Śakra, from the "Wish-Fulfilling Jewel Lamp," a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

Thinking this, their minds become filled with anguish, and they reflect, "I am unable to create obstacles." Overcome by grief and despair, and because of this, suffering physically and mentally, they become discouraged and weak. Unable to bear being tormented by such suffering, they think, "How can I cause this bodhisattva to turn back and retreat from the path of the Great Vehicle?" They then create obstacles and, in order to show the bodhisattva great terrors, they manifest various magical displays, such as setting the directions ablaze and sending down shooting stars.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: Who is that bodhisattva who, even when the Māras act in this way, cannot be caught off guard? At whatever time those bodhisattvas who are skilled in wisdom and means possess a most intense aspiration that does not deviate from the path of the Great Vehicle, they constantly, day and night, contemplate and reflect upon the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom. At the time when they do so, the body and mind of that bodhisattva move without fear of the precipices of existence and peace, like a bird moving through the sky, because they abide on the path that unites skillful means and wisdom. Therefore, how could the sinful Māras and their dark cohorts ever find an opportunity to catch such a bodhisattva off guard? They cannot.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
source: རང་གི་སྤྱོད་པ་ལ་སྐྱོན་ཞུགས་ན་གླགས་རྙེད་ཚུལ་ནི། དུས་གང་གི་ཚེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ནང་ཕན་ཚུན་ཁྲོས་ཏེ་ལུས་ཀྱིས་རྡེག་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱེད་པའི་འཐབ་པ་དང་ངག་གིས་མཚང་འབྲུ་བ་དང་རྒྱལ་པོའི་དྲུང་དུ་ཞལ་ལྕེ་གཅོད་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་ཅིང་ཕན་ཚུན་མི་མཐུན་པར་ཞེ་སྡང་གིས་ཁྲོས་པའི་སེམས་དང་ལྡན་པར་འགྱུར་པ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་སྡིག་ཅན་དེ་ནི་མཆོག་ཏུ་དགའ་ཞིང་ཉམས་བདེ་བར་འགྱུར་ཏེ། དེ་ཡི་རྒྱུ་མཚན་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་གཉིས་ཀའང་འཐབ་རྩོད་བྱས་པའི་ཉེས་པས་རྒྱལ་བའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་ནི་ཐག་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་གྱི་བར་ཆད་དུ་འགྱུར་རོ་སྙམ་པའི་ཕྱིར། དེ་ལྟར་དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལས་རིང་དུ་འགྱུར་ཞིང་རྒྱུད་མ་རུང་བར་གནོད་འཚེ་བྱེད་པའི་སྲིན་པོ་དང་ཤ་ཟ་རྣམས་དང་འདྲ་བར་འགྱུར་ལ། དེ་གཉིས་ཀ་ཡང་སེམས་ཅན་ལ་ཕན་བདེ་སྒྲུབ་པའི་རང་གི་དམ་བཅས་དེ་རྩོད་པས་ཉམས་པར་བྱེད་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །སྙིང་རྗེ་དང་བྱམས་པ་དང་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་སོགས་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་བའི་ཞེ་སྡང་དང་དེའི་གཉེན་པོ་བཟོད་པ་བསྒོམ་པ་དང་བྲལ་བ་ལ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཐོབ་པ་ག་ལ་ཡོད་དེ། ས་བོན་མེས་ཚིག་པ་ལ་མྱུ་གུ་མི་འབྱུང་བ་བཞིན་ནོ། །བྱང་སེམས་རྣམས་ཕན་ཚུན་རྩོད་པར་གྱུར་བ་དེ་ཡི་ཚེ་བདུད་རྣམས་རང་གི་འཁོར་རམ་ཕྱོགས་དང་བཅས་ཏེ་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེས་ན་བྱང་སེམས་ལ་འདོད་ཆགས་ཀྱི་ཉེས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དུས་ཡུན་རིང་བ་བྱུང་བ་ལས་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་སྐྱེས་པས་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཉམས་ཤིང་དགེ་རྩ་འཇོམས་པ་སོགས་ཉེས་དམིགས་ཆེ་བར་མདོ་ལས་རྒྱ་ཆེར་གསུངས་ཏེ། ཟླ་བ་སྒྲོན་མའི་མདོ། མད་ོབཏུས་སུ་དྲངས་པ་ལས། ཕན་ཚུན་གནོད་པའི་སེམས་སུ་གང་བྱེད་པ། དེ་ལ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཐོས་པས་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེ་བསམ་གཏན་དང་ནི་དགོན་གནས་མི་སྐྱོབ་སྟེ། སྦྱིན་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་མཆོད་པའང་སྐྱོབ་མི་བྱེད། ཞེས་དང་། འཇམ་དཔལ་རྣམ་པར་རོལ་བའི་མདོ་ལས། འཇམ་དཔལ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། བསྐལ་བ་བརྒྱར་བསགས་པའི་དགེ་བ་ཉེ་བར་འཇོམས་པར་བྱེད་པ་དེའི་ཕྱིར། ཁོང་ཁྲོ་བ་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་དང་། བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་ཆེན་པོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མདོ་ལས་ཀྱང་། ཞེ་སྡང་གི་རྩོད་པ་དང་བཅས་པའི་གནས་ལས་དཔག་ཚད་བརྒྱར་འབྱོལ་བར་བྱ་སྟེ།ཞེ་ལྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པར་མི་བྱའོ། །སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཁམས་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོད་ཤིང་བརྡེག་ལ་མཚོན་གྱིས་བཏབ་པས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཞན་ལ་ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེས་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཆེས་ཉེས་པ་ལྕི་ཞིང་དེས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་རྨས་པ་དང་ཉམས་པར་འགྱུར་ཏ་རེ། དཔེར་ན་ལྕགས་ནི་ལྕགས་ལས་གཞན་བོང་བ་སོགས་ཀྱིས་མི་ཆོད་པ་ལྟར།བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་རྩ་བ་ཡང་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཅིག་ཤོས་ཞེ་སྡང་བས་ཟད་པར་བྱེད་ཀྱིས་གཞན་གྱིས་ཟད་མི་ནུས་པས་ན། གཅིག་གིས་གཅིག་ལ་ཞེ་ས་དང་གུས་པ་དང་བཅས་པར་བྱ་སྟེ་སེམས་དང་པོ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཡང་སྟོན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་བསྐྱེད་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །ཁྱད་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་ཁྲོ་བ་ནི་ཉེས་པ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་སྟེ། ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་ལས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་མ་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ཞིག་གིས་ཕྱིར་མི་ལྡོག་པར་ལུང་བསྟན་པའམ་རྟགས་ཐོབ་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་སེམས་ཁྲོས་ནས་ལུས་ངག་གི་རྩོད་པ་རྩོམ་པར་བྱེད་ཅིང་དེ་ལ་འགྱོད་བཤགས་སོགས་མི་བྱེད་ཅིང་ཁྲོ་བའི་སེམས་མ་བཏད་ན། དགེ་བའི་ལོ་ཏོག་མི་སྐྱེ་བའི་ཞིང་ཐ་བ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐྱོན་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཁོང་ཁྲོ་སེམས་ཀྱི་སྐད་ཅིག་མ་ཅི་ཙམ་ཞིག་སྐྱེས་པ་ཇི་སྙེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་གྲངས་དང་མཉམ་པའི་བསྐལ་བར་ཞི་ནས་ལམ་ལ་བསླབ་པ་དང་ལམ་ལ་འཇུག་བའི་གོ་ཆ་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །མདོ་ཀུན་ལས་བཏུས་སུ་བྱམས་པ་སེངྒེ་སྒྲས་མདོ་དྲངས་བ་ལས་ཀྱང་། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་ལ་ལ་ཞིག་གིས། སྟོང་གསུམ་གྱི་སྟོང་ཆེན་པོའི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་ཁམས་སུ་གཏོགས་པའི་སེམས་ཅན་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་སྤྱོས་པ་དང་། བརྒྱད་པ་དང་དབྱུག་པ་དང་། ཁུར་ཚུར་གྱིས་བརྡེགས་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་མི་འགྱུར་གྱི། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ལ།ཐ་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་ཞེ་སྡང་གི་སེམས་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་ཙམ་གྱིས། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་ལ་རྨ་བྱུང་ཞིང་རྨས་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །དེ་ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ཞེ་ན། གལ་ཏེ་དེས་ཐམས་ཅད་མཁྱེན་པ་ཡོངས་སུ་མ་བཏང་ན། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་གཅིག་ཤོས་ལ་གནོད་སེམས་དང་། ཐ་བ་དང་སྡང་བའི་སེམས་ཇི་སྙད་དུ་བསྐྱེད་པ་དེ་སྙེད་ཀྱི་བསྐལ་པར་གོ་ཆ་བཟོད་ཡང་བགོ་དགོས་སོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་བས་ན་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ལམ་ཉམས་སུ་ལེན་པར་འདོད་པའི་གང་ཟག་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྲོག་ལ་བབས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོ་བོའི་གོ་སྐབས་དབྱེ་བར་མི་བྱ་ཞིང་བྱམས་སྙིང་རྗེ་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་ལ་ཉམས་ལེན་གྱི་མཐིལ་དུ་བྱའོ། །
translation: How an opportunity is found when faults enter into one’s own conduct is as follows: At whatever time bodhisattvas become angry with one another, engaging in conflicts such as striking one another with their bodies, or in disputes involving verbal abuse or litigation before a king, and, being inharmonious, possess minds inflamed by hatred, at that time the sinful Māra becomes extremely joyful and at ease. The reason for this is the thought that because those two bodhisattvas have committed the fault of engaging in conflict, they have become distant from the wisdom of the Victorious Ones and have created an obstruction to the path of the Great Vehicle. In this way, both of them become distant from the wisdom of the Buddha and become like the *rākṣasas* and *piśācas* who are wicked and cause harm, and both of them, through their conflict, cause their own vows to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings to degenerate. How could there be any attainment of enlightenment for one who is devoid of the patience that is the antidote to the hatred that causes compassion, loving-kindness, and the *bodhicitta* to degenerate? It is like a seed burned by fire, from which no sprout can emerge. At the time when bodhisattvas engage in conflict with one another, the Māras, together with their retinues or factions, become extremely joyful. Therefore, the sutras explain extensively that the faults of anger are greater than the faults of desire, for even if desire has been present for a long time, a single moment of anger causes loving-kindness and compassion to degenerate and destroys the roots of virtue. As the *Candrapradīpa-sūtra*, quoted in the *Śikṣāsamuccaya*, states: "For one who acts with a mind of malice toward another, neither the hearing of moral discipline, nor meditative concentration, nor dwelling in solitude provides protection; neither does giving nor the worship of the Buddhas provide protection." And the *Mañjuśrī-vikrīḍita-sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī, 'anger' is so called because it utterly destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over a hundred aeons; therefore, it is called 'anger'." And the *Maitreyasiṃhanāda-sūtra* also states: "One should retreat a hundred *yojanas* from a place of hateful conflict; one should not give rise to a mind of hatred. Compared to abusing, beating, and attacking with weapons all the sentient beings in a billion-fold world system, it is a far greater fault to give rise to a single thought of malice or hatred toward another bodhisattva; by this, a bodhisattva is wounded and impaired. Just as iron cannot be cut by anything other than iron, the roots of virtue of a bodhisattva are exhausted by the hatred of another bodhisattva, and cannot be exhausted by others. Therefore, one should act toward one another with respect and reverence, and one should generate the perception of a teacher even toward a bodhisattva who has just generated the mind of enlightenment." It is said that anger toward a bodhisattva who has received a prophecy is a particularly grave fault. If a bodhisattva who has not yet received a prophecy of non-retrogression from the Great Vehicle becomes angry with a bodhisattva who has received such a prophecy or the signs thereof, and engages in physical or verbal conflict without performing confession of the fault or abandoning the angry mind, then for as many moments as that angry mind—which possesses the fault of being like a barren field where the harvest of virtue cannot grow—has arisen, one must don the armor of training in the path and entering the path for an equal number of aeons. The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* also quotes the *Maitreyasiṃhanāda-sūtra*: "If a bodhisattva were to abuse, beat, or strike with a fist all the sentient beings in a billion-fold world system, by that alone the bodhisattva would not be wounded or injured. However, if a bodhisattva were to engender even a single moment of malice, harshness, or a hateful mind toward another bodhisattva, by that alone the bodhisattva is wounded and injured. Why is that? If they have not abandoned omniscience, then for as many moments as a bodhisattva has generated malice, harshness, or a hateful mind toward another bodhisattva, for that many aeons must they don the armor of patience." Thus it is said. Therefore, those individuals who wish to practice the path of the Great Vehicle should not provide an opportunity for anger, even if it costs them their lives, and should make loving-kindness, compassion, and the *bodhicitta* the foundation of their practice.

[3-263] translation already produced for this document:
Who is that bodhisattva who, even when the Māras act in this way, cannot be caught off guard? At whatever time those bodhisattvas who are skilled in wisdom and means possess a most intense aspiration that does not deviate from the path of the Great Vehicle, they constantly, day and night, contemplate and reflect upon the meaning of the supreme perfection of wisdom. At the time when they do so, the body and mind of that bodhisattva move without fear of the precipices of existence and peace, like a bird moving through the sky, because they abide on the path that unites skillful means and wisdom. Therefore, how could the sinful Māras and their dark cohorts ever find an opportunity to catch such a bodhisattva off guard? They cannot.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation:
Since the faults of anger have been explained above, the way to rely upon patience is as follows: Because the Buddhas have attained or reached great awakening through the perfection of patience, this opposing state of an angry mind is not good. One should generate the mindfulness that it destroys the roots of virtue accumulated over many eons and causes love and compassion to diminish. One should confess each instance of that negativity with intense regret, and resolve not to commit such faults again in the future. Thinking, "I must not allow this unwholesome mind to find an opportunity to arise in my continuum," one should not take delight in conflict and the like; that is how one arrives at this path of the Great Vehicle, the Buddha-Dharma. Thus it is said.

This concludes the commentary on the twenty-fourth chapter, on manifest pride, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: **རྩེ་མོའི་སྦྱོར་བ།**
translation: In order to demonstrate the two types of development—those that are primarily internal, such as the two types of development that arise because one has become a lineage-holder of the Buddhas and because one attains the fruition of Buddhahood itself—the meaning of the two verses beginning with "When training, whoever..." is as follows: When a bodhisattva is training on the path of the Great Vehicle, they do not ultimately accept any phenomena to be trained in, such as the three trainings or the six perfections. They do not perceive as true the self who is the trainee, nor the phenomena in which they are to be trained. Furthermore, they do not conceptually construct as true either the antidote—the bodhisattva’s training—or its opposing state—the non-training of anger and the like. Rather, they understand both of these as being equal in being empty of true existence. Whoever trains in this way is training without error in this perfection of wisdom, which is the phenomenon that brings about the attainment of the rank of Buddhahood.
