འདིས་ཕྱིན་དྲུག་གི་ཕན་ཡོན་དྲན་པས་དེ་ལ་མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་པ་དང་། དཀོན་མཆོག་གསུམ་དང་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་དང་ལྷ་རྗེས་སུ་དྲན་ནས་ཅི་བྱེད་དེའི་དབང་དུ་གཏོང་བ་ལས་རང་དགར་མི་འཇུག་པ་དང་། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་མེད་པར་རྗེས་སུ་དྲན་པས་སེམས་རྣམ་པར་དག་པ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནམ་སྙམ་ཞེས་གུང་ཐང་འཇམ་པའི་དབྱངས་ཀྱིས་གསུངས། མཐར་གྱིས་སྦྱོར་བ་འཆད་བྱེད་ལ། བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པར། སེངྒེའི་སྒྲ་སྒྲོགས་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་རིག་པར་བྱའོ། །ཞེས་པའི་ཚིག་འདི་ལས་མེད་ཅེས་གསུངས་སོ། །དེ་ལྟར་མཐར་གྱིས་སྦྱོར་བ་མཚོན་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཆོས་བཅུ་གསུམ་བསྟན་ཟིན་ནས་སྐབས་བསྡུ་བ་ནི། ཡོན་ཏན་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་སྡུད་པ་ཚིགས་སུ་བཅད་པའི་འགྲེལ་བ་ཟབ་མོ་རྟེན་འབྱུང་གི་དེ་ཁོ་ན་ཉིད་གསལ་བར་བྱེེད་པའི་ནོར་བུའི་སྒྲོན་མེ་སྐལ་བཟང་རེ་སྐོང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལས་སྐབས་དྲུག་པའི་འགྲེལ་བའོ།།  །།
[3-305] translation already produced for this document:
Gungthang Jamyang expressed that this shows the purification of the mind through recollecting the benefits of the six perfections, thereby exerting effort toward them; through recollecting the Three Jewels, ethical discipline, and the deities, one does not act according to one's own whims, but rather acts in accordance with what one is doing; and through recollecting the lack of intrinsic nature. Regarding the explanation of the serial application, it is said that in the *Eight Thousand Lines*, the words, "Because it roars the lion's roar, the perfection of wisdom should be known," are not present. Having thus finished explaining the thirteen factors that characterize the serial application, the conclusion of the chapter is: this is the commentary on the sixth chapter from the *Jewel Lamp Fulfilling the Wishes of the Fortunate, which Clarifies the Profound Reality of Dependent Arising, a Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection*.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
source: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།གསུམ་པ་འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ་སྟོན་པར། མངོན་པར་རྟོགས་པའི་རྒྱན་ལས། ཐུབ་པའི་ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ་ནི། །ནས། རྣམ་པ་ཉི་ཤུ་བདུན་དུ་བཞེད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། རང་ཐོབ་བྱེད་ཀྱི་ཐབས་སུ་གྱུར་པའི་མཁྱེན་གསུམ་གྱི་རྣམ་པ་བསྒོམ་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ཐོབ་པའི་འབྲས་བུ་མཐར་ཐུག །འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུའི་མཚན་ཉིད། དེ་དང་སངས་རྒྱས་དོན་གཅིག །དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། བཞི་ཡོད་དེ། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་སྐུ། ཡེ་ཤེས་ཆོས་སྐུ། ལོངས་སྐུ། སྤྲུལ་སྐུ་དང་བཞི་ཡོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། ངོ་བོ་ཉིད་ལོངས་རྫོགས་བཅས་ཏེ། དེ་བཞིན་གཞན་པ་སྤྲུལ་པ་ནི། ཆོས་སྐུ་མཛད་པ་དང་བཅས་པ། །རྣམ་པ་བཞི་ནི་ཡང་དག་བརྗོད། །ཅེས་སོ། །ས་མཚམས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱིས་ཁོ་ནར་ཡོད། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཕྲིན་ལས་སྟོན་པར། རྒྱན་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་འཁོར་བ་ཇི་སྲིད་འདིའི། །ནས། རྣམ་པ་ཉི་ཤུ་བདུན་དུ་བཞེད། །ཅེས་གསུངས། འདི་ལ་མཚན་ཉིད། དབྱེ་བ། ས་མཚམས། འཇུག་ཚུལ། ཡུན་ཚད་ལྔ་ལས། དང་པོ་ནི། རང་གི་རྒྱུར་གྱུར་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཆོས་སྐུའི་བདག་རྐྱེན་བྱས་པ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་རྣམ་དཀརགྱི་ཡོན་ཏན། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་མཚན་ཉིད། གཉིས་པ་དེ་ལ་དབྱེ་ན། བྱ་བ་ཡུལ་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་འཕྲིན་ལས། བྱེད་པ་པོ་ལ་ཡོད་པའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་གཉིས་དང་། དེ་ལས་རྒྱས་པར་དབྱེ་ན། འགྲོ་རྣམས་ཞི་བའི་ལས་ལ་འགོད་པའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ནས། མྱང་འདས་ལ་འགོད་པའི་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཀྱི་བར་ཉེར་བདུན་ཡོད། གསུམ་པ་ནི། ལམ་མ་ཞུགས་ནས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སའི་བར་དུ་ཡོད། བཞི་པ་ནི། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་འཕྲིན་ལས་གདུལ་བྱའི་རྒྱུད་ལ་འཇུག་ཚུལ་ལ་མཐའ་ཡས་པ་ཡོད་དེ། གདུལ་བྱ་རང་རང་གི་སྐལ་པ་དང་འཚམས་པར་སྐུ་གསུངས་ཐུགས་ཀྱི་འཕྲིན་ལས་རྒྱ་ཆེ་ལ་རྒྱུན་མི་ཆད་པ་དཔག་བསམ་གྱི་ཤིང་དང་ཡིད་བཞིན་གྱི་ནོར་བུ་ལྟར་འབད་མེད་ལྷུན་གྲུབ་ཏུ་འཇུག་པའི་ཕྱིར།  ལྔ་པ་ནི། ཡུན་ཚད་འཁོར་བ་མ་སྟོང་གི་བར་དུ་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་འཕྲིན་ལས་རྒྱུན་མི་ཆད་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། རྒྱན་ལས། དེ་བཞིན་འཁོར་བ་ཇི་སྲིད་འདིའི། །ལས་ནི་རྒྱུན་མི་ཆད་པར་འདོད། །ཅེས་གསུངས་པའི་ཕྱིར། འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ་དེ་ཉིད་འཆད་པར། བདག་གི་བདེ་བ་ཞེས་སོགས་ཚིགས་བཅད་གཅིག་གསུངས་པའི་དོན་ནི། དེ་ལྟར་བདག་གཞན་མཉམ་བརྗེའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་རིན་པོ་ཆེ་དེ་ཉིད་ལམ་གྱི་གཞིར་བཟུང་ནས་རྒྱལ་སྲས་ཀྱི་སྤྱོད་པ་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་དྲུག་དང་བསྡུ་བའི་དངོས་པོ་བཞི་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཉམས་སུ་བླང་པས་ས་བཅུ་ལམ་ལྔ་རིམ་གྱིས་བསྒྲོད་དེ་སྐུ་བཞི་མངོན་དུ་བྱས་ནས་ནས་མཁའ་ཇི་སྲིད་གནས་ཀྱི་བར་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལས་གཡོ་བ་མེད་པར་བཞུགས་བཞིན་དུ་དམིགས་པ་མེད་པའི་ཐུགས་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོས་བདག་གི་བདེ་བ་འདོད་པའི་སེམས་བཏང་ནས་ལན་དང་རྣམ་སྨིན་ལ་རེ་བ་མེད་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་སེམས་ཅན་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་དང་དགོས་པ་སྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་ཉིན་མཚན་རྟག་ཏུ་གཡེལ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་དུས་ལས་མི་འདའ་བར་མངོན་པར་བརྩོན་པར་མཛད་པ་དཔེར་ན་བུ་གཅིག་པ་ལམ་ནི་རྣམ་པ་ཀུན་ཏུ་སྐྱོ་བ་མེད་པའི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་རིམ་གྲོ་བྱེད་པ་ལྟར་གཞན་དོན་འབའ་ཞིག་མཛད་པའི་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་རྣམས་ལྟར་བསམ་པ་ཐག་པས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་ལ་རྣམ་པར་སྐྱོ་བ་མེད་པར་གནས་པར་བྱ་བར་ཤེས་པར་གྱིས་ཤིག །ཅེས་སོ། །འདིས་ཆོས་སྐུ་བསྟན་ཚུལ་ནི། སྐུ་བཞི་མངོན་དུ་མཛད་དེ་འཁོར་བ་མ་སྟོང་བར་དུ་སྐྱོ་བ་མེད་པར་བཞུགས་ནས་འཕྲིན་ལས་ཉེར་བདུན་གྱིས་འགྲོ་བའི་དོན་མཛད་པ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེ་ཉིད་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པར་འཆད་པའི་ཚེ། རབ་འབྱོར་གང་གིས་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་སེམས་དཔའ་ཆེན་པོས་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པར་དེ་ལྟར་རྗེས་སུ་རིག་པར་བྱེད་པ་དང་། རྣམ་པར་སྤྱོད་པ་དང་། ཞེས་པ་ནས། རྗེས་སུ་རིག་པའི་ལེའུ་སྟེ་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་དགུ་པའོ། །ཞེས་གསུངས་སོ། translation: The Resultant Truth Body. Third, in explaining the resultant Truth Body, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* states: "The nature body of the Sage is..." through to "...are asserted to be of twenty-seven types." This is the ultimate fruit attained through the power of meditating on the aspects of the three knowledges, which serve as the means for their own attainment. The definition of the resultant Truth Body is that it is synonymous with a Buddha. Regarding its divisions, there are four: the Nature Body, the Wisdom Truth Body, the Enjoyment Body, and the Emanation Body. This is because it is said: "The nature body, the complete enjoyment body, and likewise the other, the emanation body, are the Truth Body together with its activities; these four are correctly stated." Its scope is found only in a Buddha. In explaining the enlightened activity of a Buddha, the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* states: "Likewise, for as long as cyclic existence lasts..." through to "...are asserted to be of twenty-seven types." Regarding this, there are five aspects: definition, division, scope, mode of engagement, and duration. The first is the definition of a Buddha’s enlightened activity: the virtuous qualities that arise from having made the Wisdom Truth Body—which serves as its own cause—the primary condition. The second, its division, consists of two: activity residing in the object and activity residing in the agent. When divided in detail, there are twenty-seven, from the activity of establishing beings in the path of peace up to the activity of establishing them in nirvana. The third, its scope, exists from the time of not having entered the path up to the stage of Buddhahood. The fourth, the mode of engagement, is that the ways in which a Buddha’s enlightened activity enters the continuum of those to be tamed are infinite, because the enlightened activities of body, speech, and mind, which are vast and uninterrupted, engage effortlessly and spontaneously like a wish-fulfilling tree or a wish-granting jewel, in accordance with the individual capacities of those to be tamed. The fifth, its duration, is that a Buddha’s enlightened activity is uninterrupted until cyclic existence is emptied, because the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* states: "Likewise, for as long as cyclic existence lasts, the activity is considered to be uninterrupted." The meaning of the single verse beginning with "The happiness of self" that explains that very resultant Truth Body is as follows: Having taken that precious bodhicitta of exchanging self and other as the foundation of the path, and having practiced the conduct of the heirs of the Victorious One—the six perfections, the four means of gathering, and so forth—one traverses the ten stages and five paths in sequence. Having realized the four bodies, one remains without moving from the Truth Body for as long as space endures. While remaining thus, with great compassion free from conceptualization, one abandons the mind that desires one's own happiness, and with a mind devoid of hope for reward or ripening, one is constantly, day and night, diligent and never misses the time to accomplish the benefit and needs of other sentient beings. Just as a mother serves her only child with a mind that never tires in any way, you should know that one should remain without ever tiring in the benefit of sentient beings, with a sincere heart, just like the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who act solely for the benefit of others. This is how the Truth Body is shown: it indicates that having realized the four bodies, one remains without tiring until cyclic existence is emptied, and performs the benefit of beings through twenty-seven activities. When explaining this in the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*, it is said: "Subhūti, in whatever way a great bodhisattva, a great being, thus realizes the perfection of wisdom, and practices..." through to "...the twenty-ninth chapter on realization." Having thus finished explaining the four phenomena that signify the Truth Body, the conclusion of the section is: This is the commentary on the twenty-ninth chapter on realization and the eighth chapter from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, which Clarifies the Profound Reality of Dependent Origination, a Commentary on the Verses of the Precious Qualities Collection*.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation:
Beyond this point, there is no connection to the Ornament, and the master Haribhadra has refuted the system of connection that existed previously. As for our own tradition, in explaining it according to the master’s intent, since it is necessary for the eight realizations mentioned above to be generated within one’s own continuum, one must proceed by engaging in the three activities of hearing, contemplating, and meditating upon the Mother, the Perfection of Wisdom. Therefore, one should diligently seek out a qualified spiritual friend of the Great Vehicle, and by accomplishing whatever is instructed according to their command, one should please them. Then, with intense and uninterrupted perseverance that does not turn back, one should practice with great patience, without the mind becoming weary due to the hardships of the path. The manner of engaging in this, as indicated by the four verses beginning with "Whatever bodhisattva," is as follows:

Whatever bodhisattva, through great love and compassion, wishes to accomplish the task of never abandoning the work of benefiting sentient beings while remaining for an immeasurable length of time in this state of cyclic existence for the sake of others; and who is a yogi striving for the maturation of sentient beings while remaining in cyclic existence for the sake of others, as well as striving for the purification of one’s own Buddha-field and the perfection of one’s prayers—such a person will not have even a particle of a mind that arises in weariness toward the long duration of time or the hardships of the path. Thus, possessing the perfection of the three types of perseverance, such as working for the benefit of sentient beings, they will be without negligence in accomplishing the benefit of others.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: What is the fault in generating a mind of weariness? To explain that: a bodhisattva who is unskilled in means, who counts the eons by the tens of millions and thinks, "I shall strive for this long and then attain the awakening of a buddha," if they conceive of such a long duration and, through the perception of suffering in giving away their head, limbs, and so forth, strive for awakening, then at the time they are practicing the genuine Dharma to attain unexcelled awakening for the sake of others, by the power of that very perception, they will suffer for a long time and find it difficult to perform. Because of that distorted perception, they will decline from the perfection of diligence and become lazy, characterized by listlessness, self-deprecation, and the like.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one asks, "Then how should one not generate a mind of weariness?" it is because bodhisattvas who are skilled do not look at the long duration or the difficulty of the task, but rather need to generate courage like the noble Sadāprarudita. From the moment they first generate the mind for supreme awakening until they finally attain the state of a buddha—the unsurpassed, perfectly complete, great awakening—they should mentally conceive of all that time as being as easy to pass as a single day and night, and generate a perception of joy and delight. It is reasonable that a bodhisattva skilled in means, having dispelled the darkness of laziness through the clear light of wisdom that realizes all phenomena as empty of true existence and like an illusion, should engage in diligence. Thinking, "Since I have experienced intense and uninterrupted suffering in this place of saṃsāra since beginningless time without feeling weariness or disgust, why should I not endure the suffering of hardship in practicing the excellent path of the supreme vehicle, through which I will now attain the great purpose, the state of a buddha?" they generate courage and become joyful. By the power of that, they suppress the entirety of the long duration and suffering, and their diligence will increase extensively.

What is the fault in generating a mind of weariness? To explain that: a bodhisattva who is unskilled in means, who counts the eons by the tens of millions and thinks, "I shall strive for this long and then attain the awakening of a buddha," if they conceive of such a long duration and, through the perception of suffering in giving away their head, limbs, and so forth, strive for awakening, then at the time they are practicing the genuine Dharma to attain unexcelled awakening for the sake of others, by the power of that very perception, they will suffer for a long time and find it difficult to perform. Because of that distorted perception, they will decline from the perfection of diligence and become lazy, characterized by listlessness, self-deprecation, and the like.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If someone were to say to them, "Demolish this king of mountains, Mount Meru, and after you have finished demolishing it, you will attain supreme enlightenment," and if, upon hearing that, one were to think, "How could I possibly demolish this Mount Meru, which is so vast, high, and firm?" and thereby generate a mind of difficulty and weariness, or even conceive of the measure of time such as eons, then at the moment one generates such a discouraged mind, that bodhisattva has become lazy, for the mind of joy has diminished. However, if a bodhisattva thinks, "If I can attain unexcelled enlightenment by exerting this much effort, what is difficult about this?" and, without grasping at the measure of time, generates the courage and joyful mind that is capable of reducing that Mount Meru to dust in a mere instant, then that bodhisattva, who is courageous and skilled in means, has engaged in the supreme diligence. By that, they will attain the supreme enlightenment of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who leads beings out of saṃsāra, without being delayed for a long time.

[3-310] translation already produced for this document:
If one asks, "Then how should one not generate a mind of weariness?" it is because bodhisattvas who are skilled do not look at the long duration or the difficulty of the task, but rather need to generate courage like the noble Sadāprarudita. From the moment they first generate the mind for supreme awakening until they finally attain the state of a buddha—the unsurpassed, perfectly complete, great awakening—they should mentally conceive of all that time as being as easy to pass as a single day and night, and generate a perception of joy and delight. It is reasonable that a bodhisattva skilled in means, having dispelled the darkness of laziness through the clear light of wisdom that realizes all phenomena as empty of true existence and like an illusion, should engage in diligence. Thinking, "Since I have experienced intense and uninterrupted suffering in this place of saṃsāra since beginningless time without feeling weariness or disgust, why should I not endure the suffering of hardship in practicing the excellent path of the supreme vehicle, through which I will now attain the great purpose, the state of a buddha?" they generate courage and become joyful. By the power of that, they suppress the entirety of the long duration and suffering, and their diligence will increase extensively.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Even when diligence is undertaken, it is of great importance that it be free from grasping. If, while in a state of mind that grasps at signs of "self" and "other"—thinking, "I shall perform the welfare of others by maturing sentient beings through marvelous, skillful conduct that is appropriate to each, such as teaching the profound and vast Dharma, and by establishing them on the stages and paths"—one strives to accomplish the welfare of others through body, speech, and mind, then because one abides in the perception of a personal self, one is considered lazy in relation to the non-conceptual diligence that transcends the world. Being bound by the grasping of signs, one has become a discordant factor to true diligence, and thus one will be far from omniscience, just as a place is far away in terms of distance.

If someone were to say to them, "Demolish this king of mountains, Mount Meru, and after you have finished demolishing it, you will attain supreme enlightenment," and if, upon hearing that, one were to think, "How could I possibly demolish this Mount Meru, which is so vast, high, and firm?" and thereby generate a mind of difficulty and weariness, or even conceive of the measure of time such as eons, then at the moment one generates such a discouraged mind, that bodhisattva has become lazy, for the mind of joy has diminished. However, if a bodhisattva thinks, "If I can attain unexcelled enlightenment by exerting this much effort, what is difficult about this?" and, without grasping at the measure of time, generates the courage and joyful mind that is capable of reducing that Mount Meru to dust in a mere instant, then that bodhisattva, who is courageous and skilled in means, has engaged in the supreme diligence. By that, they will attain the supreme enlightenment of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who leads beings out of saṃsāra, without being delayed for a long time.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: If one asks, "In what manner should diligence be undertaken?" the Victors, who act for the benefit of beings, have declared that the perfection of diligence for bodhisattvas who desire to attain the supreme state of abandonment and realization—which is the great enlightenment where all stains of the two obscurations are pacified and never degenerate—is to engage in the way of phenomena that are empty of true existence and like illusions, without falling into the two extremes of permanence and nihilism, having completely reversed the perception of grasping the three spheres of diligence as truly existent, and while the practitioner has no perception of their own body, mind, or others as sentient beings at the time of undertaking such diligence.

Even when diligence is undertaken, it is of great importance that it be free from grasping. If, while in a state of mind that grasps at signs of "self" and "other"—thinking, "I shall perform the welfare of others by maturing sentient beings through marvelous, skillful conduct that is appropriate to each, such as teaching the profound and vast Dharma, and by establishing them on the stages and paths"—one strives to accomplish the welfare of others through body, speech, and mind, then because one abides in the perception of a personal self, one is considered lazy in relation to the non-conceptual diligence that transcends the world. Being bound by the grasping of signs, one has become a discordant factor to true diligence, and thus one will be far from omniscience, just as a place is far away in terms of distance.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The manner in which one must train in the perfection of patience—which involves not minding hardships and suffering, just as the Victor’s heir Sadāprarudita relied upon the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom—is as follows: When working for the benefit of beings, if one happens to hear many harsh words of abuse, such as others disparaging or insulting oneself, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means will think, "This is the cause of my happiness," and will rejoice, as the practice of patience arises in dependence upon an object of patience, and through the power of that, great merit will increase. Not only that, but when one examines and investigates with correct reasoning—thinking, "Who is the speaker of these harsh words, who is the one hearing them, what is the cause such as anger, and for what purpose are they spoken?"—one finds nothing at all. By realizing that they are not established in ultimate reality but are like illusions arising dependently, one possesses the supreme perfection of patience; this is the mark of the wise or the learned, for they are supreme scholars who realize that there is nothing to be angry at in phenomena that are like dreams and illusions.

If one asks, "In what manner should diligence be undertaken?" the Victors, who act for the benefit of beings, have declared that the perfection of diligence for bodhisattvas who desire to attain the supreme state of abandonment and realization—which is the great enlightenment where all stains of the two obscurations are pacified and never degenerate—is to engage in the way of phenomena that are empty of true existence and like illusions, without falling into the two extremes of permanence and nihilism, having completely reversed the perception of grasping the three spheres of diligence as truly existent, and while the practitioner has no perception of their own body, mind, or others as sentient beings at the time of undertaking such diligence.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།

[3-314] translation already produced for this document:
The manner in which one must train in the perfection of patience—which involves not minding hardships and suffering, just as the Victor’s heir Sadāprarudita relied upon the noble Dharmodgata in order to seek the perfection of wisdom—is as follows: When working for the benefit of beings, if one happens to hear many harsh words of abuse, such as others disparaging or insulting oneself, a bodhisattva who is skilled in means will think, "This is the cause of my happiness," and will rejoice, as the practice of patience arises in dependence upon an object of patience, and through the power of that, great merit will increase. Not only that, but when one examines and investigates with correct reasoning—thinking, "Who is the speaker of these harsh words, who is the one hearing them, what is the cause such as anger, and for what purpose are they spoken?"—one finds nothing at all. By realizing that they are not established in ultimate reality but are like illusions arising dependently, one possesses the supreme perfection of patience; this is the mark of the wise or the learned, for they are supreme scholars who realize that there is nothing to be angry at in phenomena that are like dreams and illusions.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The ripening result of abiding in patience is that the body becomes completely pure, like refined gold, and one comes to possess the thirty-two excellent marks, such as the wheels on the palms and soles, as well as the eighty exemplary characteristics, such as the strength of the son of Sṛdmed (Vāsudeva) and copper-colored nails, and so on, which are limitless. The result of human effort for a person who has patience with a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma is that they will proclaim the profound emptiness, which is the most supreme of all teachings, to the sentient beings to be trained. The dominant result is that in this world, all beings without exception will pay homage to that bodhisattva who possesses patience. The result of separation is that, having separated from the ignorance of not knowing, one becomes skilled in the places of what to adopt and what to discard.

If one asks what the benefits of patience are in terms of its qualities, it is this: if a bodhisattva possesses the virtuous qualities of patience—namely, being unperturbed by those who cause harm and having a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma—then, even if one were to take a person and have them fill this trichiliocosm with various precious substances such as gold and silver, and offer them to the world-knowing Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as well as to the Śrāvaka Arhats and the Pratyekabuddhas, the mass of merit from such an offering would not be able to compete even with a fraction of the merit of one who possesses the supreme practice of the perfection of patience.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: In order to teach both the patience of accepting suffering and the patience of discerning the Dharma, it is said: If a sentient being takes sandalwood powder or paste and, with a mind of great respect, smears and applies it to the body of a bodhisattva, while another person, with a mind desiring to harm, scatters impure fire upon his head—towards both of these, the bodhisattva should generate a mind that is equal and balanced, free from attachment and aversion, through the power of meditating on the selflessness of phenomena and the power of having cultivated the bodhicitta of exchanging self and other. A bodhisattva who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality, having practiced patience in this way, and having dedicated that mind of patience toward the supreme, unsurpassable enlightenment for the sake of others, becomes a great hero who is brave in accomplishing enlightenment for the sake of others. By meditating on patience that benefits all sentient beings in the world, that bodhisattva will surpass all the patience practiced by śrāvakas, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and the many various beings of the realms of sentient beings, because he is seized by a superior method.

[3-316] translation already produced for this document:
The ripening result of abiding in patience is that the body becomes completely pure, like refined gold, and one comes to possess the thirty-two excellent marks, such as the wheels on the palms and soles, as well as the eighty exemplary characteristics, such as the strength of the son of Sṛdmed (Vāsudeva) and copper-colored nails, and so on, which are limitless. The result of human effort for a person who has patience with a mind of certainty regarding the Dharma is that they will proclaim the profound emptiness, which is the most supreme of all teachings, to the sentient beings to be trained. The dominant result is that in this world, all beings without exception will pay homage to that bodhisattva who possesses patience. The result of separation is that, having separated from the ignorance of not knowing, one becomes skilled in the places of what to adopt and what to discard.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The one who practices patience should also generate this thought: Sentient beings in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of the Lord of Death—the hungry ghosts—experience many types of suffering that are difficult to endure, such as heat, cold, hunger, and thirst. All of these arise due to attachment to the contaminated objects of desire, and they experience these harms helplessly; yet, even while experiencing them, they gain not the slightest benefit for themselves or others, and they experience them entirely in vain. Therefore, thinking, "Why should I not now endure the suffering of hardship for the sake of attaining the unsurpassable enlightenment that perfectly completes the two purposes of self and others?" one should resolve to do so. A bodhisattva who thinks, "I shall endure and accept all the harms and sufferings that exist in the world," such as being scorched by iron, struck by clubs, pierced by weapons such as swords, being killed by having one's life taken, being bound by iron chains, being struck by stones or fists, having one's head severed, or having one's ears, limbs, or nose cut off—in short, all the harms and sufferings that exist in the world—will constantly remain in the perfection of patience while weeping. Thus it is said. From the "Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, Clarifying the Reality of Dependent Arising," the profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā*: this is the commentary on the thirtieth chapter, the chapter on Sadāprarudita.

[3-317] translation already produced for this document:
In order to teach both the patience of accepting suffering and the patience of discerning the Dharma, it is said: If a sentient being takes sandalwood powder or paste and, with a mind of great respect, smears and applies it to the body of a bodhisattva, while another person, with a mind desiring to harm, scatters impure fire upon his head—towards both of these, the bodhisattva should generate a mind that is equal and balanced, free from attachment and aversion, through the power of meditating on the selflessness of phenomena and the power of having cultivated the bodhicitta of exchanging self and other. A bodhisattva who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality, having practiced patience in this way, and having dedicated that mind of patience toward the supreme, unsurpassable enlightenment for the sake of others, becomes a great hero who is brave in accomplishing enlightenment for the sake of others. By meditating on patience that benefits all sentient beings in the world, that bodhisattva will surpass all the patience practiced by śrāvakas, arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and the many various beings of the realms of sentient beings, because he is seized by a superior method.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: In this way, for a suitable student who has relied upon and pleased a holy spiritual friend in the proper manner, the spiritual friend will bestow extensive instructions on the profound and the vast. Because it is the foundation of all qualities, the instruction begins with the perfection of ethical discipline, followed by the perfection of generosity and so forth. The meaning of the eighteen verses beginning with "By ethical discipline..." is as follows: First, by identifying the nature of ethical discipline, its benefits are shown. Those who desire to attain the state of peaceful nirvāṇa through the ethical discipline of restraining misconduct and so forth will attain superior qualities of the path, for that ethical discipline is like a staircase for ascending to the mansion of liberation. In particular, the statement "the ethical discipline of a bodhisattva dwells in the sphere of the ten powers" refers to the ethical discipline of training in the footsteps of the Buddha, who possesses the ten powers; because it is untainted by the defilement of the lesser vehicle’s mindset and all faults and downfalls are abandoned, the ethical discipline is not impaired. This indicates the ethical discipline of restraining misconduct. As for the ethical discipline of restraint, it follows all virtuous dharmas such as the six perfections; because it protects against all opposing factors to be abandoned and practices their antidotes, the virtuous dharmas, it is also called the ethical discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas. Furthermore, because it protects for the sake of bringing benefit and happiness to all sentient beings, and because this is dedicated to great enlightenment, it is the ethical discipline of benefiting sentient beings. Having thus briefly indicated the nature of ethical discipline, the distinction between pure and impure bodhisattva ethical discipline—even if a bodhisattva who has attained the stage of noble dharmas appears to be enjoying the five objects of desire—must be established based on whether or not there is a mindset of self-interest. If one observes ethical discipline with a mind that desires to touch or attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha or a śrāvaka arhat, then in relation to the Mahāyāna path, that person is one who has broken their ethical discipline and is unskilled in means; likewise, their thoughts and actions are inferior, and they have fallen from the conduct of a child of the Conqueror, for they will fall into the inferior path. However, if one dedicates that very observance of ethical discipline to the benefit of others, for the sake of supreme, unsurpassable enlightenment that has pacified the two obscurations, then even if that bodhisattva remains engaged in and striving within the five objects of desire, they are abiding in the perfection of ethical discipline, for they have not fallen from the Mahāyāna path.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: That which, when practiced, causes the qualities of the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment—the goal to be attained by bodhisattvas—to arise, is taught to be the meaning of the ethical discipline of bodhisattvas who possess the qualities of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. The Guide has taught that any dharma stained by the defilement of focusing on the Lesser Vehicle, even if it performs the benefit and happiness of others, is an instance of a bodhisattva’s ethical discipline being broken, as such minds are completely diminished regarding the great enlightenment that is the fruit to be attained. If a bodhisattva, even while appearing to the world to be enjoying the five objects of desire to their heart’s content, takes refuge from the depths of their heart in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Sangha, and does not separate from the intention of omniscience, thinking, "I shall attain the rank of Buddhahood for the sake of other sentient beings," then that bodhisattva, skilled in means, should be known as one who abides in the perfection of the ethical discipline of the bodhisattva vow.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Other than that, if one practices the ten paths of virtuous action for a hundred thousand million eons, yet generates a desire to attain for oneself the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha Arhat, at that time a flaw arises in the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline, and the ethical discipline that is unique to the Great Vehicle is degenerated. This is because generating a mind that abandons the benefit of others and desires to attain the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha for one’s own benefit is a fault far graver than even the four defeats (pārājika) of a bhikṣu, as it results in a degeneration from the unsurpassed enlightenment.

That which, when practiced, causes the qualities of the unsurpassed, supreme enlightenment—the goal to be attained by bodhisattvas—to arise, is taught to be the meaning of the ethical discipline of bodhisattvas who possess the qualities of accomplishing the benefit and happiness of others. The Guide has taught that any dharma stained by the defilement of focusing on the Lesser Vehicle, even if it performs the benefit and happiness of others, is an instance of a bodhisattva’s ethical discipline being broken, as such minds are completely diminished regarding the great enlightenment that is the fruit to be attained. If a bodhisattva, even while appearing to the world to be enjoying the five objects of desire to their heart’s content, takes refuge from the depths of their heart in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the noble Sangha, and does not separate from the intention of omniscience, thinking, "I shall attain the rank of Buddhahood for the sake of other sentient beings," then that bodhisattva, skilled in means, should be known as one who abides in the perfection of the ethical discipline of the bodhisattva vow.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: One guards ethical discipline and completely dedicates that very thing to supreme enlightenment, while being free from any arrogance born of grasping at that discipline as true, and one does not praise oneself nor disparage others on the basis of one’s extensive learning, ethical discipline, and so forth. If one completely abandons the perception of an inherently established "I" and the perception of sentient beings, and so forth, then that bodhisattva, who possesses the special means and wisdom, is said to abide in the perfection of ethical discipline. Regarding such ethical discipline, it is also improper to generate grasping at truth or arrogance; for if those bodhisattvas who practice the path of the Victorious One, the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, think, "These sentient beings are endowed with ethical discipline, while these are unethical," and, having grasped at the objects of adoption and rejection as true, engage with perceptions of diversity, they are bound by the grasping at characteristics and are said to be extremely unethical. Because they have divided themselves and others into categories and committed the fault of disparaging others and so forth, the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline is degenerated, and that person does not possess perfectly pure ethical discipline.

[3-321] translation already produced for this document:
Other than that, if one practices the ten paths of virtuous action for a hundred thousand million eons, yet generates a desire to attain for oneself the level of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha Arhat, at that time a flaw arises in the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline, and the ethical discipline that is unique to the Great Vehicle is degenerated. This is because generating a mind that abandons the benefit of others and desires to attain the enlightenment of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha for one’s own benefit is a fault far graver than even the four defeats (pārājika) of a bhikṣu, as it results in a degeneration from the unsurpassed enlightenment.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, to demonstrate that one should not engage in grasping at truth, it is explained: for a person who has realized and familiarized themselves with the selflessness of the person—whereby they realize all phenomena to be empty of truth and like an illusion, and for whom there is no perception of an "I" or perception of others as sentient beings—how could there be any non-restraint, that is, unethical conduct? Because there is no cause to generate it. The Guide has stated that for a person who, through knowing that all phenomena are without inherent nature, has no conceit of grasping at the two—being endowed with restraint or being without restraint and unethical—this is the bodhisattva’s restraint of ethical discipline. To say that something is "not established by inherent nature" or "empty by inherent nature" means that it is empty from its own side; it means that, apart from being merely imputed by names and conceptual thought, it is not established from the side of the object or upon the object itself.

One guards ethical discipline and completely dedicates that very thing to supreme enlightenment, while being free from any arrogance born of grasping at that discipline as true, and one does not praise oneself nor disparage others on the basis of one’s extensive learning, ethical discipline, and so forth. If one completely abandons the perception of an inherently established "I" and the perception of sentient beings, and so forth, then that bodhisattva, who possesses the special means and wisdom, is said to abide in the perfection of ethical discipline. Regarding such ethical discipline, it is also improper to generate grasping at truth or arrogance; for if those bodhisattvas who practice the path of the Victorious One, the Dharma of the Great Vehicle, think, "These sentient beings are endowed with ethical discipline, while these are unethical," and, having grasped at the objects of adoption and rejection as true, engage with perceptions of diversity, they are bound by the grasping at characteristics and are said to be extremely unethical. Because they have divided themselves and others into categories and committed the fault of disparaging others and so forth, the bodhisattva’s ethical discipline is degenerated, and that person does not possess perfectly pure ethical discipline.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Therefore, those who wish to enter the path of the supreme vehicle should rely properly upon a learned spiritual friend in order to generate within their continuum the unerring view of the middle way, which is free from extremes; they should seek extensively to hear the profound scriptures of the middle way, and exert themselves in accumulating merit, purifying obscurations, and so forth, for this should be known as the supreme essence of instruction. To demonstrate that one who is endowed with ethical discipline is also capable of engaging in the perfection of generosity, it is explained: a person whose continuum is fully ripened and purified, and who, as just explained, is free from the perception of grasping at a self and the attachment that arises due to that, and who is endowed with perfectly pure ethical discipline, is one who lacks the view of superimposing signs upon all phenomena, whether they are pleasant and desirable or unpleasant and undesirable. Thus, they give away even their head, limbs, and so forth to others, and at that time, they have no mind of attachment or despondency. By abandoning themselves and holding others dear, they give away everything they possess or have to others, and at all times they have no attachment to them; for they know that phenomena such as the body and enjoyments are empty of inherent nature, selfless, and like an illusion, arising merely from the gathering of causes and conditions and lacking any essence. Having realized this, they give away even the flesh of their own body to others without even the slightest mind of despondency arising. If that is the case, it goes without saying that they are capable of giving away external objects such as wealth and possessions. If one were to be stingy regarding such enjoyments, that would have no basis in any way—that is, it would be non-existent and have no opportunity, because there is no basis for attachment and grasping. The disadvantages of stinginess, along with the benefits of the bodhisattva’s generosity, are taught as follows: for those fools who, despite there being no "I," self, or inherently established existence, perceive a self that is inherently established and grasp at objects such as the eyes as "mine," thereby becoming attached and clinging, how could there be a mind that gives away the body, enjoyments, and so forth without regret? Such a mind does not exist. Those who are stingy will be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts, and even if, by chance, they are reborn as humans due to the power of other karma, at that time they will become poor, lacking wealth and enjoyments.

དེ་ལྟ་བས་ན་བདེན་པར་མངོན་པར་ཞེན་པར་མི་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཤད་པ། ཆོས་ཀུན་བདེན་སྟོང་སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུར་རྟོགས་ཡུལ་གང་ལ་བདག་གི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་གཞན་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་འདུ་ཤེས་མེད་པའི་གང་ཟག་གི་བདག་མེད་རྟོགས་ཤིང་གོམས་པར་བྱས་པས་བདག་ཏུ་འཛིན་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་དང་དེའི་དབང་གིས་བྱུང་བའི་འདོད་ཆགས་དང་བྲལ་བ་དེ་ལ་ནི་སྡོམ་པ་མིན་པ་སྟེ་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་འཚལ་བ་ནི་ག་ལ་ཡོད། དེ་བསྐྱེད་པའི་རྒྱུ་མེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །གང་ཟག་གང་ལ་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་རང་བཞིན་མེད་པར་ཤེས་པའི་སྒོ་ནས་སྡོམ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་དང་སྡོམ་པ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ཚུལ་འཆལ་གཉིས་སུ་འཛིན་པའི་རློམ་སེམས་མེད་པ་འདི་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་ཚུལ་ཁྲིམས་ཀྱི་སྡོམ་པ་ཡིན་པར་རྣམ་པར་འདྲེན་པས་གསུངས་སོ། །རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་མ་གྲུབ་པའམ་རང་བཞིིན་གྱིས་སྟོང་ཞེས་པ་ནི་རང་ངོས་ནས་སྟོང་ཞེས་པ་ཡིན་པས། མིང་དང་རྟོག་པས་ཕར་བཏགས་ཙམ་མ་གཏོགས་ཡུལ་གྱི་སྟེང་ནས་སམ་ཡུལ་གྱི་ནས་མ་གྲུབ་པའི་དོན་ཡིན་ནོ། །
[3-323] translation already produced for this document:
Therefore, to demonstrate that one should not engage in grasping at truth, it is explained: for a person who has realized and familiarized themselves with the selflessness of the person—whereby they realize all phenomena to be empty of truth and like an illusion, and for whom there is no perception of an "I" or perception of others as sentient beings—how could there be any non-restraint, that is, unethical conduct? Because there is no cause to generate it. The Guide has stated that for a person who, through knowing that all phenomena are without inherent nature, has no conceit of grasping at the two—being endowed with restraint or being without restraint and unethical—this is the bodhisattva’s restraint of ethical discipline. To say that something is "not established by inherent nature" or "empty by inherent nature" means that it is empty from its own side; it means that, apart from being merely imputed by names and conceptual thought, it is not established from the side of the object or upon the object itself.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: At the time when sentient beings are born into cyclic existence, bodhisattvas, knowing that these beings have become poor due to the power of being attached to enjoyments and being stingy, see the faults of stinginess and the benefits of generosity. They then aspire to give away their entire body and all their enjoyments, and through their practice, they constantly and unreservedly give away all their possessions in actuality. Even if they were to fill the four continents with the seven types of precious substances and adorn them beautifully, they would have no attachment or clinging to them; knowing them to be essence-less, like a glob of spittle, they give them to others in order to take hold of the essence of attaining complete enlightenment for the sake of others, and they themselves become extremely joyful. They do not experience such joy from acquiring or obtaining those continents themselves, because they see them as impermanent and devoid of essence.

At the time when sentient beings are born into cyclic existence, bodhisattvas, knowing that these beings have become poor due to the power of being attached to enjoyments and being stingy, see the faults of stinginess and the benefits of generosity. They then aspire to give away their entire body and all their enjoyments, and through their practice, they constantly and unreservedly give away all their possessions in actuality. Even if they were to fill the four continents with the seven types of precious substances and adorn them beautifully, they would have no attachment or clinging to them; knowing them to be essence-less, like a glob of spittle, they give them to others in order to take hold of the essence of attaining complete enlightenment for the sake of others, and they themselves become extremely joyful. They do not experience such joy from acquiring or obtaining those continents themselves, because they see them as impermanent and devoid of essence.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Those bodhisattvas, having given a gift, do not abide in a manner of being fixated upon the signs of any of the three spheres—the giver, the object to be given, and the recipient. Furthermore, those bodhisattvas never have the expectation that, "By this gift, I shall attain vast benefit and happiness as a ripening result." Instead, they give the gift along with its fruit to all sentient beings. A bodhisattva who gives in the manner just explained is skilled in giving because they possess special means and wisdom, and they give everything they possess, including the ripening fruit. Through such a method, even when giving a small object, they attain immeasurable, manifold ripening results. To teach that one should train in dedication, preceded by the overcoming of stinginess and by rejoicing, it is said: If one were to take all the sentient beings existing in the three realms—the desire, form, and formless realms—without leaving a single one out, and if those beings were to give vast gifts for an infinite eon to the special fields—the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones who know the world, the śrāvaka arhats, and the pratyekabuddhas—and if they were to seek the fruit of that giving as the enlightenment of a śrāvaka, then if a bodhisattva, a child of the Victorious One, who is skilled in the meaning of the nature of reality, skilled in means, and possesses great compassion, were to rejoice in that merit—the object of the merit of those beings just described—in a single moment of mind, and dedicate it for the sake of all sentient beings to attain the supreme, excellent rank of Buddhahood, then because they possess such a special dedication, they would surpass all the roots of virtue of all beings. For example, just as a single precious vaiḍūrya, the king of jewels, can surpass a vast heap of many gathered minor jewels, in that same way, a bodhisattva, by means of a special dedication preceded by rejoicing, surpasses all the vast heaps of merit from the giving of all sentient beings in the world.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Having explained the perfections of ethical discipline and generosity in detail, the instruction for the remaining perfections is as follows: If a bodhisattva gives generosity extensively to sentient beings, does not claim the fruit of that generosity as their own, and engages in the conduct of a conqueror’s child—giving in such a way that they have no attachment or miserliness toward the substances or objects to be given—then, from that, the vast roots of virtue, the accumulations of merit and wisdom, will be perfected, and they will possess the great power to abandon obscurations, increasing more and more. This is like the moon’s disk, which, lacking obscuring factors such as clouds, possesses extremely clear rays of light during the waxing phase. Thus, having instructed on the remaining perfections as well, it should be understood that this is the activity of a spiritual friend, just like the noble Dharmodgata. This is the commentary on the thirty-first chapter, that of Dharmodgata, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: The manner in which holy beings of fortunate capacity, having obtained profound and vast instructions and guidance from a spiritual friend, generate the supreme mind of awakening and practice the conduct of a conqueror’s child, thereby gradually traversing the ten levels, such as the first level, "the Joyous," and increasing their practice of the ten perfections, such as generosity, is explained in the five verses beginning with "By the bodhisattva’s generosity." The meaning is as follows: In this way, a bodhisattva abiding on the first level, "the Joyous," primarily obtains and practices the perfection of generosity among the ten perfections. Because they make it their primary practice, through a generosity that is unattached to anything, they sever the continuum of miserliness, which is the cause for being born in the realms of hungry ghosts, and they likewise eradicate from the root all afflictions, such as attachment and aversion, which cause poverty in terms of resources. Because they pacify all the afflictions of sentient beings—such as ignorance, attachment, and aversion—through the giving of Dharma and material things, even while the bodhisattva is engaging in the conduct of a conqueror’s child, they obtain a vast, inexhaustible, and ever-increasing abundance of desired resources that are in harmony with the Dharma throughout all their lifetimes. First, by gathering a retinue through the giving of material things, and then by placing those sentient beings who are suffering in this cycle of existence onto the Great Vehicle through the giving of Dharma, they bring them to full maturity.

[3-328] translation already produced for this document:
Having explained the perfections of ethical discipline and generosity in detail, the instruction for the remaining perfections is as follows: If a bodhisattva gives generosity extensively to sentient beings, does not claim the fruit of that generosity as their own, and engages in the conduct of a conqueror’s child—giving in such a way that they have no attachment or miserliness toward the substances or objects to be given—then, from that, the vast roots of virtue, the accumulations of merit and wisdom, will be perfected, and they will possess the great power to abandon obscurations, increasing more and more. This is like the moon’s disk, which, lacking obscuring factors such as clouds, possesses extremely clear rays of light during the waxing phase. Thus, having instructed on the remaining perfections as well, it should be understood that this is the activity of a spiritual friend, just like the noble Dharmodgata. This is the commentary on the thirty-first chapter, that of Dharmodgata, from the *Jeweled Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate*, a profound commentary on the *Ratnaguṇasañcayagāthā* that clarifies the reality of dependent origination.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Similarly, bodhisattvas abiding on the second ground, the Stainless, through their supreme practice of morality—which abandons even the appearance of impropriety in dreams—are not born into the many and varied types of animal existences. Furthermore, they abandon all eight states of non-freedom, such as being born in border regions, and through that morality, they always obtain an excellent basis endowed with the eight freedoms and ten riches. Bodhisattvas abiding on the third ground, the Luminous, through a patience that is free from all malice, obtain a supreme, beautiful, and marvelous physical form, as well as the Buddha’s body adorned with the major and minor marks; thus, they become golden in color, well-proportioned, and so attractive and pleasing that they are worthy of being gazed upon by all beings. Bodhisattvas abiding on the fourth ground, the Radiant, through a diligence free from all laziness, ensure that the qualities of the white virtues do not diminish, and by the power of all the qualities of the grounds and paths increasing and expanding ever higher, they obtain the treasury of the infinite wisdom of all-knowing awareness and the entire collection of the qualities of the abandonment and realization of the Victorious Ones.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Bodhisattvas abiding on the sixth ground, the Manifest, through the wisdom of analytical discrimination, fully realize the nature of all phenomena as emptiness just as it is, and by abandoning the root of existence—the grasping at true reality—they transcend the three realms completely and purely. Like the Buddha, the Blessed One, the King of Dharma and the best of men, they turn the precious wheel of the profound and vast Dharma without interruption, and in order to bring all suffering to a permanent end, they reveal the supreme light of the holy Dharma to all beings.

[3-330] translation already produced for this document:
Similarly, bodhisattvas abiding on the second ground, the Stainless, through their supreme practice of morality—which abandons even the appearance of impropriety in dreams—are not born into the many and varied types of animal existences. Furthermore, they abandon all eight states of non-freedom, such as being born in border regions, and through that morality, they always obtain an excellent basis endowed with the eight freedoms and ten riches. Bodhisattvas abiding on the third ground, the Luminous, through a patience that is free from all malice, obtain a supreme, beautiful, and marvelous physical form, as well as the Buddha’s body adorned with the major and minor marks; thus, they become golden in color, well-proportioned, and so attractive and pleasing that they are worthy of being gazed upon by all beings. Bodhisattvas abiding on the fourth ground, the Radiant, through a diligence free from all laziness, ensure that the qualities of the white virtues do not diminish, and by the power of all the qualities of the grounds and paths increasing and expanding ever higher, they obtain the treasury of the infinite wisdom of all-knowing awareness and the entire collection of the qualities of the abandonment and realization of the Victorious Ones.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Although Buddhaśrī makes a chapter division here by connecting it with the gradual path, according to the master’s own tradition, bodhisattvas abiding on the seventh ground, the Far-Going, through the power of having attained the perfection of skillful means to a superior degree, bring these Mahāyāna teachings, such as the ten perfections, to full completion and thereby work for the benefit of sentient beings. Bodhisattvas abiding on the eighth ground, the Immovable, through the power of having attained the perfection of aspiration to a superior degree, take hold of the complete purity of a buddhafield—which includes the pure environment of the buddhafield where they will attain buddhahood, and the pure beings within it, who are filled entirely with bodhisattvas—and so forth.

ས་ལྔ་བ་སྦྱངས་དཀའ་བ་ལ་གནས་པས་ནི་རྣམ་གཡེང་ཐམས་ཅད་དང་བྲལ་བའི་བསམ་གཏན་གྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གྱིས་ནི་འདོད་པའི་ཡོན་ཏན་ལ་སྙིང་པོ་མེད་ཅིང་ཉེས་དམིག་ཆེ་བས་དམ་པས་པའི་སྨད་པའི་འོས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་དག་འདོར་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་། སྔོན་གནས་རྗེས་དྲན་དང་གཞན་སེམས་ཤེས་པ་དང་ཟག་པ་ཟད་པའི་མངོན་ཤེས་ཏེ་རིག་པ་གསུམ་དང་། ལྷའི་མིག་དང་རྣ་བ་དང་རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་གྱི་མངོན་པར་ཤེས་པ་ལ་སོགས་པ་དང་དཔའ་བར་འགྲོ་བའི་ཏིང་ངེ་འཛིན་སོགས་མངོན་པར་སྒྲུབ་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །
[3-331] translation already produced for this document:
Bodhisattvas abiding on the fifth ground, the Difficult to Train, through the perfection of meditative concentration—which is free from all distraction—abandon those sensory qualities of desire that are devoid of essence, carry great faults, and are worthy of being disparaged by the noble ones. They also fully accomplish the three knowledges—the recollection of former abodes, the knowledge of others' minds, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of contaminants—as well as the superknowledges of the divine eye, the divine ear, and miraculous powers, and the meditative absorptions that lead to heroism.

ས་དྲུག་པ་མངོན་དུ་གྱུར་པ་ལ་གནས་པས་ནི་ཆོས་རབ་ཏུ་རྣམ་པར་འབྱེད་པའི་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱིས་ནི་ཆོས་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱི་རང་བཞིན་སྟོང་པ་ཉིད་ཇི་ལྟ་བ་བཞིན་དུ་ཡོངས་སུ་ཤེས་ནས་སྲིད་པའི་རྩ་བ་བདེན་འཛིན་སྤངས་ཏེ། ཁམས་གསུམ་མ་ལུས་པ་ལས་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པར་འདའ་བར་འགྱུར། མི་ཡི་ཁྱུ་མཆོག་ཆོས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་སངས་རྒྱས་བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་ལྟར་ཟབ་པ་དང་རྒྱ་ཆེ་བའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་འཁོར་ལོ་རིན་ཆེན་རྒྱུན་མི་ཆད་པར་བསྐོར་བར་བྱས་ནས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་མཐའ་དག་གཏན་དུ་ཟད་པར་བྱ་བའི་ཕྱིར་དུ་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་ལ་དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྣང་བ་མཆོག་ཀྱང་སྟོན་པར་འགྱུར་རོ། །
[3-332] translation already produced for this document:
Bodhisattvas abiding on the sixth ground, the Manifest, through the wisdom of analytical discrimination, fully realize the nature of all phenomena as emptiness just as it is, and by abandoning the root of existence—the grasping at true reality—they transcend the three realms completely and purely. Like the Buddha, the Blessed One, the King of Dharma and the best of men, they turn the precious wheel of the profound and vast Dharma without interruption, and in order to bring all suffering to a permanent end, they reveal the supreme light of the holy Dharma to all beings.

heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Bodhisattvas abiding on the ninth ground, the Excellent Intelligence, through the power of having attained the perfection of strength to a superior degree, teach the Dharma by way of the four perfect knowledges, thereby establishing an inconceivable number of sentient beings on the level of a buddha and upholding the buddha-continuum. Likewise, a bodhisattva abiding on the tenth ground, the Cloud of Dharma, through having attained the perfection of primordial wisdom to a superior degree, upholds the dharma-continuum by way of teaching the Dharma without interruption. Likewise, through marvelous activities that accord with the buddhas, they create limitless noble bodhisattvas, thereby upholding the sangha-continuum. Furthermore, abiding on the eleventh ground, the All-Illuminating, which is the level of a buddha, they abandon without remainder the two obscurations along with their latent tendencies, and uphold all the excellent qualities of benefit and happiness that pertain to both cyclic existence and peace. Until the end of space, they remain, performing the benefit of beings through spontaneously present activities that require no effort, just like a wish-granting tree or a wish-fulfilling jewel.

བུདྡྷ་ཤྲཱིས་མཐར་གྱིས་སྦྱོར་བ་དང་སྦྱར་ནས་འདི་ནས་ལེའུའི་མཚམས་བྱས་ཀྱང་། རང་ལུགས་སློབ་དཔོན་གྱི་བཞེད་པ་ལྟར། ས་བདུན་པ་རིང་དུ་སོང་བ་ལ་གནས་པས་ནི་ཐབས་ཀྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ལྷག་པར་ཐོབ་པའི་མཐུས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་བཅུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཆོས་འདི་རྣམས་ཡོངས་སུ་རྫོགས་པར་བྱས་ནས་སེམས་ཅན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་དོ། །ས་བརྒྱད་པ་མི་གཡོ་བ་ལ་གནས་པའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་དེ་ཡིས་སྨོན་ལམ་གྱི་ཕར་ཕྱིན་ལྷག་པར་ཐོབ་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་རང་གང་དུ་འཚང་རྒྱ་འགྱུར་གྱིས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་སྣོད་ཀྱི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པའི་ཞིང་ཁམས་དང་བཅུད་ཀྱི་སེམས་ཅན་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་བྱང་སེམས་ཤ་སྟག་གིས་གང་བ་སོགས་སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་ཞིང་ཡོངས་སུ་དག་པ་འཛིན་པར་བྱེད་དོ། །

Although Buddhaśrī makes a chapter division here by connecting it with the gradual path, according to the master’s own tradition, bodhisattvas abiding on the seventh ground, the Far-Going, through the power of having attained the perfection of skillful means to a superior degree, bring these Mahāyāna teachings, such as the ten perfections, to full completion and thereby work for the benefit of sentient beings. heading: འབྲས་བུ་ཆོས་སྐུ།
translation: Having thus explained the Mother in detail, the entrustment is made so that it may endure for a long time. The meaning of the single verse, "Healing the illnesses of beings," and so forth, is as follows: The supreme King of Physicians who eradicates and heals the illnesses of the body and mind of beings, as well as the illnesses of suffering and the defilements, is the Buddha, the Bhagavan. This is because the Tathāgatas heal all the roots of illness and suffering—namely, the ignorance of grasping at a self and the two obscurations along with their latent tendencies that arise in dependence upon it—by means of this very nectar of the Dharma, the perfection of wisdom. From the lips of such a King of Physicians, the Sage, the Buddha, the Bhagavan, this has been spoken: a teaching that takes as its primary subject the perfection of wisdom, which realizes the emptiness that is to be expressed, while implicitly teaching the entire sequence of clear realizations, such as the eight topics and seventy points. In short, it is the path of supreme enlightenment, containing all the profound and vast teachings of the Great Vehicle. The name of that meaningful sutra is "The Precious Collection of Qualities," because it contains and gathers without remainder all the precious qualities of the Great Vehicle path, including the generation of bodhicitta and its fruits. The purpose of speaking it in this way is to explain it so that all limitless sentient beings may attain such a path of the supreme vehicle. Having generated the mind for the sake of beings since before beginningless eons, having perfected the practices of completion, ripening, and purification, and having attained supreme, perfect enlightenment, the Buddha, out of great love and compassion, taught this extremely profound and difficult-to-hear Dharma to fortunate disciples, thereby establishing all limitless, space-filling beings in the state of supreme enlightenment. The way in which this summarizes the meaning of the entrustment is as follows: In the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā* (Eight Thousand Verse Perfection of Wisdom) regarding this, it is said, "From this perfection of wisdom, the omniscience of all-knowing wisdom will be perfected," and so forth. Because this is the source of the precious qualities arising from the entire path and fruit of the Great Vehicle, and because wherever this perfection of wisdom is practiced, the Buddha resides, the Dharma is taught, and the Sangha gathers, it is necessary to protect it diligently above all other sutras; thus, it was entrusted three times. Therefore, even in this sutra, the power of the words, "so that all sentient beings may attain this path," is explained in the *Dk'a 'grel* (Difficult Commentary) of the Master as follows: "The word 'attain' refers to the entrustment made to the noble Ānanda and others." Thus, it is the Buddha’s primary intention that all sentient beings attain this path, and it is for the reason that its long-term, undiminished endurance depends upon this that it was entrusted with such diligence. This is the commentary on the thirty-second chapter, the chapter on entrustment, from the *Precious Lamp that Fulfills the Wishes of the Fortunate, a Profound Commentary on the Verse Summary of the Precious Qualities Collection that Clarifies the Reality of Dependent Arising*.

Bodhisattvas abiding on the ninth ground, the Excellent Intelligence, through the power of having attained the perfection of strength to a superior degree, teach the Dharma by way of the four perfect knowledges, thereby establishing an inconceivable number of sentient beings on the level of a buddha and upholding the buddha-continuum. Likewise, a bodhisattva abiding on the tenth ground, the Cloud of Dharma, through having attained the perfection of primordial wisdom to a superior degree, upholds the dharma-continuum by way of teaching the Dharma without interruption. Likewise, through marvelous activities that accord with the buddhas, they create limitless noble bodhisattvas, thereby upholding the sangha-continuum. Furthermore, abiding on the eleventh ground, the All-Illuminating, which is the level of a buddha, they abandon without remainder the two obscurations along with their latent tendencies, and uphold all the excellent qualities of benefit and happiness that pertain to both cyclic existence and peace. Until the end of space, they remain, performing the benefit of beings through spontaneously present activities that require no effort, just like a wish-granting tree or a wish-fulfilling jewel.

translation: THE TRANSLATOR’S COLOPHON. Second, regarding the manner in which it was translated into the Tibetan language: there are two differing versions that appear. One states: "Translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian preceptor Vidyākarasiṃha—meaning 'Lion of the Source of Diligence'—and the chief editor-translator, the sole eye of the world, the monk dPal brtsegs." The other states: "This Noble Verse Summary, extracted from the Perfection of Wisdom in Eighteen Thousand Lines, was corrected and finalized by the Zhwa lu translator, the monk Dharmapālabhadra—meaning 'Good Protector of the Dharma'—by consulting both the Indian manuscript edited by the master Siṃhabhadra and accurate Tibetan manuscripts." Thus, one should know that this sūtra is non-different from the Teacher himself, and that as long as it remains in this world through hearing, contemplation, and meditation, the Teacher is known to be teaching the Dharma. Furthermore, by understanding the methods of instruction—such as the fact that by performing even a little service to this precious sūtra in this degenerate age, the Teacher himself is pleased and delighted—and by realizing that those who desire their own well-being should repay the Teacher’s kindness and that there are immeasurable temporary and ultimate benefits, such as the spontaneous accomplishment of the welfare of self and others, one should follow the excellent path of the scholars and adepts of the past. Then, just as the meaning of the precious Perfection of Wisdom sūtras was explained by the Regent Maitreyanātha and the two great charioteers, Nāgārjuna and Asaṅga, one should expand upon it within one’s own continuum and that of others.

heading: ལོ་ཙཱ་བའི་འགྱུར་བྱང་།
translation: Here it is said: The profound and vast, whose depths and limits are unfathomable, is a river of well-spoken teachings, swirling with a myriad of hidden meanings, filled with tens of millions of precious gems. It possesses a deep vortex of emptiness that strikes fear into the hearts of the unwise and childish, while being adorned with a swirling chain of waves of diverse logic. It is a place where tens of millions of the Conqueror’s children, the lords of the nāgas, who are beautifully adorned with the crests of the jewels of scripture and realization, enter with joy and delight. It is the great ocean of the Mother of the Conquerors, the wish-fulfilling jewel that brings forth the omniscient Conqueror, whose two purposes are spontaneously accomplished. It is the essence of the nectar churned from the ocean of milk of the eighty-four thousand holy teachings. It produces the supreme fruit of the four noble ones’ aspirations, which causes the lotus grove of the excellent path of the three vehicles to flourish. It is beautiful, like a thousand suns that dispel all the darkness of ignorance of beings in the three realms. There is nothing comparable to this light of the day-maker, the Dharma system of the perfection of wisdom. This is the single path traversed by the Conquerors of the three times. It is the medicinal nectar of the Dharma that heals the illnesses of the three times. It is the wish-granting tree that produces all excellence. It is the supreme captain leading to the island of the jewels of the three bodies. It is the eye of the world that illuminates the excellent path of the profound. It is the white light that dispels the suffering of existence and peace. It is the king of wish-fulfilling powers that fulfills the hopes of the fortunate. It is also the supreme teacher that points out the path to enlightenment. For countless eons, it is difficult to hear even a syllable of the Sage’s well-spoken nectar; to have a marvelous feast of enjoying it as one wishes—ah, such a fortune is extremely good! Who in this present age is capable of fully fathoming the profound and vast ocean of the Mother’s meaning? I, with my feeble intellect, have taken as my own share only a single drop, clinging to the tip of a kusha grass blade. Although the Jamyang Speech-Sun, Father and Sons, have clarified all the difficult points of the sutras and tantras, I wonder if leaving this word-commentary aside is my own allotted portion. Even if it does not benefit the foolish and ignorant who are self-conceited, whose eyes of wisdom are impaired and who are intoxicated by the poisonous water of sensory objects, it is the music of well-spoken teachings that delights the wise, and it is an offering of merit that pleases all the Conquerors and their children. However, although the intended meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom is as vast as space, the intellect of a childish person like me is as thin as a hair. Since it cannot be illustrated by the light of tens of millions of suns, may the darkness of the two obscurations of the intellect of all beings be destroyed, and may the light of omniscient wisdom flourish. May the wish-granting tree of the Conqueror’s teachings, which is the foundation of benefit and happiness, have its branches of explanation and practice fully flourish, and may the endless, wish-granting rain of excellence fulfill the hopes of beings throughout space. May the mandala of faultless view, meditation, and conduct expand, and may the thousand-rayed light of well-spoken teachings that dispels the darkness of wrong views, the treasury of the light of the marvelous Geden tradition, always shine in the sky of the Sage’s teachings. May the lotus grove of the Dharma community of explanation and practice be beautified by the countless hosts of the white lotus of scholars and adepts, who exhale the fine fragrance of supreme, pure discipline and whose hundred petals of learned intellect have blossomed. May I also, in all my lives, be cared for by the Jamyang Lama and become the foremost of his children. May I reach the pinnacle of the sevenfold wisdom, the non-forgetting retention, and supreme confidence. May I follow in the footsteps of Nāgārjuna and Asaṅga in upholding the entirety of the Conqueror’s holy Dharma, and may I learn to engage in the vast conduct just like Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. May all embodied beings who see, hear, remember, or touch me never be separated from the captain and protector, the spiritual friend. May they enter the great ship of study, reflection, and meditation, and travel to the island of the jewels of the three bodies. As long as the sun and moon cast their sidelong glances upon the beautiful face of the captivating goddess of the sky, may this lamp of the jewel of well-spoken teachings also fulfill the hopes of the fortunate disciples. From the crest of the great clouds of the blessings of the ocean of the Three Jewels and the Conquerors, may the truth-spoken Brahma-voice pour down like a rain of flowers of excellence, like the roaring of summer thunder. May the wish-granting tree of the two accumulations flourish on the ground of Samantabhadra, and may the golden ears of grain of definitive excellence arise. May the fruit of the two purposes, for oneself and others, be spontaneously accomplished and pervade with the glory of auspiciousness. This commentary on the Precious Qualities Collection, titled "The Wish-Fulfilling Lamp that Clarifies the Reality of the Profound Dependent Origination," was requested with great earnestness by the former throne-holder of the great Dharma community of explanation and practice, Sershul Monastery Thekchen Dargyeling, the ornament of the teachings in Do-Kham, the holder of the treasury of the jewels of marvelous scripture and realization, the supreme tulku Gompa Lobsang Gelek Tendhar. It was also requested by the great chant-master Lobsang Rabgye, whose intellect and analytical faculties are vast in the fields of sutra, tantra, and logic. As requested again and again by many holy beings, such as my own attendant, the former abbot Jamyang Rinchen, who is learned and speaks on logic, and the supreme tulku of Thotsa, Lobsang Tendzin Trinle, who illuminates the Geden teachings, it was composed by the monk who holds the Yellow Hat tradition, Khenrab Jamyang Lobsang Trinle, who has realized the intended meaning of the entire sutra and tantra and has perfected the profound samadhi of the two stages. It was composed at Gaden Shedrub Thubten Phelgye Ling, a place where the summer thunder of the Dharma of explanation and practice roars. The scribe was the former abbot Ganchung Jamyang Rinchen. Om Svasti. May the Omniscient One, the Lord of Dharma and gift-giver of the Second Conqueror, whose lotus-feet rest upon the crest-jewels of hundreds of thousands of the world’s scholars and adepts, protect these beings. The Mother, the Perfection of Wisdom, is the wish-granting tree that produces the fruit of the three bodies, with a firm root of the difficult-to-perform conduct of the Conqueror’s children, and with branches of completion, ripening, and purification fully perfected. The Lord of the hundred million fields, while filling all fields with the light of that method, proclaimed it to the assembly of the three types of beings, along with the miracles of samadhi, psychic power, and the manifestation of Dharma. The meaning of the Perfection of Wisdom Collection, which is the great ocean that gathers all the rivers of its profound meaning, was clarified by the holy Lama in accordance with the tradition of the great charioteers of the Land of Snows; this is marvelous. Because this opens a hundred doors to benefit and happiness, the supreme tulku Lobsang Tendzin Trinle caused this word-commentary on the Precious Qualities Collection to be printed by providing the resources. May the ocean of milk of the pure merit exerted here, accompanied by the tens of millions of waves of stainless good deeds accumulated in the three times, merge with the wish-fulfilling ocean of the three bodies. May the precious teachings of the Sage in general, and in particular the stainless tradition of the King of Dharma of the three realms, Tsongkhapa, flourish and spread for a long time, and may the activities of the beings who uphold them expand. May I and all embodied beings connected to me be born in the supreme field of the vidyādharas, Shambhala, and having perfected the journey of the five stages of the profound path, may we manifest the state of the first Buddha. This prayer of dedication was written by the ignorant Jamyang Rinchen, as requested by the supreme tulku Lobsang Trinle, the master of the ocean of supreme qualities, when he was printing this commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom Collection. Sarvada Kalyāṇa Bhavantu. Om Svasti. From the Dharma school of Gaden Shedrub Phelgye Ling, this rain of nectar, the unceasing stream of Dharma, has fallen so that the swarm of bees of the fortunate ones may enjoy the essence of the honey of explanation and practice in the lotus grove of the Conqueror’s teachings. May the merit of printing this commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom Collection, composed by the supreme tulku Khenrab Jamyang Lobsang Trinle in 1985, be a cause for the Yellow Hat tradition, the very heart of the Conqueror’s teachings, to flourish in all directions and remain for a long time.
